card.headline: Bright, alert goat chewing its cud
card.look: A healthy goat holds its head up, has bright clear eyes, and moves easily with the herd. It eats eagerly, chews its cud when resting, and passes firm, separate pellet droppings.
card.action: Check every goat once a day, at the same time and in the same order, so you notice early when one goat starts to behave differently.

aka: Dalili za mbuzi mwenye afya (signs of a healthy goat)
detail.summary: This page describes what a normal, healthy goat looks, sounds and behaves like, so you have a clear picture to compare against. Goats are good at hiding illness until it is well advanced. A farmer who knows the normal signs well will spot trouble days earlier. Early action usually means cheaper treatment, fewer deaths and less lost milk and growth.
detail.cause: Good health in goats rests on a few simple foundations. First is good feeding. Goats are browsers, which means they prefer leaves, shrubs and tree pods over short grass. They need enough roughage (fibre) to keep the rumen working. The rumen is the large first stomach on the left side of the belly, where microbes break down fibre. When the rumen is full and working well, the goat chews its cud, burps gas quietly and passes firm pellets. Second is clean water, always available, because goats drink more in hot weather and when milking. Third is minerals and vitamins, especially salt, calcium and phosphorus, which keep bones, teeth, milk production and the immune system strong. Fourth is low parasite pressure. Worms in the gut, especially the blood-sucking barber's pole worm, and external parasites such as ticks, mites and lice drain blood and energy. Fifth is dry, clean, well-ventilated housing that protects goats from rain, cold wind and damp floors, which goats handle poorly. Finally, vaccination and calm handling reduce disease and stress. When these foundations are in place, the goat's immune system can fight off most everyday germs, and the animal grows, breeds and milks well.
spread: Health problems often start after a sudden change in feed, such as moving goats onto lush green pasture after the rains, or giving large amounts of grain or kitchen waste at once.
Worm burdens rise quickly during and just after the long and short rains, when worm larvae survive well on wet grass.
Damp, muddy or crowded housing with poor airflow encourages pneumonia, foot rot and skin problems.
New goats bought from markets, or goats returning from shows, can bring in diseases such as PPR (goat plague), CCPP (contagious caprine pleuropneumonia), orf or mange.
Shared water points, dipping areas and communal grazing in pastoral areas allow ticks, worms and infections to pass between herds.
Stress from transport, weaning, kidding, extreme heat or poor handling weakens the immune system and lets hidden infections take hold.
Dirty water troughs, mouldy feed and poor feeder hygiene can upset digestion and spread germs.
detail.atRisk: Every goat benefits from a daily check, but some need closer attention. Young kids in their first weeks are the most fragile: they chill easily, can quickly become dehydrated, and depend on getting colostrum (first milk) soon after birth. Weaned kids and young stock are very vulnerable to worms. Pregnant does in late pregnancy and does in the weeks after kidding have high nutritional needs. High-yielding dairy breeds such as Toggenburg, Saanen and Alpine, and their crosses, are often more sensitive to poor feeding and parasites than hardy local breeds such as the Small East African goat and the Galla. Zero-grazed goats depend completely on the farmer for good feed, minerals and clean housing. Free-range and pastoral goats face more ticks, worms and contact with other herds. Risk rises during the rains, when worms and pneumonia increase, and during long dry seasons, when feed quality drops and goats lose condition.

early: Behaviour: the goat is alert, curious and aware of its surroundings, with head and ears up. It moves freely with the group and comes to feed eagerly.
Rectal temperature is between about 38.5 and 40 °C. It is often slightly higher in the hot afternoon, after exercise, and in young kids.
Cud chewing: when resting, the goat lies on its chest, chewing its cud steadily. It regularly brings up a ball of feed, chews it, swallows, and repeats.
Rumen: the left side behind the ribs feels full but not tight. If you press a fist there gently, you can feel the rumen contract, roughly once or twice per minute.
Droppings are firm, dark, separate pellets. Urine is clear to pale yellow, and males pass it without straining.
Eyes are bright and clear, with no heavy tears or crust. The inner lower eyelid is pink to red, which means a good blood level (FAMACHA score 1 or 2).
The coat is smooth and fairly glossy and lies flat, with no bald patches, scabs or crawling lice. The skin is supple.
Breathing at rest is quiet and regular, roughly 15–30 breaths per minute in adults. It is faster in heat and in kids. The nose may be slightly moist but has no thick discharge.
The goat walks evenly on all four feet, with no limping. Hooves are trimmed, and there is no smell or heat between the claws.
Body condition: ribs and spine can be felt under a light layer of flesh, but are not sharp or hidden under fat. The udder of a milking doe is soft, even and warm, not hot or hard.
advanced: The goat stands apart from the herd, or stays lying down when others get up. It looks dull, with head and ears down.
It refuses feed or water, or eats much less than usual. It is often the last to come to the feeder, or does not come at all.
There is no cud chewing for several hours. The left side looks swollen and tight like a drum, or looks hollow and sunken.
Rectal temperature is above about 40 °C, which suggests fever. A temperature below about 38 °C is also serious, especially in kids or does that have just kidded.
Droppings change: soft clumps or watery diarrhoea, a dirty back end, very dry small pellets, or no droppings at all. A male straining to urinate is an emergency.
The inner eyelids are pale pink or white (FAMACHA 3, 4 or 5). Look also for swelling under the jaw, called 'bottle jaw'. Both suggest anaemia, often from barber's pole worm.
Coughing, fast or laboured breathing, or thick nasal discharge. Sores around the mouth and nose, or crusty lips.
Teeth grinding, groaning, or kicking at the belly are signs of pain. Limping, a rough dull coat, weight loss, or a hot, hard or lumpy udder.

lookalikes.name: Normal rest and digestion
lookalikes.howToTell: A healthy goat lying quietly in the shade after feeding is usually chewing cud with bright eyes, and gets up readily when you approach. A sick goat lies with its head down, does not chew cud, and is slow or unwilling to rise.

lookalikes.name: A full rumen mistaken for bloat
lookalikes.howToTell: After a good feed, the left side is round but soft, and the goat chews cud and burps comfortably. In bloat, the left upper flank is tight like a drum, and the goat is uneasy, may kick at its belly, breathe with effort, or stop eating. Bloat needs urgent vet help.

lookalikes.name: Raised temperature from heat or exercise
lookalikes.howToTell: On a hot afternoon, or after goats have been chased or walked far, temperature can rise near or slightly above 40 °C in a goat that is otherwise eating and alert. Recheck after the goat has rested in the shade for some time, ideally in the cool of the morning. A true fever stays high and usually comes with dullness or poor appetite.

lookalikes.name: Heat (oestrus) behaviour and softer droppings on lush feed
lookalikes.howToTell: A doe on heat may bleat loudly, wag her tail, mount others, eat a little less, and have a clear discharge, but she stays bright and recovers within a day or two. Goats on fresh green pasture after the rains may pass softer, clumped droppings without being ill. Watery diarrhoea, a dirty tail, or dullness is not normal.

detail.diagnosis: A home health check takes only a few minutes per goat. Do it calmly and in good light. Start by watching the herd from a distance before you disturb them: who is eating, who is chewing cud, and who is standing apart? Then check each goat you are unsure about. To take the temperature, use a digital thermometer, ideally one kept only for animals. Restrain the goat gently against a wall or with a helper holding the head. Lubricate the tip with a little petroleum jelly or cooking oil. Lift the tail and slide the tip a few centimetres into the rectum, angled slightly towards the side wall. Hold it until it beeps, then read and record it. Clean the thermometer with soap and water and disinfect it afterwards. Next, check the eyes using the FAMACHA method. Gently pull down the lower eyelid and look at the colour of the inner lining. Red to pink is good. Pale pink is borderline. White means serious anaemia and needs action the same day. FAMACHA only detects anaemia from blood-sucking worms, mainly barber's pole worm. It does not show other worms such as tapeworms, or coccidia. Ideally, learn it from a trained extension officer or vet. Press your fist into the hollow on the left flank to feel rumen movement. Run your hands along the spine and ribs to judge body condition. Part the hair to look for lice, ticks and skin scabs. Look at the droppings and the back end, check the mouth and nose for sores, and check the udder of milking does. Watch the goat walk. If you find something abnormal, write down the temperature, what you saw, when it started, recent feed changes, and treatments or vaccines given. A vet or animal health assistant will use this record together with an examination, dung tests for worm eggs, blood tests, or a post-mortem on any goat that dies, to find the cause.
firstSteps: Make the daily check a habit: at morning feeding, watch every goat eat, look at droppings and bedding, and note any goat that is slow, dull or not eating.
If one goat looks unwell, move it to a clean, dry, shaded pen away from the others. It should still be able to see other goats, to reduce stress.
Take and write down its temperature, FAMACHA eye colour, appetite, droppings and breathing, with the date and time. Recheck later the same day.
Give clean, fresh water and good-quality hay or browse. Do not force-feed, and do not drench liquids into a goat that is weak or struggling to swallow.
Protect yourself: wear gloves if there is diarrhoea, discharge, abortion or mouth sores. Wash your hands well afterwards, and keep children away from sick animals.
Stop buying, selling or moving goats from the herd until you know what the problem is, especially if more than one goat is sick.
Do not give antibiotics, dewormers or other drugs by guesswork. Call your vet, animal health assistant or the County Veterinary Office and describe what you have recorded.
detail.vetTreatment: For healthy goats, the vet's role is mainly prevention. Routine vet or animal health assistant care usually includes a herd health plan: a vaccination schedule suited to your area, which in Kenya often covers PPR, CCPP, enterotoxaemia (pulpy kidney) and others your vet recommends. It also includes a parasite control plan, which uses FAMACHA scoring and dung egg counts to deworm only the goats that need it, rather than dosing everyone by routine. This slows resistance to dewormers. The vet may also advise on tick and mange control, trim hooves or show you how, check teeth and udders, castrate and disbud kids, assess body condition before breeding, and check pregnancies. Ask for advice on minerals and ration balancing for dairy goats. When a goat does fall sick, the vet examines it and may prescribe treatments such as antibiotics for bacterial infections, dewormers, anti-inflammatories or fluids. Only a vet should prescribe these. Always follow the milk and meat withdrawal periods on the label or given by your vet. Withdrawal is the time after treatment when milk must be thrown away and the animal must not be slaughtered for food. Using antibiotics only when a vet confirms they are needed, and finishing the full course, helps prevent antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines. Antibiotics do not cure viral diseases such as PPR or orf.
prevention: Vaccinate according to a plan agreed with your vet or County Veterinary Office. Join government vaccination campaigns for diseases such as PPR, and keep a record card for each goat.

Control worms strategically. Check FAMACHA scores regularly, especially during and after the rains. Deworm only the goats that need it, rotate grazing, and avoid grazing wet, short grass early in the morning, when larvae are most active.

Feed plenty of roughage and browse, and make feed changes gradually over about a week or more. Provide clean water at all times, and offer a goat mineral lick or mineral supplement suited to your area.
Keep housing dry, clean and airy. Raised slatted floors are ideal in wet areas. Remove wet bedding and droppings often, and avoid overcrowding.
Quarantine new or returning goats in a separate pen for at least two to three weeks. Watch them daily and get vet advice on vaccinating and deworming them before they mix with the herd.
Make sure newborn kids suckle colostrum within the first hours of life. Keep kid pens warm, dry and free of draughts.
Trim hooves regularly, control ticks and lice, and check the udders of milking does daily. Keep milking hygienic.
Keep simple records of births, weights, treatments, vaccinations and deaths. Records help you and your vet spot patterns early.
detail.impact: Healthy goats grow faster, reach breeding and market weight sooner, kid more regularly, and give more milk, all of which directly raise farm income. In Kenya, goats are often a household's savings account and a source of cash for school fees. Losing even one doe or a group of kids is a real setback. Most losses on smallholder and pastoral farms come from problems that are easier and cheaper to prevent or treat early, such as worms, pneumonia, kid deaths and poor nutrition. A daily check costs nothing but time. It can catch a problem while one goat is affected rather than ten, reduce spending on drugs and vet visits, protect milk sales by avoiding long withdrawal periods, and keep goats in good condition for better prices at market.
detail.humanHealth: Healthy-looking goats can still carry some infections that affect people, such as brucellosis, Q fever and orf (sore mouth). Brucellosis and Q fever are often linked to abortions and birth fluids, and orf causes scabs on the lips that can spread to hands. Wear gloves when handling birth fluids, aborted kids or mouth sores, and wash your hands with soap after handling goats. Boil or pasteurise milk before drinking it, and observe withdrawal periods after any drug treatment so residues do not reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: A goat that is well fed, dewormed only when needed, vaccinated and kept in clean, dry housing has a good chance of staying productive for many years. The biggest factor in recovery when illness strikes is how early it is noticed. Goats often show only small changes at first, such as eating a little less or skipping cud chewing, before they collapse. Farmers who check daily and act on small changes usually lose far fewer animals. Even with good care, some losses can happen, so regular vet contact and good records remain important.

faqs.q: Do I need to take every goat's temperature every day?
faqs.a: No. Watching each goat eat, chew cud, move and pass droppings every day is usually enough. Take the temperature of any goat that looks dull, is off feed, has diarrhoea or is breathing fast. It also helps to take a few normal readings from healthy goats in your herd, so you know what is normal on your farm in the morning and afternoon.

faqs.q: How long should a goat spend chewing cud?
faqs.a: Healthy goats spend several hours each day chewing cud, mostly when resting and at night. You should see most resting goats chewing at any time. If a goat has not chewed cud for several hours and is also eating poorly, check its temperature and rumen, and call your vet.

faqs.q: Can I rely only on FAMACHA to decide when to deworm?
faqs.a: FAMACHA is a very useful tool for barber's pole worm, the most dangerous worm in many Kenyan goat herds, and it helps you avoid dosing goats that do not need it. However, it does not detect other worms, coccidia or tapeworms. Combine it with body condition, a check of the back end for diarrhoea, and occasional dung egg counts from your vet or a lab.

faqs.q: My goat's droppings became soft after the rains started. Is it sick?
faqs.a: Fresh green grass after the rains often makes droppings softer and clumped, and this can be normal if the goat stays bright and eats well. Watery diarrhoea, a dirty tail, weight loss, pale eyelids or dullness are not normal. They may point to worms, coccidia or other infection and need a vet's advice.

faqs.q: Why does my healthy goat grind its teeth sometimes?
faqs.a: Occasional light grinding while chewing cud can be normal. Loud, repeated grinding, especially with a hunched back, groaning, kicking at the belly or poor appetite, is a sign of pain. It needs a full check and a call to your vet.

products.role: A dicalcium phosphate supplement that can help supply calcium and phosphorus for bones, teeth and milk production. This is especially useful where browse or pasture is poor, or for growing kids and milking does. Use it as part of a balanced ration agreed with your vet or nutrition adviser.

Can help cover vitamins A, D3 and E during long dry seasons, when green feed is scarce, and around breeding and late pregnancy. These vitamins support eyesight, bones, fertility and immunity. Use it on vet or agrovet advice as a supplement to good feeding, not a replacement for it.

card.headline: Crusty discharge from eyes and nose
card.look: Several goats suddenly have a high fever, stop eating, and develop runny eyes and nose that turn thick, yellow and crusty, often with mouth sores, very bad breath and watery diarrhoea. Many animals in the herd fall sick within days, and some begin to die.
card.action: Isolate the sick goats immediately, stop all movement of animals on and off your farm, and report to your County Veterinary Officer today, because PPR is a notifiable disease.

aka: Kitimoto cha mbuzi (local descriptive name, varies by area)
detail.summary: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) is a highly contagious viral disease of goats and sheep. Goats are usually hit harder than sheep. It causes fever, crusty eye and nose discharge, mouth sores, diarrhoea and pneumonia, and in a herd that has never met the virus, most animals can fall sick and a large share may die. It is one of the most damaging diseases of goats in Kenya and East Africa, it is notifiable by law, and it can be prevented with a cheap, effective vaccine.
detail.cause: PPR is caused by a virus called small ruminant morbillivirus (often just called PPR virus). It belongs to the same family as the virus that once caused rinderpest in cattle and measles in people. When a goat breathes in the virus, it first multiplies in the throat and nearby lymph nodes (the glands that help fight infection), then spreads through the blood to the whole body. The virus attacks the lining of the mouth, nose, eyes, lungs and gut, killing cells and causing the sores, discharges and diarrhoea farmers see. It also badly weakens the immune system, the body's defence system. This is why many goats with PPR also get bacterial pneumonia (lung infection) on top of the virus, and that pneumonia is often what kills them. Death usually comes from a mix of dehydration from diarrhoea, starvation because the mouth is too painful to eat, and severe lung damage. Goats that survive develop strong immunity and are not usually infected again.
spread: Close contact between sick and healthy goats is the main route: the virus is in tears, nasal discharge, saliva, coughs and droppings of sick animals.
Sick goats cough and sneeze out tiny droplets that healthy goats breathe in when they are housed or herded tightly together, for example in night bomas or crowded pens.
Buying new goats, especially from livestock markets, is one of the commonest ways PPR enters a farm, because infected animals may look healthy for a few days before signs show.
Communal grazing areas, shared watering points, and dips bring goats from many herds together and let the virus pass between flocks.
Moving animals during drought, trade, dowry or festive seasons carries the virus to new villages and counties.

Contaminated feed troughs, water containers, bedding, and people's hands, clothes and boots can carry the virus for a short time, although the virus does not survive long outside the animal, especially in sunlight and heat.
Goats returning unsold from a market can bring the infection home to the rest of the herd.
detail.atRisk: All goats that have not been vaccinated and have never had PPR are at risk, whatever the breed. Young goats, roughly from about three months old (when the protection they got from their mother's milk fades) up to about a year, often suffer the most severe disease and highest deaths. Local breeds such as Small East African goats and Galla goats, and improved or dairy breeds such as Toggenburg, Saanen and their crosses, can all be badly affected. Sheep can also catch PPR, though they are usually less severely affected than goats. Pastoral systems in northern and eastern Kenya, where herds move, mix at water points and are sold at large markets, have historically been hard hit, but zero-grazing and smallholder farms are also at risk when they buy new stock. Outbreaks often follow times of animal movement and stress, such as drought, the start of the rains when herds mix again, and busy market periods before holidays. Poor nutrition, worm burdens and cold, wet weather make the disease worse.

early: A sudden high fever: the goat feels hot to the touch, especially under the tail and inside the ears, and a thermometer reading is well above normal.
The goat becomes dull, stands apart with its head down, and stops eating or eats very little.
The hair coat looks rough and stands up.
A clear, watery discharge runs from the eyes and nose, and the goat may sneeze.
The gums and inside of the eyelids look redder than normal.
Several goats in the herd fall sick within a few days of each other, rather than one animal alone.
advanced: The eye and nose discharge becomes thick, yellow and pus-like, then dries into crusts that block the nostrils and glue the eyelids shut.
Greyish or whitish sores and patches of dead tissue appear on the gums, lips, tongue and inside the cheeks; the mouth is painful, the goat drools and struggles to eat.
The breath smells very foul and rotten.
Severe watery diarrhoea starts, often very smelly and sometimes with blood or mucus, soiling the tail and back legs.
Coughing, fast and laboured breathing, and noisy breathing show that pneumonia has developed.
The goat becomes dehydrated, with sunken eyes and skin that stays tented when pinched, and loses weight quickly.
Pregnant does may abort.
Body temperature may drop below normal shortly before death; badly affected goats often die within about a week to ten days of first showing signs.

lookalikes.name: Contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP)
lookalikes.howToTell: CCPP is a bacterial lung disease that causes fever, coughing and painful, laboured breathing, and can also kill many goats. However, it does not usually cause mouth sores, thick crusty eye discharge or severe diarrhoea. In PPR, the mouth sores, foul breath and diarrhoea alongside breathing problems are the key clues. CCPP is also notifiable, so report both to the vet.

lookalikes.name: Orf (contagious ecthyma, sore mouth)
lookalikes.howToTell: Orf causes thick, warty scabs on the lips, nose and sometimes udder, mainly in kids. The goats are usually otherwise bright, without high fever, diarrhoea or pneumonia, and deaths are few unless kids cannot suckle. PPR sores are inside the mouth, the goats are very sick with fever, and many die.

lookalikes.name: Pasteurellosis (shipping fever pneumonia)
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial pneumonia often follows stress such as transport, and causes fever, nasal discharge and coughing. It does not usually cause mouth sores and severe diarrhoea, and spreads less dramatically through the herd. It is also a common secondary infection in PPR, so a vet may need lab tests to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Foot-and-mouth disease and bluetongue
lookalikes.howToTell: Foot-and-mouth disease causes blisters in the mouth and on the feet, so goats limp, and cattle on the same farm are usually affected too. Bluetongue, spread by biting midges, is mostly seen in sheep and causes a swollen face, lips and tongue and lameness. Neither typically causes the crusty eye and nose discharge with severe diarrhoea that marks PPR. Both are notifiable, so the vet should confirm.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will strongly suspect PPR from the pattern on the farm: many goats falling sick quickly with fever, eye and nose discharge, mouth sores, diarrhoea and pneumonia, with deaths, especially after new animals arrived or goats visited a market. Because PPR is notifiable, confirmation by a laboratory is important. The vet or County Veterinary Officer will take swabs from the eyes, nose and mouth of goats in the early fever stage, blood samples, and, if a goat has died, tissue samples such as lung, lymph nodes, spleen and intestine. These are tested at a government laboratory, such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional veterinary investigation laboratory, using tests such as PCR (which detects the virus's genetic material) and ELISA (which detects virus or antibodies). Rapid pen-side test kits are sometimes used in the field to give a quick result. At post-mortem, the vet may see mouth erosions, pneumonia, and dark red stripes in the lining of the large intestine, often called 'zebra stripes'. To help, the farmer should record how many goats are sick and how many have died, when signs started, ages of affected animals, recent purchases, market visits or contact with other herds, and vaccination history. Do not open dead goats yourself; keep carcasses covered and away from dogs and other animals until the vet advises.
firstSteps: Separate all sick goats from healthy ones straight away, in a pen or area downwind and away from the rest of the herd, and keep sheep away from them too.
Stop all movement: do not sell, buy, lend, take goats to market or to communal grazing and water points until the vet tells you it is safe.
Call your County Veterinary Officer, local veterinary office or a private vet today, because PPR must be reported by law and fast reporting helps protect neighbouring herds.
Give sick goats clean, fresh water at all times in a container they can reach easily, as dehydration from diarrhoea kills quickly.
Offer soft, tasty feed such as fresh green leaves, soft grass or soaked feed, since mouth sores make chewing painful.
Keep sick goats in a dry, clean, shaded and draught-free shelter, protected from rain and cold at night, with clean bedding.

Gently wipe crusts from the eyes and nostrils with a clean cloth dipped in clean, lukewarm water so the goat can see and breathe more easily, using a separate cloth per goat and washing your hands afterwards.
Use separate boots, clothes and equipment for the sick pen, wash hands well, and do not visit other farms until the outbreak is over.
Write down each sick and dead animal, the date signs started, and any recent purchases or market visits, so the vet can trace the source quickly.
Do not slaughter, sell or move sick or dead goats, and do not give any drugs unless a vet prescribes them.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the PPR virus, and antibiotics do not cure the virus itself. Treatment is supportive, meaning it helps the goat's body survive while its immune system fights off the infection. A vet may prescribe antibiotics, such as oxytetracycline or other drug classes they judge suitable, to control the secondary bacterial pneumonia and gut infections that often kill goats with PPR. They may also use anti-inflammatory drugs to reduce fever and pain, fluids for dehydration, and gentle care for mouth and eye sores. All treatment must be prescribed by a vet, who will decide which animals to treat, which drugs to use and for how long. Antibiotics should only be used when a vet advises, and the full course must be followed, because misuse of antibiotics leads to antimicrobial resistance, where drugs stop working for animals and people. Any drug used will have a milk and meat withdrawal period, a set time during which milk must be thrown away and the goat must not be slaughtered for food; ask the vet and follow it strictly. Because PPR is notifiable, the government veterinary service will also take control measures. These can include putting the farm or area under quarantine (no animals in or out), restricting movement and closing local markets, vaccinating healthy goats and sheep in the surrounding area (ring vaccination), and tracing where infected animals came from. Vaccinating goats that are already sick will not save them, so the focus is protecting the healthy ones. Even with good care, some goats will die, especially young ones and those with severe pneumonia.
prevention: Vaccinate all goats and sheep against PPR. A single dose of the live PPR vaccine, produced in Kenya by KEVEVAPI and available through veterinary services and agrovets, gives long-lasting, usually lifelong protection; ask your vet about the right schedule for your herd.

Vaccinate kids born after the main herd vaccination once their mother's protection fades, usually from around three to four months of age, as your vet advises, and join government vaccination campaigns when they come to your area.
Keep any new goats or sheep in a separate pen for at least two to three weeks before mixing them with your herd, and watch them closely for fever, discharge or diarrhoea.
Buy animals from known, healthy farms with a vaccination history where possible, rather than from unknown market sources, and ask for movement permits.
Keep goats that come back unsold from the market separate for a period before they rejoin the herd.
Limit contact with other herds at communal grazing, water points and dips during outbreaks in your area, and listen to announcements from your County Veterinary Officer.
Keep goats strong with good nutrition, clean water, regular deworming and tick control, as well-fed, parasite-free goats cope better with any disease.
Provide dry, well-ventilated housing that is not overcrowded, and clean pens, troughs and water containers regularly.

Report any suspected PPR quickly, as early reporting allows ring vaccination and movement control that protect your neighbours and your own future herd. Kenya is part of the global effort to eradicate PPR by 2030, and every vaccinated herd helps.
detail.impact: PPR can wipe out a large part of a goat herd within weeks, especially among young stock, which means the loss of future breeding does, milk, meat and income. For many Kenyan families, particularly pastoralists and women smallholders, goats are savings for school fees, medical bills and emergencies, so an outbreak can push a household into hardship. Goats that survive lose a lot of weight and take weeks to recover condition, which lowers their sale price. Pregnant does may abort, so the next kid crop is lost. Dairy goat farmers lose milk sales during illness and during drug withdrawal periods. Quarantine and market closures mean farmers cannot sell animals even when they need cash, and whole areas can lose trade. Treating secondary infections costs money, while vaccination is cheap by comparison, which makes prevention by far the better investment.
detail.outlook: The outlook for goats with PPR is often poor, especially in herds that have never been vaccinated and among young goats, where many of the sick may die. Survival is better in older goats, well-fed animals, and those that receive early supportive care and vet-prescribed treatment for secondary pneumonia. Goats with severe diarrhoea, heavy pneumonia, or a temperature that drops below normal are less likely to survive. Goats that recover usually have lifelong immunity to PPR, though they may stay weak and thin for several weeks and need good feeding to regain condition. The outlook for the herd as a whole improves greatly when the outbreak is reported quickly, sick animals are isolated, movement is stopped and healthy animals are vaccinated.

faqs.q: Can PPR infect people, and can we eat the meat or drink the milk?
faqs.a: PPR is not known to infect people. However, you should never slaughter or sell sick or dead goats during an outbreak. Moving carcasses and meat breaks quarantine rules and can spread the virus to other goats through blood, discharges and contaminated hands and tools. Sick goats may also be carrying other diseases or drug residues. Follow your vet's advice on disposing of dead animals, usually by deep burial or burning.

faqs.q: If I vaccinate my goats, how long are they protected?
faqs.a: The PPR vaccine used in Kenya is a live vaccine that gives strong, long-lasting protection, usually for life, after a single dose. Kids born later still need to be vaccinated once the protection from their mother's milk fades, usually from around three to four months old. Your vet or County Veterinary Officer will advise on the best timing and whether any repeat vaccination is needed in your area.

faqs.q: Can I vaccinate my goats now that some are already sick?
faqs.a: The vaccine will not cure goats that are already sick, and it takes some days to build protection in healthy goats. In an outbreak, the government veterinary service decides how and where to vaccinate, often by vaccinating healthy herds in a ring around the infected area. Call the vet first rather than vaccinating on your own, so the response is coordinated and the vaccine is handled and used correctly.

faqs.q: Why must I report PPR, and what will happen if I do?
faqs.a: Kenyan law requires anyone who suspects a notifiable disease like PPR to report it to the County Veterinary Officer or the Directorate of Veterinary Services. Reporting allows the vets to confirm the disease, vaccinate nearby herds and stop it spreading across the county. The vet may place your farm or area under quarantine, which means no goats or sheep can move in or out, and local markets may close for a time. This can be hard, but it protects your neighbours and helps end the outbreak sooner. Ask your County Veterinary Officer whether any support is available, as this varies and is not guaranteed.

faqs.q: Can my sheep and cattle catch PPR from my goats?
faqs.a: Sheep can catch PPR and should be vaccinated along with goats, though they are usually less severely affected. Cattle and camels can sometimes become infected without showing much illness, but they are not considered important in spreading the disease. Keep sheep away from sick goats and include them in your vaccination plan.

faqs.q: Can a goat that recovered from PPR get it again or spread it?
faqs.a: Goats that recover from PPR usually develop lifelong immunity and are not expected to get sick with it again. They can still shed virus for a short time after recovery, so keep them separated until your vet says the outbreak is over. Recovered goats are not considered long-term carriers, but follow the quarantine rules before selling or moving any animal.

ppr.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a dull, thin brown East African goat standing with its head lowered in a rural Kenyan homestead pen, with thick yellowish crusted discharge around its nostrils and matted, crusty eyelids, soft natural daylight.
ppr.seoDescription: PPR (goat plague) in goats: spot fever, crusty eye and nose discharge, mouth sores and diarrhoea, act fast, report to the vet and prevent with vaccination.

card.headline: Goats gasping with neck stretched out
card.look: Several goats have a high fever, cough painfully and breathe fast and hard with the neck stretched forward, the mouth often open, and froth at the nose or mouth. They stop eating, stand apart and may grunt with each breath.
card.action: Keep the whole herd at home, separate the sick goats, and call your County Veterinary Officer today because CCPP is a notifiable disease that must be reported.

aka: Homa ya mapafu ya mbuzi (Swahili, descriptive: goat lung fever)
detail.summary: Contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP) is a severe and highly contagious lung disease of goats caused by a mycoplasma, a very small type of bacterium. It spreads quickly through the air between goats kept close together and causes high fever, painful coughing and breathing trouble. In a herd that has never met the disease, most goats can fall sick and many can die within days or weeks. It is a notifiable disease in Kenya and one of the most costly goat diseases in pastoral and smallholder areas of East Africa.
detail.cause: CCPP is caused by Mycoplasma capricolum subspecies capripneumoniae, often shortened to Mccp. Mycoplasmas are tiny bacteria that have no cell wall, so some common antibiotics such as penicillin do not work on them. When a goat breathes in droplets from an infected goat, the organism settles in the lungs. It causes strong inflammation of the lung tissue (pneumonia) and of the pleura, the thin skin that lines the chest and covers the lungs (pleurisy). The chest fills with straw-coloured fluid and yellow, sticky clots called fibrin, and the lung becomes hard and stuck to the chest wall. Often one side of the chest is worse than the other. Because the lung cannot expand properly, the goat struggles to get enough air, which is why it stretches its neck, opens its mouth and breathes hard. The damage stays mostly in the chest; unlike some other goat diseases it does not usually cause diarrhoea, mouth sores or swollen joints. Goats that survive may keep damaged, scarred lungs, and some may carry the organism and pass it to others. The disease affects goats; sheep are rarely if ever affected in the field, and some wild relatives of goats can be affected.
spread: The main route is breathing in droplets coughed or breathed out by sick goats, so close contact is the biggest risk.
Crowding goats together at night in bomas, small sheds or during transport lets the organism pass very quickly from goat to goat.
Bringing in new goats from markets, other herds or areas with the disease is the most common way it enters a clean herd.
Recovered goats that look healthy may still carry the infection and can start a new outbreak when mixed with other goats.
Livestock markets, watering points, dips and shared grazing where many herds mix help the disease jump between herds.
Stress from cold, wet weather, long treks, drought migration, poor feeding and transport makes outbreaks more likely and more severe.
The organism does not survive long outside the goat, so spread through the environment, feed or equipment is much less important than live goat contact.
Once inside a goat it usually takes around one to two weeks before signs show, though this can vary, so a goat bought last week may look healthy and still be incubating the disease.
detail.atRisk: Goats of all ages and breeds can be affected, including Galla, Small East African, Toggenburg, Saanen and crossbred dairy goats. Herds that have never been exposed or vaccinated suffer the worst losses, and kids and pregnant does are especially vulnerable; pregnant does may abort. The disease is well established in pastoral areas of northern and eastern Kenya such as Turkana, Marsabit, Wajir, Mandera, Garissa, Isiolo and Samburu, and in rangelands of Kajiado and Narok, but it can reach any county through goat trade. Outbreaks often follow the cold, wet weather of the long and short rains, and periods of drought when herds trek long distances and mix at water points. Large herds kept tightly in night bomas, goats moved through markets, and zero-grazing units that buy in goats without quarantine are all at higher risk.

early: A high fever, often above 41°C, measured with a thermometer in the rectum; the goat feels hot to the touch, especially at the ears and inside the thighs.
The goat goes off feed, stops chewing the cud, looks dull and stands apart from the herd.
Fast breathing, with the flanks moving more than usual even at rest.
A cough that starts soft and becomes frequent and painful, often heard most at night or when goats are moved.
Milk yield drops sharply in dairy does.
Several goats in the herd showing similar signs within a few days, which is a key clue that this is a contagious disease.
advanced: Very laboured breathing with the neck stretched forward, the head held low and the mouth open.
Grunting or groaning with each breath, showing chest pain.
Frothy saliva hanging from the mouth and a frothy or thick discharge from the nose.
Standing with front legs spread apart and refusing to lie down, or lying down and being unable to rise.
Pain when the chest is pressed, and the goat may resist being handled.
Pregnant does aborting during the outbreak.
Rapid weakness and death, sometimes within a few days of the first signs, with many deaths across the herd.

lookalikes.name: Pneumonic pasteurellosis (shipping fever, caused by Mannheimia and Pasteurella bacteria)
lookalikes.howToTell: Pasteurellosis usually affects a smaller number of goats, often after a stress such as transport or a cold night, and sheep in the same herd may also get sick. CCPP tends to sweep through most of the goat herd, spares sheep, and causes heavy chest fluid at post-mortem. Only a vet and laboratory can tell them apart with certainty.

lookalikes.name: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR, goat plague)
lookalikes.howToTell: PPR also causes fever and pneumonia, but goats usually have sores in the mouth, a bad smell from the mouth, sticky discharge from the eyes and nose, and watery diarrhoea. CCPP stays in the chest with no mouth sores or diarrhoea. PPR also affects sheep. Both are notifiable, so report either.

lookalikes.name: Lungworm (verminous pneumonia)
lookalikes.howToTell: Lungworm causes a slow, long-lasting cough, usually without high fever, and goats stay fairly alert and keep eating. Signs build over weeks, not days, and deaths are few. CCPP is sudden, with high fever and many goats very ill at once.

lookalikes.name: Mycoplasma mycoides infection (MAKePS: mastitis, arthritis, keratitis, pneumonia, septicaemia)
lookalikes.howToTell: This related mycoplasma can cause pneumonia, but it often also brings swollen painful joints, cloudy eyes and mastitis in does. CCPP is mostly limited to the lungs and chest. Laboratory tests are needed to separate them.

detail.diagnosis: The vet will look at the history of the outbreak, how many goats are sick, how fast it spread, and whether new goats were brought in. They will take temperatures, listen to the chest and look for pain and breathing trouble. A post-mortem on a goat that has just died is very useful: CCPP typically shows a lot of straw-coloured fluid in the chest, yellow fibrin clots, lungs stuck to the chest wall and hard, granular lung tissue, often worse on one side. Because the mycoplasma is difficult to grow, the vet will send samples of lung tissue and chest fluid to a laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional veterinary laboratory for confirmation by PCR (a test that detects the organism's genetic material) or culture. Blood samples from sick and recovered goats can be tested for antibodies using tests such as complement fixation, latex agglutination or ELISA to confirm the herd has been exposed. To help, the farmer should keep a dead goat whole, cool and covered away from dogs and scavengers until the vet arrives, and write down when signs started, how many goats are sick or dead, their ages, any recent purchases or movements, and vaccination history.
firstSteps: Stop all movement: do not sell, buy, lend, slaughter for sale or take any goats to market or to shared grazing and water points until the vet advises.
Report the outbreak to your County Veterinary Officer or the nearest government veterinary office, because CCPP is a notifiable disease and reporting is required by law.
Separate sick goats from healthy ones as far apart as possible, ideally in a different shelter with no nose-to-nose contact.
Give the sick goats shade, shelter from wind, rain and cold, and a dry, well-ventilated space; avoid closed, stuffy sheds that make breathing harder.
Make clean, fresh water and soft palatable feed such as fresh browse or good hay easy to reach, without forcing feed or water into the mouth of a goat that is struggling to breathe.
Handle sick goats calmly and as little as possible, because stress and chasing can make breathing collapse.
Keep a simple written record of each sick or dead goat, the date signs started, temperatures if you have a thermometer, and any goats bought or moved in the last month.
Do not give antibiotics or other drugs on your own; wait for the vet, who will decide what treatment is right and allowed during an official response.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be decided and prescribed by a veterinarian, and during a notifiable disease outbreak the County Veterinary Services may direct how the herd is handled. CCPP can respond to certain antibiotics if treatment starts early, before the lungs are badly damaged. Drug classes commonly used include tetracyclines such as oxytetracycline and macrolides such as tylosin; in some places other classes may be used under veterinary direction. Penicillins do not work against mycoplasmas. Goats that are already very sick may not recover even with treatment, and goats that do recover can keep scarred lungs and may still carry the infection. For this reason, treatment is usually combined with vaccination of healthy goats in the herd and surrounding area, and strict movement control. The vet may also give anti-inflammatory drugs to ease fever and pain. Antibiotics should only be used as the vet directs and for the full course prescribed, because misuse encourages antimicrobial resistance, meaning the drugs stop working for future outbreaks. All these drugs have milk and meat withdrawal periods: milk from treated does and meat from treated goats must not be sold or eaten until the withdrawal time on the label, as explained by your vet, has passed.
prevention: Vaccinate: a killed (inactivated) CCPP vaccine is produced in Kenya by KEVEVAPI and is available through government veterinary services and agrovets; ask your vet about vaccinating all goats and giving boosters as recommended, usually yearly, ideally before the rains.
Join vaccination campaigns run by the County Veterinary Services, especially in pastoral areas, because protecting whole communities of herds stops the disease circulating.
Quarantine every new goat for at least three to four weeks away from your herd, watch it for cough and fever, and buy only from herds with known vaccination history.
Avoid overcrowding in night bomas and sheds; give goats enough space and good ventilation while still protecting them from cold wind and rain.
Reduce stress during the rains and drought by providing shelter, good nutrition, clean water and shorter treks where possible.
Limit contact with other herds at markets, water points and shared grazing during outbreaks in your area, and listen to local veterinary alerts.
Keep goats in good body condition with balanced feeding, mineral licks and regular deworming, so that their immune systems are strong.
Report coughing and sudden deaths early, because rapid action in the first cases saves the rest of your herd and your neighbours' herds.
detail.impact: CCPP can be devastating on a Kenyan goat farm. In a herd that has not been vaccinated, losses can be very heavy within a few weeks, wiping out years of breeding work and savings, since for many pastoral families goats are their bank account, school fees and food security. Survivors often grow slowly, lose weight and condition, and dairy does give much less milk. Abortions mean fewer kids the following season. Quarantine and movement restrictions stop sales at markets, sometimes for weeks, which hurts income at the time families most need it. There are also costs for vet visits, drugs and vaccines. Across counties, CCPP limits goat trade and export, so prevention through vaccination is far cheaper than dealing with an outbreak.
detail.humanHealth: CCPP does not infect people. The main human health concern is drug residues: milk and meat from goats treated with antibiotics must not be consumed or sold until the withdrawal period advised by the vet has passed. Goats that are sick or have died of disease should not be sold or eaten; follow the vet's instructions for disposal.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends heavily on how early the disease is recognised and whether the herd has been vaccinated. Goats treated early by a vet can recover, but very sick goats with severe breathing trouble often die even with treatment. Many survivors keep damaged lungs, grow poorly and may carry the infection. In vaccinated herds, outbreaks are much rarer and milder. Fast reporting, strict movement control and vaccination of healthy goats give the best chance of stopping losses.

faqs.q: Why must I report CCPP? Will the government kill my goats?
faqs.a: CCPP is a notifiable disease in Kenya, which means the law requires farmers, vets and agrovet staff to report suspected cases to the County Veterinary Officer or Directorate of Veterinary Services. Reporting lets the veterinary team confirm the disease, vaccinate herds around you and stop it spreading through your area. The usual response focuses on quarantine, treatment under vet guidance and vaccination rather than mass slaughter, but the exact measures are decided by the veterinary authorities for each outbreak. Hiding an outbreak usually makes losses much bigger for you and your neighbours.

faqs.q: What do movement restrictions mean for me?
faqs.a: When your farm or area is placed under quarantine, you cannot move goats in or out, sell them at markets, or take them to shared grazing and water without permission. Livestock markets in the area may be closed for a time. Moving animals usually needs a movement permit from the veterinary office. These rules stay until the vets are satisfied that the disease is under control. They are hard on income, but they are the fastest way to stop the disease reaching more herds.

faqs.q: Can I buy antibiotics from the agrovet and treat my goats myself?
faqs.a: No. CCPP needs a vet's diagnosis, and during an outbreak treatment should be prescribed and supervised by a vet. Some common antibiotics, such as penicillins, do not work against mycoplasma at all, and wrong use wastes money, leaves drug residues in milk and meat, and builds antimicrobial resistance. Late or incomplete treatment can also leave goats as carriers that spread the disease later. Call the vet early, when treatment has the best chance of helping.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine, and how often should I vaccinate?
faqs.a: Yes. A killed CCPP vaccine is made in Kenya by KEVEVAPI and is used in government campaigns and sold through agrovets. It protects goats from developing severe disease but needs to be given before an outbreak reaches your herd and repeated, commonly once a year. Your vet will advise on the right age for kids and the best timing, often before the rains. Keep the vaccine cold as instructed, because a vaccine that gets warm may not work.

faqs.q: Can my sheep or cattle catch CCPP from my goats?
faqs.a: CCPP is a goat disease. Sheep kept with goats are rarely if ever affected in the field, and cattle are not affected. Cattle have their own similar disease, contagious bovine pleuropneumonia (CBPP), caused by a different mycoplasma. If your sheep are also coughing and sick, tell the vet, because another disease such as PPR or pasteurellosis may be involved.

faqs.q: My goats recovered. Are they safe to mix with new goats?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Goats that recover from CCPP can keep the organism in their lungs and pass it on, especially under stress. Ask your vet before mixing them with new or unvaccinated goats. Vaccinating the whole herd, including newcomers, and quarantining new goats are the safest steps. Recovered goats may also grow poorly because of lung scarring, so some farmers choose to cull poor doers once the vet allows movement.

ccpp.imagePrompt: A thin brown East African goat standing in a dusty thornbush boma with its neck stretched forward, mouth slightly open, front legs spread apart and frothy discharge at its nose, other goats resting in the background under soft daylight.
ccpp.seoDescription: CCPP in goats: spot fever, cough and laboured breathing early, report to your County Vet, isolate the herd and prevent outbreaks with yearly vaccination.

card.headline: Raised lumps and scabs on hairless skin
card.look: A feverish, dull goat develops round, firm lumps that turn into dark scabs on the lips, nostrils, eyelids, udder, under the tail and inside the thighs. Often it also has a runny nose, watery eyes, swollen glands and laboured breathing.
card.action: Isolate the sick goat, stop all goat movement on and off the farm, and report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, because goat pox is a notifiable disease.

detail.summary: Goat pox is a highly contagious viral disease of goats. It causes fever, painful lumps across the skin, sores in the mouth and airways, and sometimes pneumonia. Young kids and goats never exposed or vaccinated can die in large numbers, and survivors lose weight, milk and skin value. It is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so every suspected case must be reported to the veterinary authorities.
detail.cause: Goat pox is caused by a capripoxvirus, a member of the pox virus family. It is closely related to the sheep pox virus and to the lumpy skin disease virus of cattle. Many East African strains can infect both goats and sheep, although some strains affect one species more than the other. After the virus enters through the nose, mouth or broken skin, it multiplies in the local tissue. It then travels in the blood to the skin, lymph nodes (the 'glands' that filter infection, felt under the jaw, in front of the shoulder and in the flank) and internal organs such as the lungs and gut. In the skin it damages small blood vessels and skin cells. This first causes red patches, then raised firm nodules, and finally dead tissue that dries into a scab. Similar lesions form inside the mouth, nose, windpipe and lungs. That is why some goats struggle to breathe and develop pneumonia. Open lesions are easily invaded by bacteria and fly maggots, which makes the goat sicker. The time from infection to signs (the incubation period) is usually around one to two weeks, but it can be up to three weeks.
spread: Direct contact between sick and healthy goats or sheep, such as sharing a pen, nose-to-nose contact at night bomas or crowding at water points.
Breathing in virus from the nasal discharge, saliva and breath of sick animals, especially in closed, poorly ventilated housing.
Scabs falling off healed or sick goats carry live virus. It can survive for months in dry, shaded pens, bedding and soil around the boma.
Contaminated items such as feeding troughs, water buckets, ropes, vehicles, shearing or castration tools, clothing and shoes of people moving between flocks.
Biting flies, especially stable flies, can carry the virus mechanically on their mouthparts from one goat to another.
Buying goats from markets, or mixing flocks during trade, dowry exchange, communal grazing or pastoral migration, is a common way the disease enters new areas.
Recovered goats do not stay long-term carriers in the way some diseases do, but their shed scabs can keep a pen infectious long after the sick animals have healed.
detail.atRisk: All breeds and ages of goats can be infected. Young kids, very old goats, pregnant does and animals that are thin, sick or heavily wormed suffer most. Imported or improved breeds such as Saanen, Toggenburg, Alpine and Boer crosses, and goats from areas where the disease has not recently circulated, often get more severe disease than local East African breeds. Unvaccinated flocks are at greatest risk. Outbreaks are more common where many flocks mix: livestock markets, pastoral and agro-pastoral areas, communal grazing and watering points, and along trade and migration routes. Droughts push herds together and weaken animals, and wet seasons with many biting flies help spread. Zero-grazing dairy goat units are not safe either if new stock is brought in without quarantine. Sheep kept with goats can also be infected.

early: Fever: the goat feels hot, especially at the ears and inside the thighs. It stands apart, hunched and dull, and eats less.
Watery eyes and a clear runny nose that soon becomes thicker, together with drooling or a wet mouth.
Swollen lymph nodes, felt as firm lumps in front of the shoulder, under the jaw or in the flank, often before skin lumps appear.
Small red, flat patches on hairless or thinly-haired skin: lips, nostrils, eyelids, ears, udder and teats, scrotum, under the tail and inside the thighs.
Within a day or two these patches become raised, firm, round lumps (nodules), usually a few millimetres to about a centimetre across.
Faster breathing and reluctance to move, and does may suddenly drop in milk.
advanced: Lumps turn grey or dark in the middle, the tissue dies and forms hard brown-black scabs that later fall off and leave scars.
In severe cases lumps cover large parts of the body, including the woolly or hairy skin, and the eyelids swell shut.
Sores in the mouth, tongue and nostrils make eating and drinking painful, so the goat loses weight fast.
Laboured, noisy breathing, coughing and thick nasal discharge as lesions develop in the airways and lungs (pneumonia).
Sores on the teats and udder make does refuse to let kids suckle, and mastitis can follow.
Pregnant does may abort, and young kids may die suddenly, sometimes before many skin lesions are seen.
Infected wounds may smell bad and attract flies and maggots, and very sick goats go down and cannot rise.

lookalikes.name: Orf (contagious ecthyma, 'scabby mouth')
lookalikes.howToTell: Orf mainly causes thick, crusty, wart-like scabs around the lips, mouth corners, nostrils and sometimes teats, mostly in kids. Goats are usually bright with little or no fever, and there are no lumps spread over the body or breathing problems. Goat pox causes fever, swollen glands and firm nodules on many body sites. Only a lab can be sure, so report if unsure.

lookalikes.name: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR, goat plague)
lookalikes.howToTell: PPR also causes fever, eye and nose discharge, mouth sores and pneumonia, but its key signs are severe, often watery diarrhoea and grey dead tissue on the gums and tongue, without firm lumps across the skin. PPR is also notifiable, so either way call the vet.

lookalikes.name: Mange (skin mites)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange causes intense itching, rubbing, hair loss and thickened, crusty or wrinkled skin that spreads slowly over weeks. Goats usually have no fever and no firm round nodules, and breathing is normal.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (streptothricosis) and insect or tick bites
lookalikes.howToTell: Dermatophilosis gives raised tufts of matted hair with crusts that lift off like a paintbrush, usually on the back after rains, and goats stay fairly well. Bite reactions are small, itchy bumps that fade in days without fever or swollen glands.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will first examine the flock, take temperatures, feel the lymph nodes, look at the skin, mouth and eyes, and listen to the lungs. The typical picture of fever plus nodules on hairless skin, swollen glands and spread through the flock makes goat pox strongly suspected. Because it is notifiable and looks like other diseases, confirmation is done in a government laboratory. The vet or veterinary officer will take samples such as small skin biopsies or scabs from fresh lesions, nasal swabs and blood. These are tested with PCR (a test that detects the virus's genetic material), and sometimes by virus isolation, microscope examination of tissue, or blood tests for antibodies. If a goat dies, a post-mortem may show pox lesions in the lungs, windpipe and gut. Do not cut open lumps or bury dead goats before the vet arrives unless told to. To help, write down the number of goats, how many are sick or dead, when signs started, any recent purchases, market visits or mixing with other flocks, and your vaccination history with dates. Keep sick animals penned and ready for examination.
firstSteps: Isolate every goat that shows fever or skin lumps in a separate shaded pen, downwind and away from the healthy flock and any sheep.
Report immediately to your County Veterinary Officer, area veterinary officer or the nearest Directorate of Veterinary Services office. Goat pox is notifiable, and reporting is a legal duty.
Stop all movement of goats and sheep on and off the farm: no selling, buying, lending bucks, taking animals to market or communal grazing until the vet advises.
Give sick goats clean water at all times and soft, palatable feed such as fresh cut grass, leaves or soaked feed, because mouth sores make eating painful.
Keep the pen dry, clean and well ventilated, and provide shade so feverish goats can rest. Separate kids from does with teat sores if suckling is too painful, and hand-feed if needed.
Protect against flies, for example by keeping the pen clean and removing dung and wet bedding, because flies spread the virus and infest wounds.
Wear gloves or wash hands well with soap after handling sick goats. Use separate boots, clothes and buckets for the sick pen, and handle healthy goats first.
Record each goat's signs, temperature if you have a thermometer, and any deaths with dates. Keep carcasses covered and do not sell or eat meat from sick goats until the vet gives guidance.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no medicine that kills the goat pox virus, and antibiotics do not cure it. Treatment aims to keep the goat alive and comfortable while its own immune system fights the virus. A vet may prescribe antibiotics, such as oxytetracycline or penicillin-streptomycin combinations, to control bacterial infection in skin sores and pneumonia. These should only be used on a vet's prescription and given as a full course, because careless antibiotic use breeds resistant bacteria (antimicrobial resistance) that make future treatments fail. Anti-inflammatory or fever-reducing drugs may be used to ease pain and fever and help the goat eat. Wounds may be cleaned and treated with antiseptics and fly repellents to prevent maggot infestation, and eye lesions may need care. Supportive care, including water, soft feed and shelter, is just as important as drugs. All drugs have milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time after treatment when milk and meat must not be sold or eaten. Your vet will tell you how long these are. Because goat pox is notifiable, the veterinary authorities will also lead the outbreak response. This may include quarantining the farm, movement controls in the area, vaccinating healthy goats and sheep on your farm and neighbouring farms (ring vaccination), and in some situations culling severely affected animals. Expect recovery in surviving goats to take several weeks, with scabs falling off over three to six weeks and scars remaining.
prevention: Vaccinate goats and sheep against sheep and goat pox. In Kenya a live vaccine is produced locally and available through veterinary offices and agrovets. Follow your vet on the right age for kids, how often to boost and how to keep the vaccine cold.
Quarantine every new goat for at least three weeks in a separate pen before mixing it with your flock, and buy from known, healthy, vaccinated flocks where possible.
Avoid mixing your goats with other flocks at markets, water points and communal grazing, especially when outbreaks are reported in your area. Listen to local veterinary alerts.

Keep pens clean and dry, and remove dung, old bedding and shed scabs regularly. After an outbreak, clean thoroughly and disinfect with a vet-recommended product, and leave pens empty for as long as advised.
Control biting flies by keeping manure away from the pens, drying out wet areas and using fly control methods your vet recommends.
Keep goats strong with good feeding, clean water, regular deworming and tick control, because thin, wormy animals suffer more severe disease.
Do not share tools, ropes, buckets or vehicles with other farms without cleaning them, and ask visitors and traders to keep out of pens.
Respect quarantine and movement restrictions announced by veterinary authorities. Moving sick or exposed goats is how the disease spreads to new counties.
detail.impact: Goat pox can be very costly for a Kenyan farm. In an unvaccinated flock many goats fall sick at once, and deaths can be high in kids and improved dairy or meat breeds. Dairy does drop sharply in milk, and teat sores can lead to mastitis and lost udders. Pregnant does may abort, so the next kid crop is lost. Sick goats lose weight quickly and take weeks to regain condition. Scarred skins fetch lower prices from tanneries. Treatment, labour and vet costs add up. Quarantine and movement bans mean you cannot sell goats for school fees, ceremonies or emergencies until the area is cleared. At a wider level, outbreaks disrupt livestock markets and export trade, which hits pastoral communities that depend on goats for income and food security.
detail.humanHealth: Goat pox is not considered a disease of people, and mainstream veterinary references do not regard it as a meaningful risk to human health. However, orf (scabby mouth), which looks similar, can infect people and cause painful sores on the hands. So wear gloves or wash hands well with soap when handling goats with skin lesions. Do not sell or consume milk or meat from goats under treatment until the withdrawal period your vet gives you has passed, because drug residues can harm consumers and are illegal.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on the goat's age, breed, condition and immunity, and on the virus strain. Adult local-breed goats with mild skin lesions often recover over three to six weeks with good nursing. They are then usually protected for a long time, although they may stay thin for a while and keep scars. Kids, pregnant does, improved breeds and goats with lesions in the lungs or widespread lesions have a much poorer outlook, and many may die. Quick reporting, isolation, good supportive care, control of secondary bacterial infection and fly strike, and rapid vaccination of healthy animals all improve the chances for the rest of the flock. Once a flock is fully vaccinated, outbreaks are uncommon.

faqs.q: Can I treat goat pox myself with antibiotics from the agrovet?
faqs.a: No. Goat pox is caused by a virus, and antibiotics cannot kill viruses. A vet may prescribe antibiotics to stop bacteria infecting the sores and lungs, but guessing drugs and doses yourself wastes money, can leave harmful residues in milk and meat, and encourages drug-resistant bacteria. Because it is notifiable, you must also report it so the veterinary authorities can stop it spreading.

faqs.q: What happens when I report goat pox to the County Veterinary Officer?
faqs.a: An officer will visit, examine your goats and take samples for laboratory confirmation. If goat pox is suspected or confirmed, your farm and possibly the surrounding area will be placed under quarantine. This means goats and sheep cannot be moved, sold or taken to markets without permission. Healthy animals nearby may be vaccinated. These rules protect your neighbours and the wider livestock trade, and reporting early usually means a shorter, smaller outbreak.

faqs.q: Should I vaccinate my goats during an outbreak?
faqs.a: Vaccination of healthy, unexposed animals is a key tool in controlling outbreaks, and veterinary authorities often carry out ring vaccination around affected farms. However, vaccination must be planned by the vet. Goats already incubating the virus may still fall sick, and using clean needles is important so you do not spread infection. Do not wait for an outbreak: routine vaccination is far more effective.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk or eat meat from a goat with goat pox?
faqs.a: Goat pox is not regarded as a human disease, but you should not sell or eat meat or milk from visibly sick goats, and you must follow any instructions from the veterinary officer during quarantine. If goats have been treated with drugs, respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods the vet gives you. Never slaughter sick goats for sale to avoid losses, as this spreads the disease and can break the law.

faqs.q: Can goat pox spread to my sheep and cattle?
faqs.a: Many East African strains infect both goats and sheep, so keep sheep away from sick goats and vaccinate both species where advised. Cattle get lumpy skin disease, which is caused by a related but different virus. Goat pox is not usually considered a cattle disease, but good hygiene across all your livestock is still wise during an outbreak.

faqs.q: How long should I keep pens empty after an outbreak?
faqs.a: The goat pox virus can survive for months in dry scabs, dung and bedding, especially in shaded pens. Remove and burn or bury bedding and dung as your vet advises, scrub surfaces, use a vet-recommended disinfectant, and leave pens empty as long as the veterinary officer suggests before bringing in new stock. Make sure new goats are vaccinated and quarantined first.
