goat-pox.seoDescription: Goat pox in Kenya: spot fever, skin lumps and scabs on lips, udder and tail early. Learn first steps, reporting rules, vaccination and prevention.

card.headline: Very pale or white inner eyelids
card.look: Gently pull down the lower eyelid: instead of a healthy bright pink-red, the inside is pale pink or almost white. The goat may also be weak, lag behind the herd, or have a soft swelling under the jaw (bottle jaw).
card.action: Keep the pale goat calm, handle it gently, and call your vet or animal health assistant today so the right dewormer can be chosen and given correctly.

detail.summary: Barber's pole worm (Haemonchus contortus) is a small worm that lives in the goat's fourth stomach and sucks blood. A heavy burden causes anaemia, which means too little blood, so the goat becomes pale, weak and swollen under the jaw, and can die suddenly. It is one of the most common and costly killers of goats in Kenya, especially during and after the long and short rains. Many dewormers no longer work well against it because of drug resistance, so careful checking and targeted treatment matter a great deal.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Haemonchus contortus, a roundworm about two to three centimetres long. The female worm looks like a red-and-white barber's pole because her blood-filled gut twists around her white egg tubes. The worms live in the abomasum, the goat's fourth or 'true' stomach, where they pierce the stomach lining and suck blood. Each worm takes only a little blood, but a goat can carry thousands of worms, and the wounds keep bleeding after the worm moves on. The goat slowly loses red blood cells (causing anaemia and pale gums and eyelids) and blood protein (causing fluid to leak into tissues, seen as bottle jaw, a soft swelling under the jaw). When blood loss is fast, the goat may die before the farmer notices anything. Unlike many other worms, barber's pole worm usually does not cause diarrhoea, so goats can look normal from behind while being seriously ill. Female worms lay thousands of eggs every day, which pass out in the droppings and contaminate the pasture very quickly.
spread: Eggs pass out in the droppings of infected goats, sheep and sometimes other ruminants, and hatch on the ground into tiny larvae (immature worms).
In warm, wet weather the larvae develop into the infective stage in about a week or less, and climb up wet grass blades in films of moisture.
Goats swallow these infective larvae while grazing, especially short grass close to the ground and grass wet with early-morning dew or after rain.
Once swallowed, larvae grow into adult egg-laying worms in roughly three weeks, so heavy pasture contamination builds up fast during the rains.
In dry or cold weather some larvae inside the goat go into a resting state and resume development when conditions improve, causing outbreaks when the rains return.
Does around kidding and while nursing have weaker immunity and shed many more eggs, contaminating pasture for their young kids.
Overstocking, grazing the same small plot all year, and grazing low-lying wet areas or around water points greatly increase spread.
Buying in goats that carry resistant worms is a common way to bring dewormer-resistant barber's pole worm onto a farm.
detail.atRisk: All goats can be affected, but kids and young goats after weaning, pregnant and nursing does, and thin or poorly fed goats are at greatest risk. Goats generally build weaker immunity to worms than sheep, so even adult goats stay vulnerable. Risk is highest during and just after the long rains (roughly March to June) and short rains (roughly October to December), when pasture is warm and wet. Goats that graze short pasture, tethered goats kept on the same patch, and herds sharing grazing with sheep are at high risk, while goats that mostly browse shrubs and trees pick up fewer larvae. Zero-grazed goats fed cut grass can still be infected if grass is cut close to the ground from contaminated areas. Some exotic dairy breeds and crosses (such as Toggenburg, Saanen and Alpine) may suffer more than hardy local breeds like the Small East African goat, although individual animals vary a lot within any breed.

early: Inner lower eyelids, gums and the inside of the vulva look paler pink than normal when checked in daylight.
The goat tires easily, walks slowly, and lags behind the herd when driven to grazing or water.
Gradual loss of weight and body condition even though feed seems adequate.
Rough, dull, staring coat and a generally unthrifty look.
Drop in milk yield in dairy does and slower growth in kids.
Droppings usually stay as normal firm pellets, which is why the problem is easily missed.
advanced: Inner eyelids very pale or almost white (FAMACHA score 4 or 5).
Bottle jaw: a soft, cool, fluid-filled swelling under the lower jaw, often bigger in the evening after the head has been down grazing, and smaller in the morning.
Marked weakness, lying down a lot, reluctance to stand, or collapse when chased or handled.
Fast breathing and a fast heartbeat, especially after small effort.
Swelling of the lower belly or legs from fluid in some cases.
Sudden death, sometimes of apparently good-looking goats, especially in young animals during the rains.

lookalikes.name: Liver fluke (fasciolosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Liver fluke also causes pale eyelids, weight loss and bottle jaw, but it is linked to grazing in swampy areas, around dams, rivers or irrigation where water snails live, and usually develops more slowly. A vet confirms it with a special faecal sedimentation test for fluke eggs, or by finding flat leaf-shaped flukes in the liver at post-mortem, whereas barber's pole worms are found in the fourth stomach. Both can occur together.

lookalikes.name: Trypanosomiasis (nagana)
lookalikes.howToTell: This tsetse-borne disease also causes anaemia and wasting, but often comes with fever, swollen lymph nodes (glands) and occurs in tsetse areas such as parts of the coast, Lake Victoria basin and some rangelands. A vet confirms it with a blood test, while a faecal egg count will be high in haemonchosis.

lookalikes.name: Anaplasmosis and other tick-borne blood diseases
lookalikes.howToTell: These cause anaemia too, but often with fever, yellowish eyelids or gums (jaundice), and heavy tick loads. Bottle jaw is more typical of worms. A vet uses a blood smear to find the blood parasite.

lookalikes.name: Other stomach and gut worms and coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Worms such as Trichostrongylus and coccidia (tiny gut parasites common in kids) mainly cause diarrhoea, soiled tails and weight loss rather than severe paleness. If the goat is scouring but eyelids are fairly pink, barber's pole worm is less likely to be the main problem, though mixed infections are common.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually starts by examining the goat: checking the colour of the inner eyelid with a FAMACHA chart (a colour card scoring from 1, red and healthy, to 5, white and severely anaemic), feeling for bottle jaw, scoring body condition and listening to the heart and breathing. A faecal egg count, where a small sample of fresh droppings is examined under a microscope, shows how many worm eggs are being passed; some labs can also culture the eggs to confirm which worm type is present. A blood test for packed cell volume (the share of the blood made up of red cells) measures how anaemic the goat is. If a goat has died, a post-mortem is very useful: the vet opens the fourth stomach and can often see many thin red-and-white worms moving in the contents, with pale tissues and watery fluid in the body. To check whether your dewormer still works, the vet may do a faecal egg count reduction test, taking samples before and about 10 to 14 days after deworming. You can help by collecting fresh droppings straight from the rectum or just-dropped pellets into a clean, labelled bag, keeping them cool (not frozen), and noting which goats are affected, their ages, FAMACHA scores, recent deaths, when and with what product you last dewormed, and where the herd has been grazing.
firstSteps: Check the inner eyelids of every goat in the herd, not just the sick one, in good daylight, and write down which animals are pale, so you know how widespread the problem is.
Handle pale or weak goats very gently and slowly, because severely anaemic goats can collapse and die from the stress of chasing, catching or long walks.
Keep affected goats in a shaded, sheltered, dry pen close to home, away from wet pasture, so they stop picking up more larvae.

Give clean drinking water and good-quality feed such as fresh browse, good hay, and if available a protein-rich supplement like dairy meal or legume leaves (lucerne, desmodium, leucaena or calliandra), to help the body rebuild blood.
Call your vet or animal health assistant promptly, especially if any goat has very pale or white eyelids, bottle jaw or cannot stand, and tell them which dewormers you have used recently.

Do not guess or buy random dewormers at high or low amounts; a wrong product or underdosing wastes money and speeds up resistance, so let the vet choose the product and dose by the goat's actual weight.
Collect a few fresh dropping samples in clean labelled bags and keep them cool for the vet, and if a goat dies, keep the carcass cool and covered for a post-mortem.
Wash your hands after handling goats and droppings as basic good hygiene.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed by a vet, who will choose a dewormer based on the farm's history, local resistance patterns and, ideally, faecal egg count results. Common drug groups used against barber's pole worm include benzimidazoles (such as albendazole and fenbendazole), levamisole, macrocyclic lactones (such as ivermectin, doramectin and moxidectin), closantel (which targets blood-feeding worms and also liver fluke), and newer groups such as monepantel where available. Resistance to albendazole, levamisole and ivermectin has been reported in goats and sheep in Kenya and East Africa, so a product that worked years ago may now fail. Goats break down many dewormers faster than sheep or cattle, so the correct goat dose can differ from the label dose for other species; only the vet should decide this, and goats should be weighed or weight-taped rather than guessed. The vet may combine two drug groups or advise treating only the goats that need it (targeted selective treatment) to slow resistance. Severely anaemic goats may also receive supportive care such as iron and B-vitamin injections, good nutrition and rest, and in rare valuable cases a blood transfusion. Expect pale goats to take several weeks to regain normal eyelid colour as new blood is made; bottle jaw often eases within days to a couple of weeks. Every dewormer has a milk and meat withdrawal period, the time you must wait before milk or meat is safe for people; some products are not allowed at all in milking does, so always ask your vet and follow the label.
prevention: Check eyelid colour with a FAMACHA chart every one to two weeks during the rains and every three to four weeks in the dry season, and deworm only goats scoring 4 or 5, and those scoring 3 if they are kids, pregnant or nursing does, or thin, as advised by your vet.
Use the Five Point Check along with FAMACHA: eyelid colour, bottle jaw, body condition, a dirty tail (scouring) and nasal discharge, to decide which goats really need treatment.
Leave some healthy goats untreated when it is safe, so that worms still sensitive to dewormers survive on the pasture (called refugia); this slows the spread of resistance.
Weigh goats or use a weight tape before dosing, calibrate the dosing gun, and never underdose, which is a major cause of dewormer resistance.

Ask your vet to do a faecal egg count reduction test once a year or when treatment seems to fail, and change dewormer groups based on the results, not on brand names, since many brands contain the same active ingredient.

Rotate grazing so goats do not return to the same paddock for several weeks, avoid grazing very short grass, low-lying wet ground and areas around water points, and delay grazing until the morning dew has dried.
Encourage browsing on shrubs and trees and, for zero-grazing, cut fodder well above ground level and avoid cutting from contaminated grazing areas.

Feed well, especially protein, during pregnancy, around kidding and for weaned kids, because well-nourished goats cope with worms much better; tannin-rich forages such as leucaena, calliandra and some acacias may also help reduce worm burdens.
Quarantine newly bought goats for two to three weeks, deworm them as advised by your vet, and check droppings before mixing them with the herd so you do not bring in resistant worms.
Keep records of FAMACHA scores and treatments, and cull or avoid breeding from goats that repeatedly need deworming, while keeping goats that stay healthy with little treatment.
detail.impact: Barber's pole worm is a leading cause of goat deaths and poor performance on Kenyan farms, from zero-grazed dairy goat units in central Kenya to pastoral herds in the rangelands. Losses come from sudden deaths during the rains, slow growth of kids and weaners, lower milk yields in dairy does, poor fertility, weak kids born to anaemic does, and lower market prices for thin goats. Farmers also spend money on repeated dewormers, and when worms become resistant, that money is wasted while goats keep dying. For a smallholder whose goats are savings, school fees or milk for the family, losing even a few animals in one rainy season can be a serious setback.
detail.humanHealth: Barber's pole worm does not infect people. The main human risk comes from dewormer residues: milk or meat from goats treated with dewormers can contain drug traces if sold or eaten before the withdrawal period has passed. Always follow the withdrawal time on the label or given by your vet, keep records of treatment dates, and discard milk during the withdrawal period. Store dewormers safely away from children and food.
detail.outlook: Goats caught early, with mild to moderate paleness and no collapse, usually recover well once given an effective dewormer, rest and good feed, although regaining full blood levels and body condition takes several weeks. Goats with white eyelids, severe bottle jaw or that cannot stand have a guarded outlook and may die even with treatment, especially if stressed during handling. Recovery also depends heavily on whether the chosen dewormer still works on your farm, so failure to improve within one to two weeks should be reported to the vet. Without changes to grazing and monitoring, reinfection in the next rainy season is very likely.

faqs.q: How often should I deworm my goats?
faqs.a: There is no single correct calendar, and deworming the whole herd every month is one of the fastest ways to create resistant worms. A better approach is to check eyelid colour with a FAMACHA chart regularly, every one to two weeks in the rains, and deworm only the goats that are pale or otherwise showing signs, plus vulnerable groups as your vet advises. Your vet can help plan strategic treatments around the rains and kidding that suit your area.

faqs.q: I dewormed but my goats are still pale and dying. Why?
faqs.a: The most common reasons are dewormer resistance, underdosing because the goat's weight was guessed, a fake or expired product, or immediately returning goats to heavily contaminated pasture. Anaemia also takes weeks to correct, so goats may stay pale for a while even when worms are killed. Another disease such as liver fluke or a tick-borne infection may be involved. Ask your vet to do a faecal egg count before and after treatment to find out whether the drug is working.

faqs.q: Where can I get a FAMACHA chart and is it hard to use?
faqs.a: FAMACHA charts are usually available through vets, county livestock offices, training programmes and some agrovets; only genuine laminated cards should be used because printed copies may show wrong colours. It is easy to learn: in good daylight, press down the upper eyelid and pull the lower one down to see the inner pink lining, then match the colour to the card. Training from a vet or extension officer is recommended so your scoring is accurate. Remember FAMACHA only detects blood-sucking worms like barber's pole worm, not all worms.

faqs.q: Can I use a sheep or cattle dewormer on my goats?
faqs.a: Many dewormers are used in several species, but goats break down several of them faster than sheep or cattle, so the correct dose for a goat can differ from what is printed for other animals. Some products are also not suitable for milking goats. Never guess. Ask your vet which product and dose to use, and weigh the goats before dosing.

faqs.q: Is the milk safe to drink after I deworm?
faqs.a: The worm itself does not infect people, but the drug can pass into milk and meat. Every dewormer has a withdrawal period, which is the number of days you must wait before milk or meat can be used. During that time the milk should be discarded, not sold or given to children. Check the label and confirm with your vet, as some products cannot be used in lactating does at all.

faqs.q: Do herbal or traditional dewormers work?
faqs.a: Some plants, especially tannin-rich fodders like leucaena, calliandra and certain acacias, may help reduce worm burdens and support goats when fed as part of the diet, and research on others continues. However, results vary and most traditional remedies have not been proven to clear a dangerous barber's pole worm burden. Do not rely on them alone for a pale, weak goat; get vet advice and use good grazing management and nutrition alongside any natural approaches.

haemonchosis.imagePrompt: Close-up photograph of a brown East African goat's eye with a hand gently pulling down the lower eyelid to reveal a very pale, almost white inner lining, soft natural daylight, farm background blurred.
haemonchosis.seoDescription: Barber's pole worm in goats: spot pale eyelids and bottle jaw early, use FAMACHA scoring, act before the vet arrives and prevent dewormer resistance.

card.headline: Kids with dirty, scouring back ends
card.look: Kids aged about 3 weeks to 5 months have soft to watery droppings, sometimes with mucus or blood, stuck to the tail and hind legs. They strain often, eat less, look dull and hunched, and stop growing well.
card.action: Move scouring kids to a clean, dry pen, give them clean water, and call your vet the same day, because dehydration can kill kids quickly.

aka: Kid scours (general term that also covers other causes)
detail.summary: Coccidiosis is a gut disease of young goats caused by tiny single-celled parasites called Eimeria. It is one of the most common reasons goat kids in Kenya scour, stop growing or die between weaning age and about five months. Many kids carry a few of these parasites with no harm, but crowded, wet and dirty pens let numbers build up until the gut is badly damaged. Even kids that survive can stay stunted for months, so prevention pays far more than treatment.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by several species of Eimeria, a protozoan parasite. A protozoan is a microscopic single-celled organism, not a worm, and it cannot be seen with the eye. Goats have their own Eimeria species. The ones from chickens, cattle or sheep do not cause coccidiosis in goats. Infected goats pass huge numbers of tiny egg-like stages called oocysts in their droppings. In warm, damp bedding these oocysts mature within a few days and become infective. A kid swallows them when it licks dirty walls, feeds from soiled troughs or suckles a dirty udder. Inside the kid, the parasites invade the cells lining the intestines, multiply and burst out, destroying the cells as they go. One swallowed oocyst can produce very many new parasites, so a heavy dose can strip large areas of the gut lining. The damaged gut cannot absorb water and nutrients properly. The result is diarrhoea, loss of fluids and salts, bleeding in severe cases, pain and straining. Because the damage happens before the new oocysts appear in the droppings, a kid can be sick before a dung test turns positive. Older goats usually build up immunity through repeated light exposure. They still shed some oocysts and keep the pen contaminated for the next batch of kids.
spread: Kids swallow mature oocysts from droppings that contaminate bedding, floors, walls, feed troughs and water containers.
Adult does that look healthy still shed oocysts, so kids born into a pen used by adults are exposed from their first weeks.
Wet, warm bedding and mud around water points help oocysts mature fast and survive for many months, so the pen itself becomes the source.
Overcrowding raises the number of oocysts each kid swallows, and the dose decides how sick a kid gets.
Feeding hay or concentrates on the floor, where kids stand and drop dung, is one of the most common ways infection builds up.
Stress makes outbreaks more likely, including weaning, transport, sudden feed changes, mixing groups, cold wet weather and other diseases such as worms.
Oocysts resist many common disinfectants and can be carried on boots, wheelbarrows and feeding tools between pens.
detail.atRisk: Kids between about 3 weeks and 5 months old are most at risk, with the peak often around weaning. Kids born in a batch, or kept in groups in the same pen year after year, face heavy contamination. Zero-grazed and intensively housed dairy goats such as Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine and their crosses often suffer badly because of crowding and pens with built-up dung. Galla and Small East African goats on free-range or pastoral systems are also affected, especially around bomas, night enclosures and water points that stay muddy. Outbreaks are most common during and after the long and short rains, when bedding and yards stay wet. Bought-in kids, recently weaned kids, orphans on bottle feeding, and kids that are thin or carrying worms are at extra risk. Adult goats rarely show disease unless they are very stressed or have never been exposed before.

early: Droppings change from firm pellets to soft clumps, then pasty, then runny.
The tail, back end and hocks become stained and dirty with dung.
The kid eats less, drinks less milk or creep feed, and stays behind when the group moves.
The kid is less playful, stands hunched, and the coat looks rough and dull.
The kid gains weight slowly or stops growing compared with others of the same age.
Several kids in the same pen or age group start showing loose droppings within days of each other.
advanced: Watery diarrhoea, often dark or greenish, that may contain mucus, streaks of blood or dark clotted blood.
Frequent straining with little coming out, sometimes with the back arched and the tail raised, which can occasionally push out part of the rectum (rectal prolapse).
Sunken eyes and a dry mouth. A pinch of skin on the neck stays up instead of springing back, which shows dehydration.
Marked weakness, unsteady walking, lying down for long periods and refusing to get up.
Fast weight loss, a pot-bellied but bony shape, and pale gums if there has been much blood loss.
Cold legs and ears, collapse and death, which can come within days in heavily infected young kids.
Kids that survive a bad attack often stay stunted and pot-bellied for months.

lookalikes.name: Worms (especially barber's pole worm and other roundworms)
lookalikes.howToTell: Barber's pole worm usually causes pale eyelids and gums, weakness and swelling under the jaw (bottle jaw), often without much diarrhoea. Other roundworms can cause scouring in older kids and adults on pasture. Coccidiosis mainly hits housed or crowded kids under about 5 months and may include blood and straining. Both often occur together, and only a dung test can tell them apart for sure.

lookalikes.name: Cryptosporidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: This is another tiny parasite, but it usually affects much younger kids, in their first one to three weeks of life. The diarrhoea is usually yellow and very watery, without blood. It can also infect people. A lab test on dung is needed to confirm it.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia (pulpy kidney, overeating disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: This usually strikes the biggest, fastest-growing kids after a sudden change to rich feed or lots of milk or grain. It often causes sudden death, or violent signs such as convulsions and paddling, within hours. It is not the slow scouring and wasting of coccidiosis. It is largely preventable by vaccination.

lookalikes.name: Bacterial or nutritional scours (for example E. coli, Salmonella, or overfeeding milk)
lookalikes.howToTell: Overfeeding milk or sudden feed changes cause pale, pasty scours that often settle once feeding is corrected. Bacterial infections such as Salmonella can cause fever, very foul-smelling diarrhoea, and illness in adults as well as kids. Your vet may need dung samples or a post-mortem to tell them apart from coccidiosis.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will look at the kids' age, the pen conditions and the pattern of illness in the group, then examine sick kids for dehydration, fever and blood loss. The main test is a dung test, called faecal flotation, where a lab counts oocysts under a microscope. Results need careful reading. Healthy kids can shed many oocysts of harmless species, while a very sick kid may show few oocysts because the damage comes before shedding. Some labs can identify which Eimeria species are present, which helps show whether they are the harmful kinds. Your vet may also check for worms in the same sample, because the two often occur together. If a kid dies, a post-mortem is very useful. It often shows a thickened, inflamed gut wall with small white or grey spots or patches, and sometimes blood in the intestine. Scrapings of the gut wall can confirm the parasites. To help your vet, collect fresh droppings from several affected kids and a few healthy ones. Put them straight from the rectum or fresh off the ground into clean, labelled containers or gloves tied shut, and keep them cool but not frozen. Note the kids' ages, when signs started, how many are sick or have died, what they eat, any recent weaning, moves or feed changes, and any treatments already given.
firstSteps: Separate scouring kids into a clean, dry, draught-free pen with fresh bedding so they stop swallowing more oocysts and do not contaminate healthy kids.
Make sure every sick kid has easy access to clean, fresh water. Keep weak kids warm and out of rain and cold wind, because dehydrated kids chill easily.
Keep milk-fed kids suckling or bottle-feeding unless your vet advises otherwise. Milk gives energy, and stopping it suddenly can weaken them.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day, especially if you see blood, straining, sunken eyes or kids that cannot stand. Collect fresh dung samples to show them.
Remove wet, soiled bedding from the main kid pen, scrape out dung, and raise feed and water containers off the floor so kids cannot dirty them.
Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap after handling scouring kids and their dung. Other causes of kid diarrhoea can infect people.
Write down each sick kid's identity, age, signs and the date. This record helps your vet decide on treatment and whether the whole group needs it.
Do not give leftover drugs, human medicines or antibiotics without a vet's advice. The wrong drug wastes money, may harm the kid and can delay the right treatment.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed by a vet, who will choose the drug based on the kids' age, how sick they are and what is available and approved locally. The main medicines are anticoccidial drugs, which kill or stop the parasites multiplying. Commonly used active ingredients include toltrazuril and diclazuril, usually given by mouth. Others are amprolium, and sulfonamides such as sulfadimidine, which are a type of antibiotic that also acts against coccidia. Because all kids in a pen are usually exposed, vets often treat the whole age group, not just the ones showing signs. Some of these drugs work best when given early, before the gut is badly damaged. Badly dehydrated kids need fluids and salts, given by mouth or, in severe cases, by drip or injection under the skin by the vet. The vet may also give supportive care such as vitamins, and may treat worms or other infections found at the same time. Where sulfonamides or other antibiotics are used, they must be given exactly as prescribed. Using them carelessly or too often encourages antimicrobial resistance, which means the drugs stop working on the farm and beyond. Overusing anticoccidial drugs can also make coccidia resistant. All of these drugs have milk and meat withdrawal periods. This is the time after treatment when milk and meat must not be sold or eaten, so ask your vet and follow the label. Expect sick kids to start improving within a few days if treatment starts early. Kids with severe gut damage may still die or recover slowly, because the gut lining needs time to heal.
prevention: Keep kid pens dry and clean. Remove dung and wet bedding often, add fresh dry bedding, and fix leaking roofs and water spills, especially during the long and short rains.
Use raised slatted floors for housed goats where possible, with gaps that let droppings fall through, so kids are kept away from their own dung.
Put feed in raised troughs or hay racks and water in containers kids cannot climb into or dirty. Never feed concentrates or hay on the floor.
Avoid overcrowding, and keep kids in small groups of similar age. Do not keep young kids in pens with older, shedding goats or in pens that have just held another batch.
Rest and clean pens between batches of kids. Scrape out all dung and let the pen dry in the sun. Common disinfectants kill few oocysts, so physical cleaning and drying matter most.
Clean does' udders and keep kidding areas clean so newborns do not swallow oocysts in their first weeks.
Reduce stress at weaning. Wean gradually, avoid moving, mixing, dehorning or castrating kids all at once, and change feeds slowly.

On farms with repeated problems, ask your vet about a prevention plan. This may include planned treatment of kids at a high-risk age, or feed additives such as decoquinate or ionophores like monensin. Only use these on vet advice, because some, such as monensin, are dangerous if fed to dogs or horses, or if mixed wrongly.
Keep kids well fed with colostrum at birth, good milk or creep feed, clean water and minerals, and control worms. Strong, well-nourished kids cope better with exposure.
Isolate newly bought goats, especially kids, for two to three weeks and watch their droppings before mixing them with your herd.
detail.impact: Coccidiosis costs Kenyan goat farmers money in several ways. Kids may die, often the most valuable dairy or improved breed kids kept in houses. Many survivors grow slowly, take longer to reach market weight or breeding size, and need more feed to get there. In dairy goat units, stunted doelings may breed later and produce less milk over their lives. Vet visits, drugs, extra labour cleaning pens and lost sales of kids or milk during withdrawal periods all add up. Because the parasite stays in the pen, a farm that does not fix housing and hygiene can lose kids batch after batch, season after season. The good news is that relatively cheap changes, such as raised floors, raised feeders and dry bedding, can cut losses a lot.
detail.humanHealth: Goat coccidia (Eimeria) are specific to goats and do not infect people. However, other causes of kid diarrhoea that look similar, such as Cryptosporidium and Salmonella, can infect humans, especially children, so wash hands with soap after handling scouring kids or dung and keep children from playing in kid pens. Drugs used to treat coccidiosis leave residues, so milk and meat from treated goats must not be sold or eaten until the withdrawal period your vet gives you has passed.
detail.outlook: Kids treated early, while they are still eating and only mildly dehydrated, usually recover well. Kids that already have bloody diarrhoea, severe dehydration or cannot stand are at real risk of dying even with good treatment. Some survivors stay stunted because the damaged gut takes weeks to heal and absorbs food poorly in the meantime. The outlook for the whole herd depends mostly on management. Treating sick kids without improving pen hygiene, dryness, space and feeding usually means the problem comes back with the next batch. Older goats build immunity, so once kids pass about five to six months in good health, serious disease becomes much less likely.

faqs.q: Can I use the coccidiosis drug I bought for my chickens on my goats?
faqs.a: No, not without a vet's advice. Chicken coccidia are different species from goat coccidia and do not infect goats. Many poultry products are made and dosed for birds in drinking water, and the strength, safety and withdrawal periods for goats can be very different. Some poultry additives can be harmful to goats if wrongly mixed. Ask your vet to prescribe a product and amount suitable for goat kids.

faqs.q: My adult goats look healthy. Why do my kids keep getting coccidiosis?
faqs.a: Most adult goats carry some coccidia and pass oocysts in their droppings without getting sick, because they have built up immunity. Those oocysts build up in bedding, floors and yards, especially when they are damp. Young kids have no immunity yet and swallow large numbers, so they fall sick. Keeping kids in clean, dry pens away from built-up dung, and raising feeders off the floor, breaks this cycle.

faqs.q: Will deworming my kids treat coccidiosis?
faqs.a: Usually not. Coccidia are protozoa, not worms, and most common dewormers do not kill them. Worms and coccidiosis often happen together and can look similar, so ask your vet for a dung test that checks for both. Treat each problem with the right medicine at the right time.

faqs.q: Is it enough to treat only the kids that are scouring?
faqs.a: Often not. By the time a few kids show signs, the rest of the same age group have usually swallowed oocysts and may be about to fall sick. Vets often advise treating the whole group at risk. They will also tell you to clean the pen, otherwise the treated kids are reinfected straight away. Your vet will judge what is right for your herd.

faqs.q: How long do coccidia survive in my goat house?
faqs.a: Oocysts are very tough. In shaded, damp bedding and soil they can survive for many months, and they resist many common disinfectants. Sunlight and drying help kill them. Removing all dung and bedding, scraping floors, letting the pen dry fully and resting it between batches of kids does more than spraying disinfectant alone.

faqs.q: Can a kid that recovered from coccidiosis still grow well?
faqs.a: Many do, especially if treated early. A kid that had severe gut damage may grow slowly for weeks or months while the gut lining heals. Give recovering kids good-quality feed, clean water, minerals, shelter and protection from worms. Watch their weight, and talk to your vet if they stay thin or pot-bellied.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help replace water and salts lost through diarrhoea in scouring kids. Use it alongside the anticoccidial treatment your vet prescribes, not instead of it. Kids that are badly dehydrated or cannot swallow need the vet.

A vitamin A, D3 and E supplement that can support recovering kids during convalescence. Vitamin A helps maintain the gut lining. Use it only as part of vet-guided recovery care alongside proper treatment and clean housing; it does not kill coccidia.

card.headline: Best-growing kid found suddenly dead
card.look: Your fattest, fastest-growing kid is found dead or dying, often after a feed change, grain or lush pasture. Others may stagger, lie on their side paddling, cry out, convulse or pass watery diarrhoea.
card.action: Call your vet immediately, and stop all grain and concentrate feeding to the whole herd while you keep the other goats calm on plain hay and water.

detail.summary: Enterotoxaemia is a sudden, often fatal disease caused by a poison (toxin) made by bacteria that normally live harmlessly in a goat's gut. When feed changes suddenly, or a goat eats too much grain, concentrate or lush green feed, these bacteria multiply fast and release toxin that damages the gut, brain and blood vessels. It typically kills the healthiest, best-fed kids first, often before the farmer sees any sign. The good news is that it is largely preventable with regular vaccination and careful feeding.
detail.cause: The cause is Clostridium perfringens type D, a bacterium found in soil, manure and the normal intestines of healthy goats. In small numbers it does no harm. The trouble starts when a lot of starch or sugar, from grain, dairy meal, bread, kitchen waste, lush young pasture or a large milk meal, passes undigested from the rumen (the first, largest stomach) into the small intestine. There the bacteria feed on it, multiply very quickly and produce a powerful poison called epsilon toxin. This toxin is absorbed into the blood. It makes blood vessels leaky, so fluid builds up in the brain, lungs, heart sac and gut. Damage to the brain causes staggering, blindness, convulsions and death. In goats, unlike sheep, the gut itself is often badly inflamed (enterocolitis), which causes diarrhoea and belly pain. The name 'pulpy kidney' comes from the soft, mushy kidneys often seen at post-mortem, mainly in sheep; in goats this sign is less consistent. Because the toxin acts so quickly, many animals die within hours.
spread: It is not passed from goat to goat like a cold. The bacteria are already in the gut and the environment, and disease is triggered by what and how the goat eats.
Sudden changes in diet are the main trigger, for example moving goats from dry grazing to lush green pasture after the long or short rains start.
Feeding grain, maize, dairy meal, sorghum, bread or concentrates in large amounts, or starting them without a gradual build-up, is a common cause.
Goats breaking into a feed store or a maize field and gorging themselves can cause outbreaks within a day or two.
Irregular feeding, such as skipping a meal and then giving a large one, or uneven feeding where bossy goats eat more than their share, raises the risk.
In kids, heavy suckling from high-yielding does, or large irregular bottle feeds of milk or milk replacer, can trigger disease.
Stress, transport, other illness and heavy worm burdens can slow the gut and make overgrowth more likely.
Bacteria from the manure of affected animals build up in pens and soil, so dirty, crowded housing increases the overall load.
detail.atRisk: Young, fast-growing kids are most at risk, especially those from about a few weeks to several months old that are fed well, suckle heavily or receive concentrates. Kids born to unvaccinated does get little or no protection from colostrum (first milk). Weaned kids being fattened for market, dairy goats on high-concentrate rations, and show or breeding animals being pushed for growth are also at high risk. Adult goats can be affected too, often with a longer-lasting form that causes repeated diarrhoea and weight loss. Dairy breeds such as Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine and their crosses kept in zero-grazing units with heavy feeding are commonly affected, but Galla, Small East African and crossbred meat goats on improved feeding are not immune. Risk rises at the start of the rains when pasture suddenly becomes lush, after harvest when goats get access to stover with spilled grain, and whenever a farmer changes feed quickly. Goats that were vaccinated long ago are also at risk, because protection in goats fades faster than in sheep.

early: Often there are no early signs at all: the first thing seen may be a dead kid that looked perfectly healthy the evening before.
A goat that stops eating suddenly, stands apart from the herd, looks dull and does not want to move.
Signs of belly pain: kicking at the belly, grinding teeth, crying out, lying down and getting up repeatedly.
Soft to watery diarrhoea, sometimes with mucus or streaks of blood.
Staggering, wobbly walking, head pressing against walls, or seeming blind and walking into things.
A bloated or tense belly in some cases.
advanced: Lying flat on the side, unable to rise, with legs paddling as if running.
Convulsions (fits), with the head and neck pulled back, foaming at the mouth and jerking.
Very fast, heavy breathing and a weak pulse as the goat goes into shock.
Coma and death, often within a few hours of the first signs in kids.
In adult goats with the longer-lasting form: repeated bouts of diarrhoea, weight loss, poor appetite and falling milk yield over days to weeks.
Several of the best kids in the group dying over a few days after the same feed change.

lookalikes.name: Anthrax
lookalikes.howToTell: Anthrax also causes sudden death, but dark, tarry blood that does not clot may ooze from the nose, mouth or anus, and the carcass may swell and stiffen poorly. Anthrax is notifiable and dangerous to people. If a goat dies suddenly with bleeding from openings, do not open the carcass; call the vet, who will check before any post-mortem is done.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater (cowdriosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Heartwater, spread by bont ticks, also causes fever, circling, high stepping, paddling and convulsions. It usually affects goats of any age with tick exposure, often with a high fever beforehand, and is not linked to a feed change. Enterotoxaemia mostly hits well-fed kids after diet changes and the goat may not have a fever. A vet can tell them apart with a brain smear at post-mortem.

lookalikes.name: Grain overload (rumen acidosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Both follow eating too much grain, and they can occur together. With acidosis the goat has a swollen, sloshy left belly, severe dehydration, sunken eyes and very sour-smelling, watery dung, and it gets sick over several hours to a day. Enterotoxaemia tends to cause nervous signs and sudden death more quickly.

lookalikes.name: Polioencephalomalacia (thiamine or vitamin B1 deficiency)
lookalikes.howToTell: This also causes blindness, star-gazing, head pressing and fits, and can follow diet changes. It usually develops more slowly, the goat often stays alert and keeps trying to stand, and diarrhoea is uncommon. Vets often treat suspected cases with thiamine and watch for improvement, which helps tell the two apart.

detail.diagnosis: Diagnosis is often made from the history and post-mortem, because live cases die so quickly. The vet will ask about recent feed changes, grain or concentrate feeding, lush pasture, vaccination dates and which goats died. A key clue is that the best-conditioned kids are affected. On examining a sick goat the vet looks for nervous signs, diarrhoea and belly pain; a urine test strip showing sugar in the urine supports the diagnosis, though this is less reliable in goats than in sheep. At post-mortem the vet may find a fluid-filled heart sac, wet swollen lungs, an inflamed, bloody or watery small intestine and colon, and sometimes soft kidneys. Confirmation needs laboratory testing of fresh gut contents for epsilon toxin, often at a county or regional veterinary laboratory. Samples must be taken soon after death because clostridia multiply quickly in a carcass and can give misleading results. The vet will also rule out anthrax before opening a carcass that died suddenly. To help, note the time of death and first signs, write down what all goats were fed over the past week, keep vaccination records ready, keep the carcass in a cool, shaded place covered from dogs and flies, and do not open it yourself.
firstSteps: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer straight away and describe the sudden deaths, signs and recent feed changes; this is an emergency and minutes matter.
Stop all grain, dairy meal, bread, kitchen waste and other concentrates for the whole herd immediately, and move goats off lush pasture onto good dry hay or mature grass with clean water.
Move sick goats to a quiet, shaded, well-bedded pen away from the others, and handle them gently; avoid chasing, which worsens shock.
Do not pour water or drenches into the mouth of a goat that is convulsing, lying flat or cannot swallow, because liquid can go into the lungs and kill it.
Check the rest of the herd closely every few hours, especially the best-fed kids, and note any that stop eating, stagger or develop diarrhoea.
If a goat has died, do not open the carcass, especially if there is blood from the nose, mouth or anus, as this could be anthrax; keep it cool, covered and away from dogs until the vet sees it.
Wear gloves when handling sick or dead animals and wash your hands with soap afterwards.
Write down which goats are affected, their ages, when signs started, what they ate, and when they were last vaccinated, so the vet can act quickly.
Do not give antibiotics or other drugs from the agrovet on your own; treatment and emergency vaccination of the herd must be decided by your vet.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment is difficult because the disease moves so fast, and many goats are dead or dying by the time help arrives. For goats that are still alive, a vet may use a combination of approaches. Clostridium perfringens type C and D antitoxin, where it can be obtained, neutralises toxin already in the blood; availability in Kenya can be limited. Antibiotics such as penicillins may be given to reduce the number of bacteria in the gut. Anti-inflammatory and pain-relieving drugs such as flunixin or meloxicam help with pain and shock. Fluids by drip or by mouth, once the goat can swallow safely, are used to correct dehydration. The vet may also give thiamine (vitamin B1) in case the problem is actually polioencephalomalacia, and may give medicines to settle the gut. Goats with severe nervous signs usually have a poor chance even with treatment. The vet will also advise on the rest of the herd: cutting back feed, and vaccinating all goats, sometimes together with antitoxin, to protect them while vaccine immunity builds over the following weeks. Antibiotics must only be used on a vet's prescription and given exactly as directed, because misuse breeds resistant bacteria (antimicrobial resistance) that make future infections harder to treat in animals and people. Every drug has a milk and meat withdrawal period, the time you must wait before selling or using milk or slaughtering the goat; your vet will tell you how long, and you must keep to it.
prevention: Vaccinate every goat with a clostridial vaccine that covers Clostridium perfringens type D (often sold as 'CD&T' or multi-strain clostridial vaccines at agrovets), following the label and your vet's advice.

Give the first vaccination course with a booster a few weeks later, then keep up regular boosters; protection fades faster in goats than in sheep, so many vets advise boosting goats more often than once a year, especially in heavily fed herds.
Vaccinate pregnant does a few weeks before kidding so their colostrum protects newborn kids, and make sure every kid drinks colostrum within the first hours of life.
Vaccinate kids on the schedule your vet recommends, starting earlier if the dam was not vaccinated, and vaccinate new goats on arrival before they join the herd.
Store vaccine in a fridge, not the freezer, carry it in a cool box, use clean needles and do not use expired or warm vaccine, because damaged vaccine gives no protection.
Change feed slowly, over about two weeks, whenever you introduce grain, dairy meal, new pasture or a new ration, starting with small amounts and increasing gradually.
Always give enough roughage such as hay, Napier grass or crop residues before concentrates, feed concentrates in small, regular meals, and provide enough trough space so bossy goats cannot gorge.
Lock feed stores securely and fence maize and other grain fields so goats cannot break in and overeat.
When the rains bring lush pasture, give hay before turning goats out and limit grazing time for the first days.
Feed milk and milk replacer to kids in regular, moderate meals, keep a steady deworming and tick-control programme, and keep pens clean and dry to reduce bacterial build-up.
detail.impact: Enterotoxaemia hits Kenyan goat farmers hard because it kills the most valuable animals: the fastest-growing kids being raised for sale, breeding or dairy. Losing several kids in a few days can wipe out a season's profit, especially for smallholders with small herds who rely on goat sales for school fees or emergencies. Dairy goat farmers lose milk income when adult does develop the longer-lasting form, with repeated diarrhoea, weight loss and falling yield. There are also costs for vet visits, emergency vaccination of the herd, possible drug withdrawal periods for milk and meat, and lost time. Group projects and farmers investing in improved dairy breeds and concentrate feeding can lose expensive animals. Compared with these losses, routine vaccination and careful feeding cost very little.
detail.humanHealth: Clostridium perfringens type D enterotoxaemia is not considered a disease that spreads from goats to people. However, do not eat or sell meat from goats that died suddenly or were very sick: sudden death can also be caused by anthrax, which is deadly to people, and meat from sick or dead animals is unsafe and spoils quickly. Wear gloves when handling dead or sick animals and wash hands well with soap. If a goat has been treated with antibiotics or other drugs, respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods your vet gives you so that drug residues do not reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: The outlook for a goat already showing nervous signs such as convulsions, paddling or coma is poor, and many die within hours even with treatment. Goats caught early, with mild diarrhoea or belly pain and no nervous signs, have a better chance if a vet treats them quickly and feeding is corrected. Adult goats with the longer-lasting form often recover with treatment and diet change, though they may lose condition for some time. The outlook for the rest of the herd is good: once feed is corrected and goats are vaccinated, outbreaks usually stop, although protection from vaccine takes some time to build. Herds kept on regular vaccination and steady feeding rarely see the disease again.

faqs.q: Why does it always kill my best, fattest kids?
faqs.a: Because the disease is driven by feed. The strongest, greediest kids drink the most milk or eat the most grain and concentrate, so more undigested starch reaches their intestines. That gives the bacteria more food to multiply and make toxin. Weak or poorly fed kids eat less and are less likely to be affected. So when your best kids die suddenly, enterotoxaemia should be high on your list.

faqs.q: I vaccinated my goats. Why did one still die?
faqs.a: Several things can cause this. Protection in goats fades faster than in sheep, so if boosters were missed or given too long ago, immunity may have worn off. Kids need a first course with a booster, and one dose alone may not protect them. Vaccine that got warm or frozen, or was expired, may not work. Very heavy grain feeding can also overwhelm partial immunity. Ask your vet to check your vaccination programme, confirm the cause of death, and help you plan regular boosters.

faqs.q: Is enterotoxaemia contagious? Should I separate the rest of the herd?
faqs.a: It does not spread from goat to goat like a cough. The bacteria are already in every goat's gut and in the soil. Goats get sick when the same feeding problem affects them all. That is why the whole herd needs feed changes and often vaccination after a death. Isolating sick goats is still sensible, so they rest quietly and you can watch them, and so you can rule out other diseases with your vet.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell the meat of a goat that died of this?
faqs.a: No. Meat from a goat that died suddenly or was very sick is not safe or fit to eat. You cannot be sure without a vet that it was not anthrax, which can kill people. Meat from such animals also spoils quickly. If the goat was treated with drugs, there may be residues in the meat. Let the vet examine the carcass, then bury it deeply or dispose of it as the vet advises.

faqs.q: Can adult goats get enterotoxaemia, or only kids?
faqs.a: Adults can get it too, especially dairy does on heavy concentrate feeding or goats that break into grain. In adults it often takes a longer form, with repeated diarrhoea, weight loss, poor appetite and falling milk, rather than sudden death. Vaccinating adults and feeding them steadily protects them and also protects their kids through colostrum.

faqs.q: How should I start feeding dairy meal or grain without causing this?
faqs.a: Make sure the goats are vaccinated first. Then start with a very small amount and increase it slowly over about two weeks. Always give hay or other roughage before concentrates. Split the daily amount into two or more small meals instead of one big one, and give enough trough space so each goat gets its share. Never let goats have free access to grain, and do not suddenly double the ration. Ask your vet or extension officer how much concentrate suits your goats.

products.role: Once a vet has seen the goat and it is standing and swallowing normally, this oral rehydration solution can help replace fluid and salts lost through diarrhoea during recovery. It does not neutralise the toxin or treat the infection, and must never be given to a goat that is convulsing or lying flat.

Can be used as digestive and liver support for recovering goats and the rest of the herd while feed is being brought back to a steady, roughage-based diet after an outbreak. It supports recovery alongside vet treatment, vaccination and careful feeding; it does not prevent or cure enterotoxaemia.

card.headline: Coughing goat with runny nose, fast breathing
card.look: The goat stands apart with drooping ears, breathes fast with its flanks heaving, coughs, and has thick white or yellow discharge from the nose. It may refuse feed and feel hot.
card.action: Move sick goats to a dry, draught-free, well-aired pen, give clean water, and call your vet the same day.

aka: Homa ya mapafu (Swahili, general term for lung fever)
detail.summary: Pneumonia in goats is an infection and swelling of the lungs. It is very often caused by bacteria called Mannheimia haemolytica and Pasteurella multocida, which normally live harmlessly in the nose and throat. They invade the lungs after the goat is stressed by transport, cold and wet weather, crowding, poor ventilation or another infection. It is one of the most common causes of illness and death in goats in East Africa, especially in kids. Early treatment by a vet usually works well, but delay can be fatal.
detail.cause: The main bacteria are Mannheimia haemolytica and Pasteurella multocida, and sometimes a related germ called Bibersteinia trehalosi. Most healthy goats carry small numbers of these bacteria in the nose and tonsils without getting sick. When a goat is stressed, its natural defences in the airways weaken. Stress can come from a long lorry journey to market, sudden cold rain, chilly nights, weaning, overcrowding, dusty feed, or ammonia fumes from dirty bedding. A viral infection (such as PPR or other respiratory viruses) or lungworms can damage the lining of the airways first and open the way. The bacteria then multiply quickly and move down into the lungs. Mannheimia produces a toxin (a poison) that kills the white blood cells meant to fight infection. This causes the lung tissue to swell, fill with fluid and pus, and become firm and dark red, so the goat cannot take in enough oxygen. Sometimes a sticky layer called fibrin forms on the lung surface and sticks the lung to the chest wall. In young kids the bacteria can also enter the blood (septicaemia, meaning blood poisoning) and cause sudden death before obvious lung signs appear.
spread: Stress is the main trigger: transport, mixing goats from different sources, market visits, weaning, castration, dehorning and sudden changes in feed all weaken the goat's defences.
Cold, wet and windy weather, especially at the start of the long and short rains and on cold highland nights, often comes just before outbreaks.
Poorly ventilated, damp or overcrowded houses let germs build up in the air and allow ammonia from urine and dung to irritate the airways.
Sick goats cough and sneeze bacteria into the air and onto feed troughs and water, so close contact in a shared pen spreads infection to the others.
Newly bought goats that look healthy may carry the bacteria and shed them after the stress of the journey.
Other diseases such as PPR, lungworm, heavy worm burdens, malnutrition and mineral or vitamin shortages lower resistance and make pneumonia more likely.
Dust from dry hay, dusty kraals in the dry season and smoke from cooking fires near housing can irritate the lungs and set the stage for infection.
detail.atRisk: Kids, especially from birth to around six months and at weaning, are most at risk and are most likely to die suddenly. Goats that have just been transported, bought at market or mixed into a new herd are at high risk in the first two to three weeks. Thin, wormy or poorly fed goats, does around kidding, and goats recovering from another illness are also vulnerable. Outbreaks are common during the onset of the long and short rains, during cold spells in highland areas such as Nyandarua, Nyeri, Kericho and the Mt Kenya region, and in damp seasons when animals are housed. Dairy goats kept zero-grazed in closed, poorly aired sheds can suffer when bedding is wet and ammonia builds up. In pastoral systems, long treks, crowded night bomas and trucking to livestock markets are typical triggers. All breeds can be affected, including Small East African, Galla, Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine and their crosses, though exotic dairy breeds kept in cold, damp housing may suffer more.

early: The goat is dull, stands apart from the herd, with ears drooping and head held low.
Appetite drops; the goat eats less, stops chewing the cud, and may drink less.
Fever: the goat feels hot and a thermometer in the rectum often reads above about 40°C (normal for a goat is roughly 38.5–39.7°C).
Clear nasal discharge that soon becomes thick, white, yellow or green.
Breathing is faster and shallower than normal, even when the goat is resting in the shade.
An occasional moist cough, often heard when the goats are moved or first let out in the morning.
Watery eyes and a slightly reduced milk yield in milking does.
advanced: Laboured breathing with the flanks heaving, mouth open, and sometimes a grunt with each breath.
The goat stands with neck stretched forward and elbows turned out to ease breathing, or lies down and refuses to rise.
Frequent, deep or painful cough, with crusted pus around the nostrils.
Marked weight loss, sunken eyes and dry skin from dehydration because the goat has stopped eating and drinking.
Pale or bluish gums and tongue in severe cases, showing lack of oxygen.
Temperature may fall below normal just before death, which is a very bad sign.
Sudden death of kids or young goats, sometimes with frothy fluid at the nose, before clear signs were seen.
Goats that survive without proper treatment may become chronic poor-doers with a lasting cough and stunted growth.

lookalikes.name: Contagious caprine pleuropneumonia (CCPP)
lookalikes.howToTell: CCPP is caused by Mycoplasma capricolum subsp. capripneumoniae and is a notifiable disease in Kenya, so it must be reported. It spreads very fast through the whole herd, often with many goats sick within days and very high deaths in all ages. Goats show very high fever, severe painful breathing, grunting and standing with neck stretched out. At post-mortem one lung is often stuck to the ribs with thick straw-coloured fluid in the chest. Pasteurella pneumonia usually affects fewer goats, often after a clear stress, and responds better to treatment. Only a lab test can tell them apart for certain, so report any fast-spreading pneumonia to the County Veterinary Officer.

lookalikes.name: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR, goat plague)
lookalikes.howToTell: PPR is a notifiable viral disease. As well as fever, cough and nasal discharge, goats get sores and dead skin on the gums, lips and tongue, bad-smelling breath, sticky eye discharge and severe watery diarrhoea. Pasteurella often follows PPR as a secondary infection, so a goat may have both. Antibiotics do not cure the PPR virus. Report suspected PPR immediately.

lookalikes.name: Lungworm infection
lookalikes.howToTell: Lungworms cause a slow, persistent dry cough, gradual weight loss and mild breathing difficulty, often in goats grazing wet pastures. There is usually little or no fever and goats keep eating. The vet can find larvae in a dung sample. Heavy lungworm burdens can make goats more likely to get bacterial pneumonia.

lookalikes.name: Nasal bots (Oestrus ovis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Fly larvae living in the nose cause sneezing, head shaking, rubbing the nose on the ground and a thick nasal discharge, sometimes with blood. Goats usually have no fever, breathe normally and keep eating. Signs are often worse in the hot, fly season.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will first look at the whole herd, ask about recent transport, purchases, weather and vaccinations, and then examine sick goats. They take the rectal temperature, count the breathing rate, and listen to the chest with a stethoscope for crackles, wheezes or silent areas where the lung is solid. Because CCPP and PPR can look similar and are notifiable, the vet may take nasal swabs, blood samples or fluid from the chest and send them to a laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a regional veterinary lab for culture (growing the germ) or PCR (a DNA test). A post-mortem on a goat that has died is one of the most useful tools: pasteurellosis typically shows firm, dark red areas in the lower front parts of the lungs, sometimes with a fibrin coating, while CCPP often shows one-sided lung damage with a lot of straw-coloured fluid. Samples from the lung can confirm which germ is involved and which antibiotics will work. To help the vet, write down how many goats are sick and dead, when signs began, their ages, recent movements or purchases, vaccines and dewormers given, and any drugs already used. If a goat dies, keep the carcass in a cool, shaded place covered from dogs and flies, and call the vet quickly so samples are fresh.
firstSteps: Separate coughing, feverish or fast-breathing goats into a dry, clean pen away from the rest of the herd to reduce spread.
Make the pen draught-free but well aired: block cold wind and rain, but keep openings high up so fresh air moves and ammonia escapes.
Provide dry, clean bedding and remove wet, dirty bedding that gives off ammonia fumes.
Give plenty of clean, fresh water that is not ice cold, and offer soft, tasty feed such as fresh leaves, good hay or a little dairy meal to encourage eating.
Avoid moving, trucking, chasing or handling sick goats more than necessary, as stress and exertion worsen breathing.
Take and record rectal temperatures of sick goats and any in-contact goats if you have a thermometer, and note breathing rate, appetite and number affected.
Stop buying in, selling or moving goats until the vet has seen the herd, especially if several goats fell sick quickly, because CCPP or PPR must be ruled out.
Call your vet or the County Veterinary Officer the same day; do not give antibiotics or other drugs left over from before without the vet's advice, and wash your hands after handling sick goats.
detail.vetTreatment: Pasteurella pneumonia is a bacterial infection, so a vet will usually prescribe an antibiotic. Commonly used options in goats include oxytetracycline, penicillin-based products (sometimes combined with streptomycin), florfenicol, and in some cases macrolides such as tulathromycin or tilmicosin, or ceftiofur. Note that tilmicosin can be dangerous if given wrongly and must only be used under strict vet direction. The vet chooses the drug, route and length of treatment based on the goat, the local resistance pattern and, where possible, lab results. Treatment must be prescribed by a vet; do not guess doses or stop the course early, because under-treatment and misuse of antibiotics breeds resistant bacteria (antimicrobial resistance) that make future outbreaks harder to control. The vet may also give an anti-inflammatory painkiller, such as meloxicam or flunixin, to bring down fever and lung swelling so the goat breathes and eats more easily. Severely affected goats may need fluids and supportive care. In an outbreak, the vet may advise treating in-contact goats that are already running a fever. Goats that are treated early, while still eating, often improve within one to three days, but a few may need a second course or a change of drug. Every antibiotic and anti-inflammatory has a withdrawal period, the time you must wait after the last treatment before milk or meat can be used for people. Ask the vet for the exact withdrawal times, write them down, mark treated goats, and do not sell or drink their milk or slaughter them before the time is up. If PPR or CCPP is involved, antibiotics may help with secondary bacteria, but they do not cure the PPR virus, and CCPP control is directed by the veterinary authorities.
prevention: Reduce transport stress: move goats in the cooler part of the day, avoid overcrowding vehicles, give water and rest on long journeys, and do not transport sick or weak goats.
Quarantine newly bought goats for at least two to three weeks in a separate pen, watching for cough, fever and discharge before mixing them with your herd.
Build or improve housing so it is dry, raised or well drained, protected from cold wind and rain, but with good airflow near the roof to remove ammonia and damp air.
Clean out wet bedding and dung regularly, avoid overcrowding, and keep kids in a warm, dry, draught-free area, especially during cold nights and the rainy seasons.
Feed well: good forage, clean water, and suitable minerals and vitamins keep the immune system strong; make sure newborn kids get colostrum (first milk) within the first hours of life.

Vaccinate against PPR and CCPP as advised by your County Veterinary Officer, because these diseases cause severe lung problems and pave the way for Pasteurella; ask your vet whether a Pasteurella or Mannheimia vaccine is available and suitable for your area, as availability in Kenya varies.
Control worms, lungworms and ticks with a regular programme planned with your vet or agrovet, because parasite-weakened goats are more likely to develop pneumonia.
Plan stressful jobs such as weaning, castration and dehorning so they do not happen together or during cold, wet weather or just after transport.
detail.impact: Pneumonia is one of the leading causes of kid deaths on Kenyan goat farms, and each lost kid is a lost future sale, breeding doe or source of milk. Sick goats stop eating and lose condition quickly, so meat goats take longer to reach market weight and fetch lower prices. Dairy goats can drop sharply in milk yield, and milk must be discarded during treatment withdrawal periods, cutting daily income. Treatment costs include the vet visit, antibiotics and anti-inflammatories, and labour for nursing sick animals. Goats that recover poorly may stay stunted with a chronic cough and become unprofitable. Traders and pastoralists who buy, truck and resell goats can lose several animals after a single stressful journey. An outbreak also raises the worry that CCPP or PPR may be present, which can lead to movement restrictions and lost market access until the vet rules these out.
detail.humanHealth: Goat pneumonia caused by Mannheimia and Pasteurella is not considered a significant risk to people through normal contact. Pasteurella multocida can occasionally infect people through animal bites or scratches, and people with weak immune systems should take extra care. Wear gloves or wash hands well with soap after handling sick goats, nasal discharge or carcasses. The bigger human-health concern is drug residues: milk and meat from goats treated with antibiotics or anti-inflammatories must not be used until the withdrawal period given by the vet has passed, as residues can cause allergic reactions and help create antibiotic-resistant bacteria that affect people.
detail.outlook: With early diagnosis and the right antibiotic from a vet, most goats with Pasteurella pneumonia recover, often showing improvement within a few days. The outlook is much poorer when treatment is delayed, when the goat has stopped eating and drinking, when the temperature has dropped below normal, or when breathing is very laboured. Young kids can die very quickly, sometimes before signs are noticed. Goats with another disease at the same time, such as PPR, CCPP, heavy worms or poor nutrition, are less likely to recover well. Some survivors keep permanent lung damage, with a chronic cough, poor growth and a higher chance of getting pneumonia again. Good nursing, a dry warm pen and fixing the stress that triggered the outbreak make a real difference to recovery.

faqs.q: How do I know if it is ordinary pneumonia or CCPP?
faqs.a: You cannot be fully sure by looking. CCPP usually spreads very fast through the herd, makes many goats of all ages very sick within days, and kills many of them, with severe grunting and painful breathing. Ordinary Pasteurella pneumonia usually follows a clear stress such as transport or cold rain and affects fewer goats. Because CCPP is notifiable and very damaging, report any outbreak where several goats fall sick quickly to your County Veterinary Officer so samples can be tested.

faqs.q: Can I just buy an antibiotic at the agrovet and inject my goats?
faqs.a: It is best not to. Treatment must be prescribed by a vet, who will choose the right drug, confirm it is not CCPP or PPR, and tell you the correct course and withdrawal period. Wrong drugs, wrong doses or stopping too early waste money, can fail to save the goat, and build up antibiotic resistance on your farm. Call the vet early; a quick visit is often cheaper than losing goats.

faqs.q: Why do my goats get sick after I bring them from the market?
faqs.a: The journey, crowding, lack of water, mixing with strange goats and change of feed all stress the animals. Stress weakens the natural defences in the airways, so the Pasteurella bacteria they already carry can multiply and invade the lungs. This is why it is sometimes called shipping fever. Transport gently, give water and rest, and keep new goats in quarantine for two to three weeks.

faqs.q: Should I close the goat house completely to keep them warm?
faqs.a: No. Goats need protection from cold wind and rain, but a fully closed house traps damp air, germs and ammonia from urine, which damages the lungs. Close the lower walls on the windy side and keep openings high up near the roof so stale air can escape. Keep bedding dry and change it often.

faqs.q: Can a goat that recovered from pneumonia get it again?
faqs.a: Yes. Recovery does not give strong lasting protection, and goats with lung damage from a previous attack may be more likely to get sick again. Reducing stress, good housing, good feeding, parasite control and vaccinating against PPR and CCPP help lower the chance of repeat attacks.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk from a goat that has pneumonia?
faqs.a: The pneumonia germ itself is not a major risk through milk, but sick goats often give poor milk and may be on drugs. If the goat has been treated with antibiotics or anti-inflammatories, throw away the milk until the withdrawal period given by your vet has passed. Always boil goat milk before drinking.

products.role: Oral rehydration support for goats that are drinking and eating less because of fever and laboured breathing; it helps replace lost fluids and electrolytes during recovery, alongside vet-prescribed treatment and good nursing, and is not a cure for the infection.

A plant-extract supplement labelled to relieve respiratory problems and stress; it can be used as supportive care to help goats cope during recovery and in stressful periods such as after transport, but only alongside vet treatment, vaccination and improved housing, never as a replacement for antibiotics when the vet prescribes them.
