card.headline: Crusty, wart-like scabs on the lips
card.look: Thick brown or grey crusts form around the mouth, lips and nostrils, sometimes on the teats or feet. Affected kids drool, eat slowly and struggle to suckle.
card.action: Separate affected goats and wear gloves when you handle them, because orf spreads to people.

detail.summary: Orf is a very contagious viral skin disease of goats and sheep. It causes painful, crusty, wart-like scabs, mainly on the lips, nostrils, gums, teats and sometimes the feet. Most goats recover on their own in about three to four weeks. It still matters because young kids can starve when they cannot suckle, does with sore teats may refuse their kids or get mastitis, and the virus easily infects the hands of the people who handle the goats.
detail.cause: Orf is caused by the orf virus. It belongs to a group called parapoxviruses, which are distant relatives of the poxviruses. The virus enters through small breaks in the skin, such as scratches from thorny browse like acacia, rough dry feed, or teeth coming through in young kids. It then multiplies in the outer layer of the skin. The skin first turns red. Small raised bumps called papules appear, then blisters, then pus-filled spots called pustules. These finally dry into thick, crusty scabs that can heap up and look like warts or cauliflower. The sores are painful, so goats do not want to eat or suckle. The damaged skin is also an easy entry point for bacteria and for fly larvae (maggots). That is where many of the serious problems come from. The virus itself rarely kills. The scabs that fall off are full of virus, and it can survive in dry scab material on the ground, in pens and on feeding equipment for many months. This is why orf often returns to the same farm year after year.
spread: Direct contact between an infected goat and a healthy one, especially when goats nuzzle, share feed or crowd at troughs.
Kids with sore mouths pass the virus to their mothers' teats when suckling, and does with infected udders pass it to other kids.
Scabs that drop off infected goats contaminate bedding, pens, feed troughs, water points and pasture, where the virus can survive for months.
Thorny browse, thistles, rough hay and stubble scratch the lips and give the virus a way into the skin.
Bringing in new goats from markets or other farms that are carrying the virus, even if their scabs have nearly healed.
Shared equipment, feeding bottles, drenching guns, ear-tagging tools and the hands or clothes of people moving between goats.
detail.atRisk: Kids and young goats from a few weeks to about six months old are most often affected, and they suffer the most. Goats that have never met the virus, such as a newly bought herd, can be affected at any age. Does nursing infected kids often develop sores on the teats and udder. Outbreaks are common where many goats are crowded together. This includes zero-grazing units, holding pens at markets, and the dry season, when goats in pastoral areas browse heavily on thorny bush and gather at watering points. Weak, thin or poorly fed goats, and those carrying heavy worm burdens, may have more severe and longer-lasting sores. All breeds can be affected, including Small East African, Galla, Toggenburg, Saanen and their crosses. Kienyeji herds kept with sheep can pass the virus between the two species.

early: Red, slightly swollen patches at the corners of the mouth, on the lips or around the nostrils.
Small raised bumps or blisters that soon fill with pus and burst.
A kid that sniffs at the teat or feed but pulls away, eats slowly or chews carefully.
Drooling or wet lips, and the goat may rub its mouth on objects.
In does, red spots or small blisters on the teats, and the doe kicking or walking away when the kid tries to suckle.
Occasionally, sores on the skin just above the hooves, causing slight lameness.
advanced: Thick, brown-grey, crusty scabs that heap up like warts or cauliflower around the lips, nose and sometimes eyelids or ears.
Scabs that crack and bleed slightly when the goat eats, with a bad smell if bacteria have infected them.
Kids that lose weight, look hollow-sided and weak because they cannot suckle or eat properly.
Hard, hot, swollen udder halves or abnormal milk in does, which suggests mastitis (udder infection) on top of orf.
Maggots in the sores during warm, wet weather when flies are active.
Rarely, sores spreading inside the mouth, onto the gums and tongue, or down the throat. In weak kids this can lead to pneumonia or death.

lookalikes.name: Goat pox (sheep and goat pox)
lookalikes.howToTell: Goat pox causes fever, dullness and raised lumps spread over the whole body, especially where hair is thin. Orf sores stay mainly on the lips, nose, teats and feet, and the goat is usually bright apart from being sore. Goat pox is notifiable, so call the vet urgently if you see body-wide lumps with fever.

lookalikes.name: Peste des petits ruminants (PPR, goat plague)
lookalikes.howToTell: PPR causes high fever, thick discharge from the eyes and nose, raw ulcers inside the mouth, severe diarrhoea and often rapid deaths across the herd. Orf causes crusty scabs on the outside of the lips with little fever, and deaths are uncommon. PPR is notifiable and must be reported immediately.

lookalikes.name: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)
lookalikes.howToTell: FMD causes blisters inside the mouth and between the claws, sudden lameness, fever and drooling, and it often affects cattle on the same farm too. Orf produces heaped, crusty scabs rather than burst blisters and raw patches, and cattle are not affected. FMD is notifiable.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (streptothricosis) or bacterial skin infection
lookalikes.howToTell: Dermatophilosis gives 'paintbrush' tufts of matted hair with scabs over the back and body, often after long rains. Orf concentrates on the mouth and teats. A vet may need samples to tell them apart, and the two can occur together.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually recognises orf from the typical crusty sores on the lips and teats of young goats, together with how the outbreak has spread through the herd. The vet will check the mouth, feet, udder and whole body. This rules out more serious notifiable diseases such as goat pox, PPR and FMD, which can look similar in the early stages. The vet will also check for fever. If there is doubt, the vet can send scabs or swabs to a laboratory, such as a county or regional veterinary laboratory, for virus testing. To help the vet, note when the first goat showed signs and how many goats are affected. Record their ages, whether any new goats were recently brought in, and whether any have died. Keep affected goats penned so they can be examined easily, and take clear photos of the sores if the vet will be some time arriving.
firstSteps: Separate goats with sores, and their nursing kids, from the rest of the herd. Keep them in their own pen with their own feed and water containers.
Wear gloves, or at least wash your hands well with soap and water, every time you touch an affected goat. Cover any cuts on your hands, because people catch orf easily.
Do not pick or scrape off the scabs. This is painful, delays healing and spreads virus into the environment.
Check that every kid is actually getting milk. If a kid cannot suckle, call the vet or extension officer for advice on bottle feeding or other ways to feed it.
Offer soft, palatable feed such as fresh young grass, soaked or softened feed, and clean water within easy reach. Remove thorny browse and rough, stalky hay for now.
Check the udders of nursing does daily. Look for hardness, heat, swelling or abnormal milk, and report any changes to the vet, as mastitis needs prompt treatment.
Watch the sores for maggots or a bad smell, especially in warm, wet weather, and tell the vet at once if you see them.
Stop selling or moving affected goats, and do not bring new goats in, until the outbreak has settled. Write down which goats are affected and when.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no drug that kills the orf virus. Antibiotics do not cure orf itself, and most uncomplicated cases heal on their own within about three to four weeks. The vet's job is to confirm it is orf and not a notifiable disease, then to prevent and treat complications. The vet may advise gently cleaning the sores with a mild antiseptic. They may prescribe an antibiotic spray or ointment if the sores are infected with bacteria, and a fly repellent or wound dressing to prevent maggots. Injectable antibiotics are only used when there is serious bacterial infection, such as badly infected sores, mastitis or pneumonia. Using antibiotics without a real need speeds up antimicrobial resistance, which means the drugs stop working when you truly need them. Any antibiotic or other drug must be prescribed by a vet. You must also observe the milk and meat withdrawal period stated for that product, which is the time you must wait before milk or meat from the treated goat can be used or sold. The vet may also advise on feeding weak kids, pain relief, and treating does with mastitis. Expect the scabs to dry and drop off over a few weeks. The skin underneath usually heals without lasting scars.
prevention: Check every new goat carefully before buying, and keep new arrivals apart for at least three to four weeks before mixing them with your herd.
Clean and disinfect pens, feed troughs and equipment after an outbreak. Remove and burn or bury bedding and scabs, because the virus survives for a long time in dry scab material.
Reduce sharp, thorny browse and rough feed for young kids where possible, and avoid overcrowding at feeding and watering points, to limit scratches around the mouth.
Keep goats in good body condition with good nutrition, minerals and regular deworming, so their skin and immune system are strong and sores heal faster.

Ask your vet about orf vaccination. Live vaccines exist, but availability in Kenya varies. The vaccine contains live virus that can infect people and bring orf onto a clean farm, so it is normally only used on farms that already have the disease, under veterinary advice.
Handle goats with gloves during outbreaks and wash hands and equipment between groups. This protects both people and the rest of the herd.
Goats that recover usually have good protection for a while. Even so, keep a careful eye on each new crop of kids, because the virus often reappears on the same farm.
detail.impact: Orf rarely kills adult goats, but it can cost a Kenyan farmer real money. Kids that cannot suckle or eat lose weight, grow slowly and sometimes die, especially when the sores become infected or maggots get in. Does with sore teats may refuse their kids, give less milk, or develop mastitis that can permanently damage an udder half. That hurts dairy goat keepers who depend on daily milk sales. Goats with visible scabs fetch lower prices or are turned away at markets. Sales may need to be delayed until they heal, and buyers may avoid a farm known to have orf. There is also the cost of vet visits, any treatment needed for complications, and time spent hand-feeding kids. Family members who catch orf on their hands may lose working days.
detail.humanHealth: Orf is a zoonosis, meaning it can spread from goats to people. People usually catch it on the hands or fingers through cuts or scratches while handling infected goats, scabs, feeding bottles or contaminated equipment. It may also spread from the live vaccine. In people it causes one or a few firm, painful lumps that can blister and crust. The lump may be accompanied by mild fever or swollen glands in the armpit. It usually heals by itself over several weeks. People with weak immune systems, such as those on cancer treatment or with poorly controlled HIV, can have larger, slower-healing sores. To protect yourself, wear gloves when handling affected goats or their scabs, and cover any cuts. Wash your hands well with soap afterwards, and keep children from touching sick kids. Anyone who develops a sore on the hand after handling goats should see a health worker and mention contact with goats with orf. Spread from person to person is very rare.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for most goats. Uncomplicated sores normally dry and fall off within about three to four weeks, and the skin heals well. Recovery is slower, and the risk of death higher, in very young or weak kids that cannot feed. It is also worse when sores become infected with bacteria or maggots, when the sores spread inside the mouth or throat, and when does develop mastitis. Good nursing makes a big difference, especially making sure kids get milk, offering soft feed and watching closely for complications. Recovered goats usually have useful immunity for a period, though reinfection can occur and is generally milder.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics cure orf?
faqs.a: No. Orf is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. Most goats heal on their own in a few weeks. A vet may prescribe antibiotics only if bacteria have infected the sores or the udder, or if a kid develops pneumonia. Using antibiotics when they are not needed wastes money and helps create resistant bacteria.

faqs.q: Can I catch orf from my goats?
faqs.a: Yes. Orf commonly infects the hands of people who handle sick goats, bottle-feed kids or touch scabs. It causes a painful lump that usually heals in several weeks. Wear gloves, cover cuts and wash your hands with soap. See a health worker if you develop a sore, and tell them you have been handling goats with orf.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drink milk or eat meat from goats with orf?
faqs.a: Orf is mainly spread through skin contact, not through food. Still, milk from does with infected teats or mastitis should not be used, because it may be poor quality or contaminated. Always boil milk before use. If any goat has been treated with drugs, you must follow the withdrawal period your vet gives before using its milk or meat. Handle carcasses and skins with gloves.

faqs.q: Why does orf keep coming back on my farm every year?
faqs.a: The virus survives for months in scabs that fall onto bedding, soil and feeding areas. Each new group of kids that has never met the virus can then become infected. Thorough cleaning after an outbreak helps. So does removing old bedding, cutting down sharp browse for young kids, and quarantining new goats. Vaccination may be worth discussing with your vet on farms where orf returns regularly.

faqs.q: Should I scrape off the scabs or apply home remedies like used engine oil?
faqs.a: Do not scrape the scabs. This is painful, causes bleeding, slows healing and spreads the virus. Avoid engine oil, paraffin, battery acid or other harsh home remedies, which damage the skin and can poison the goat. Ask your vet whether a mild antiseptic or fly-repellent dressing is suitable.

faqs.q: Can goats with orf be sold or mixed with other goats?
faqs.a: It is best not to. Goats with scabs are infectious and will spread orf to other farms, and buyers often reject them. Keep affected goats at home and separate until the scabs have completely dropped off and the skin has healed. Then clean the pen before using it for other animals.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help support fluid and energy intake in kids and goats that are drinking or suckling poorly because of painful mouth sores, especially in hot weather. It is supportive care only, used alongside the vet's advice and proper milk feeding. It does not treat the orf virus.

Vitamins A, D3 and E support normal skin health and general resilience. Your vet or agrovet may advise them for thin or poorly fed goats during recovery, particularly in the dry season when green feed is scarce. This is a nutritional aid alongside good feeding and vet care, not a cure for orf.

card.headline: Limping goat grazing on its knees
card.look: One or more goats limp, hold up a foot or kneel on their front legs to graze. Between the claws the skin is red, wet and smells rotten, and the hoof horn may be loose.
card.action: Separate lame goats onto dry, clean ground, look at every foot, and call your vet or animal health officer to confirm foot rot and plan treatment for the whole herd.

detail.summary: Foot rot is a contagious bacterial infection of the skin between the claws and the hoof of goats and sheep. It causes painful lameness, a strong rotten smell and, in bad cases, separation of the hoof horn from the foot. It spreads quickly through a herd in wet, muddy conditions, especially during the long and short rains. It rarely kills, but it causes weight loss, less milk, poor kid growth and a lot of work, so early action and good prevention pay off.
detail.cause: Foot rot is caused mainly by a bacterium called Dichelobacter nodosus. It cannot live long in soil, but it survives for a long time inside the feet of infected or carrier goats. It works together with a second bacterium, Fusobacterium necrophorum, which lives naturally in dung and soil. When the skin between the claws stays wet and soft from mud, dung or wet grass, it gets damaged and these bacteria get in. First the skin becomes red, moist and inflamed; this early stage is often called scald (interdigital dermatitis, meaning inflammation of the skin between the toes). Dichelobacter nodosus produces enzymes that break down the horn and the tissue that holds it to the foot. The infection then 'under-runs' the hoof, meaning it spreads underneath the horn of the sole and heel so the horn separates and becomes loose. The dead tissue gives off the typical foul smell. Some strains are mild (benign) and only cause scald; others are virulent and cause severe under-running. In goats, under-running is often less extensive than in sheep, but the lameness and pain can still be serious.
spread: Infected goats shed the bacteria from their feet onto pasture, paths, pens and bedding, and healthy goats pick it up when they walk on the same ground.
Wet, warm conditions are the main trigger: muddy yards, soaked bedding, wet grass during the rains and areas around water troughs and gates keep feet soft and easy to damage.
Buying or borrowing goats from markets or other farms is the most common way the disease enters a clean herd, because carrier animals can look normal while carrying bacteria in their feet.
Sharing grazing, communal watering points, trucks or holding pens with other herds spreads the bacteria between farms.
Small injuries from stones, thorns, stubble and long overgrown hooves give the bacteria an entry point.
The bacteria do not survive long on pasture once dry or without goats, but they persist in the feet of untreated or chronically infected animals, which keep re-infecting the herd.
detail.atRisk: All ages can get foot rot, but adult goats and those kept in groups are most often affected. Dairy goats such as Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine and their crosses in the wetter highlands (for example Meru, Nyeri, Kiambu, Murang'a and the Rift Valley) are at high risk because of high rainfall and confinement. Zero-grazed goats in pens with wet, dirty floors and no raised slatted floor are especially vulnerable. Goats with overgrown, poorly trimmed hooves, goats in poor body condition and those recently bought from markets are more likely to get infected. Risk peaks during and just after the long and short rains. In drier pastoral areas, outbreaks usually appear around muddy watering points and night enclosures (bomas) during the wet season. Sheep grazed with goats can share and spread the same infection.

early: Mild limping on one or more feet, often worse after the goat has been lying down.
Goat stands with a foot lifted, shifts weight from foot to foot or is slow to follow the herd.
The skin between the two claws is red, swollen, moist and may have a thin greyish-white layer on it.
A slightly unpleasant smell when you lift and look closely at the foot.
Goat spends more time lying down and eats a little less than usual.
advanced: Marked lameness, with goats kneeling on their front knees to graze or walk, which can cause hairless, thickened or sore knees.
A strong, rotten, unmistakable smell from the feet.
The horn of the sole and heel becomes loose and separates from the foot; you can see grey, soft, smelly tissue underneath.
Several feet are often affected, and many goats in the herd become lame at the same time.
Weight loss, drop in milk yield, poor coat and reluctance to move to grazing or water.
Bucks may refuse to mount, and heavily pregnant does may struggle to walk and lie down for long periods.
In neglected cases the hoof becomes misshapen, and flies may lay eggs in the wounds, causing maggot infestation (fly strike).

lookalikes.name: Foot abscess (toe or heel abscess)
lookalikes.howToTell: An abscess usually affects one foot of one goat, comes on suddenly and causes very severe lameness. The foot is hot and swollen above the hoof and may burst and drain pus. Foot rot usually affects many goats and several feet, with a foul smell between the claws rather than a hot swelling.

lookalikes.name: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)
lookalikes.howToTell: FMD is a notifiable viral disease. Goats have fever, blisters or raw sores in the mouth, on the tongue and along the top of the hoof (coronary band), drooling and sudden lameness in many animals, often with cattle on the farm also affected. Foot rot has no mouth sores and no high fever. If you see mouth sores or drooling with lameness, report immediately to the County Veterinary Officer.

lookalikes.name: Overgrown hooves or laminitis
lookalikes.howToTell: Overgrown hooves look long, curled or folded under, and lameness improves after careful trimming; there is no rotten smell or wet red skin. Laminitis (inflammation inside the hoof, often after too much grain) makes goats walk stiffly on all feet, often after a feeding change, with hot hooves but healthy skin between the claws.

lookalikes.name: Scald (benign interdigital dermatitis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Scald is the mild early stage: red, moist skin between the claws with little smell and no loose horn. It can progress to full foot rot if virulent bacteria are present, so treat it seriously and ask your vet to check whether the horn is under-run.

detail.diagnosis: Foot rot is usually diagnosed on the farm. The vet or animal health officer will watch the goats walk, catch lame animals, clean and examine each foot, check for the typical smell, red moist skin between the claws and loose or under-run horn, and score how severe each foot is. They will rule out conditions like foot abscess, FMD and laminitis. In some cases they may take swabs from the feet for laboratory tests to identify Dichelobacter nodosus and whether the strain is mild or virulent, which helps plan an eradication programme, though this testing is not always easily available. To prepare, keep lame goats in a small dry pen, have a clean area and good light for examination, write down how many goats are lame, when it started, which goats were bought or moved recently, and what treatments or foot baths you have already used.
firstSteps: Separate lame goats into a clean, dry pen or paddock so they stop contaminating the ground where healthy goats walk.
Look at every goat's feet, not just the obviously lame ones, and write down which goats and which feet are affected.
Move the herd off muddy, wet areas; clean out soaked bedding and give dry bedding or a raised slatted floor where possible.
Gently clean mud and dung from affected feet with clean water so the vet can see the lesions; avoid deep cutting or digging into the foot yourself.
Make sure lame goats can easily reach water and feed, bringing fodder and water close to them if they are reluctant to walk.
Wear gloves when handling infected feet, and wash your hands, tools and boots afterwards to avoid carrying the infection to other goats or farms.
Stop selling, buying or mixing goats with other herds until the problem is under control.
Call your vet or animal health officer to confirm the diagnosis and agree a treatment plan for the whole herd.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment usually combines foot care, foot baths and, for more severe cases, antibiotics prescribed by a vet. Feet are cleaned and only loose, under-run horn is carefully removed; modern advice is to avoid heavy trimming that draws blood, because it slows healing and can spread infection. Infected goats are often stood in a foot bath, commonly containing zinc sulphate, copper sulphate or, less often, formalin, prepared at the strength and contact time your vet or the product label advises. After bathing, goats should stand on a clean, dry surface for some time before returning to pasture. Formalin and copper sulphate are hazardous to people and the environment and must be handled with care. For moderate to severe or under-running cases, a vet may prescribe an injectable antibiotic such as long-acting oxytetracycline or a penicillin-based product, sometimes alongside a topical antibiotic spray. Many goats improve within days of correct antibiotic treatment, but the vet will plan follow-up checks. All drugs and doses must be prescribed by a vet. Respect the milk and meat withdrawal periods on every product, meaning the time you must wait before selling or drinking milk or slaughtering. Use antibiotics responsibly and only as prescribed: misuse helps bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance), making future treatment harder. Goats that keep getting foot rot despite repeated treatment are often recommended for culling because they remain a source of infection. Vaccines against foot rot exist in some countries, but they are not widely available in Kenya and tend to give weaker protection in goats than in sheep; ask your vet about current options.
prevention: Check and trim hooves regularly, for example every few months and before the rains, so they do not grow long and trap mud and dung; use clean, sharp trimmers and disinfect them between goats.
Keep housing dry: use raised slatted floors in zero-grazing units, clean out dung often, replace wet bedding and fix leaking roofs and water troughs.
Avoid grazing goats on waterlogged or muddy land, especially in the long and short rains, and put gravel or murram around gates, troughs and feeding points.
Quarantine new goats for about three to four weeks, examine their feet, and foot-bathe or treat them as advised by your vet before mixing them with your herd.
Buy goats from trusted farms with no history of foot rot, and avoid shared trucks, markets and communal pens where possible.
Use a foot bath routinely during high-risk wet periods, following your vet's advice on product, strength and how often, and dispose of used solution safely away from water sources.
Cull goats that repeatedly develop foot rot, because chronic carriers keep re-infecting the herd.
Feed a balanced diet with good-quality forage and minerals to keep goats in good body condition, which supports healthy skin and hoof horn.
If you also keep sheep, apply the same foot care and biosecurity to them, since both species share the infection.
detail.impact: Foot rot hits goat income in several ways. Lame goats graze and browse less, so they lose weight and condition. Dairy does produce less milk, which hurts farmers selling goat milk in towns. Kids grow more slowly, and bucks with sore feet may refuse to serve, delaying kidding. Pregnant does that cannot move well may have problems around kidding. Affected goats fetch lower prices, and some buyers avoid herds known to have foot rot. There are costs for foot-bath chemicals, vet visits, antibiotics and the labour of catching, trimming and bathing goats again and again. Milk from treated goats must be thrown away during the withdrawal period. On farms where the disease becomes established, repeated outbreaks every rainy season and culling of chronic cases can seriously reduce profits.
detail.humanHealth: Foot rot bacteria are not known to cause disease in people. The main human risks come from treatment. Foot-bath chemicals, especially formalin and copper sulphate, can burn skin and eyes and irritate the lungs; wear gloves, boots and eye protection, mix them in a well-ventilated place and keep them away from children, food and water sources. Antibiotics used for foot rot can leave residues in milk and meat, so never drink or sell milk, or slaughter treated goats, before the withdrawal period stated on the product and confirmed by your vet has passed. Always wash hands after handling infected feet.
detail.outlook: Most goats recover well when foot rot is caught early, the whole herd is treated and conditions are kept dry. Mild scald often clears quickly with foot bathing and dry housing. Goats with severe under-running, several affected feet or long-standing infection take longer to heal and may need repeated treatment. Recovery is slower in wet seasons, in muddy housing and when lame goats are left untreated, because they keep spreading the bacteria. Some goats become chronic carriers that relapse again and again; culling these helps protect the rest of the herd. With good hoof care, quarantine of new animals and dry housing, many farms can greatly reduce or even eliminate foot rot over time, though results vary from farm to farm.

faqs.q: Can I just cut away all the rotten part of the hoof myself?
faqs.a: It is best not to do heavy trimming. Removing only loose, dead horn helps, but cutting deep into the foot until it bleeds causes pain, slows healing and can spread infection. Ask your vet or an experienced animal health officer to show you how to trim properly, and always disinfect your trimmers between goats.

faqs.q: Why does foot rot keep coming back every rainy season?
faqs.a: Usually because some goats remain carriers, holding bacteria in their feet even when they look fine, and wet conditions in the rains let the infection spread again. Regular foot checks, treating every lame goat promptly, culling repeat cases, quarantining new animals and keeping pens dry all help break this cycle.

faqs.q: Do I need to treat the whole herd or only the lame goats?
faqs.a: Your vet will guide you, but usually the whole herd needs attention. Healthy-looking goats may have early infection, so all feet should be checked and the group is often run through a foot bath. Lame goats may need extra treatment such as antibiotics prescribed by the vet.

faqs.q: Can I drink or sell milk from a goat being treated for foot rot?
faqs.a: Not if the goat has been given antibiotics. You must wait for the full milk withdrawal period on the product label, as advised by your vet, before drinking or selling milk. This protects your family and customers from drug residues and helps fight antimicrobial resistance.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for foot rot in Kenya?
faqs.a: Foot rot vaccines are used in some countries, mainly for sheep, but they are not commonly available in Kenya and generally protect goats less well. Prevention here depends mostly on good hoof care, dry housing, foot baths and careful buying of new goats. Ask your County Veterinary Officer or vet about any current vaccine options.

faqs.q: Can my sheep and goats give foot rot to each other?
faqs.a: Yes. The same bacteria infect both sheep and goats, and they share it through pasture, pens and paths. If you keep both, check and treat both species, and use the same quarantine and foot-bath routine for all new animals.

products.role: Vitamins A, D3 and E support normal skin, horn and immune function, so AD3E can be used, with your vet's agreement, as a supportive supplement for goats in poor condition while they recover from foot rot. It does not treat the infection and must be used alongside vet-prescribed treatment, foot care and dry housing.

foot-rot.seoDescription: Foot rot in goats: spot lameness, knee grazing and foul-smelling red skin between toes, act fast, and prevent it with trimming, foot baths and dry pens.

card.headline: Firm lumps under jaw, neck or shoulder
card.look: Your goat has one or more round, firm lumps the size of a marble to an orange, often below the ear, under the jaw, in front of the shoulder or near the udder or scrotum. Some lumps lose hair, soften and burst, leaking thick, cheesy, greenish-white pus.
card.action: Separate the goat with the lump from the herd straight away, and do not squeeze or burst it yourself. Call your vet to drain it safely.

aka: Lumps or boils (often called 'jipu', the Swahili word for abscess)
detail.summary: Caseous lymphadenitis (CL) is a long-lasting, contagious bacterial infection of goats and sheep. It causes abscesses in the lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are the small glands that filter infection, found under the jaw, in front of the shoulder, in the flank and elsewhere. Abscesses can also form inside the body in the lungs, liver and other organs. CL rarely kills quickly, but it spreads quietly through a herd and lowers the value of breeding stock, meat and skins. Once it is on a farm it is hard to get rid of, so early recognition matters.
detail.cause: CL is caused by a bacterium called Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis. It enters the body through breaks in the skin, such as scratches from thorny fences, ear-tagging, castration, dehorning, shearing or clipping wounds, and fighting. It can also enter through the mouth or nose. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node. There they hide inside white blood cells and are protected from the body's defences. The body walls off the infection with a thick capsule, and a slowly growing abscess forms. It is filled with pus that becomes thick and cheesy, which is what 'caseous' means. In goats the pus is often pasty and cream to greenish in colour. When an abscess bursts, the pus carries huge numbers of bacteria onto the skin, the ground, feeders and walls. In some goats abscesses also form in internal lymph nodes and organs, mostly the lungs. These cannot be seen from outside. They slowly cause weight loss, coughing and poor production. This hidden form is sometimes called 'thin goat' or 'wasting' disease.
spread: Pus from a burst abscess is the main source of infection. It contaminates bedding, soil, feed troughs, water points, fences and walls where goats rub.
The bacteria can survive in the environment for months, especially in shaded, damp or dusty bedding and on wooden structures. A contaminated pen stays risky long after the sick goat has gone.
Goats pick up infection through small wounds. Common ones are thorn and wire scratches, ear-tag and tattoo holes, castration and dehorning wounds, and injection sites made with dirty needles.
Shared equipment spreads it from goat to goat. This includes clippers, shears, hoof knives, needles and tagging pliers that are not cleaned and disinfected between animals.
Head-butting and rubbing against each other, feeders and posts spread pus between goats, especially in crowded pens and at feeding time.
Goats with abscesses in the lungs can cough out bacteria. Nearby goats in close housing can then breathe them in.

Buying an infected goat, often one that looks healthy because the abscess has not yet appeared, is the commonest way CL first arrives on a farm. Shows, markets and borrowed breeding bucks are also high-risk.
detail.atRisk: Any goat can be infected, but signs are most often seen in adult goats over about one year old. The abscesses take weeks to months to grow, so infections caught when young often show up later. Herds that buy in animals from markets or other farms without checking them are at higher risk. So are herds that share bucks or use communal grazing and watering points. Dairy goats in zero-grazing units are at risk because they are housed close together and share feeders. Commercial meat herds that are handled often for tagging and castration are at risk too. Thorny bush grazing in pastoral and semi-arid areas leads to many skin scratches that let the bacteria in. Sheep kept with goats can carry and spread the same infection. There is no strong seasonal pattern. Spread can rise when animals are crowded, such as in dry-season holding pens or wet-season indoor housing, and after handling events like castration, dehorning or shearing of sheep.

early: A single firm, round lump appears under the skin at a lymph node site. Common places are below the ear, under the jaw, at the angle of the jaw, in front of the shoulder, in the flank in front of the hind leg, above the udder or near the scrotum.
The lump grows slowly over weeks and is usually not very painful. The goat often keeps eating and behaving normally.
The skin over the lump may start to thin and lose hair. The centre may feel softer than the edges as the pus matures.
More than one lump may appear on the same goat, or similar lumps show up on several goats in the herd over months.
Some goats show no outside lumps at all but slowly lose condition despite good feeding. This can be an early sign of internal abscesses.
advanced: The abscess bursts and leaks thick, cheesy, cream to greenish pus with little smell. This leaves a wet, crusted, hairless patch.
Burst abscesses often heal over and then come back at the same site or at another lymph node months later.
Large abscesses near the throat can press on the windpipe or gullet. This causes noisy breathing or difficulty swallowing.
The goat loses weight steadily, has a dull coat and a lower milk yield, even while still eating. This happens when abscesses form in the lungs, liver, kidneys or internal lymph nodes.
A chronic cough, faster breathing or tiring easily can point to abscesses in the lungs.
An abscess in the udder area can lower milk yield and may affect milk quality.
In severe internal cases the goat becomes very thin and weak and may eventually die. This is slow, usually over many months.

lookalikes.name: Abscesses from other bacteria or dirty injections
lookalikes.howToTell: Many bacteria can cause lumps, especially at injection sites on the neck or thigh. These usually appear soon after an injection or wound, not at a lymph node, and often have smelly, runnier pus. Morel's disease, caused by a Staphylococcus germ, looks very similar to CL. Only a lab culture of the pus can tell them apart for certain.

lookalikes.name: Bottle jaw from worms (haemonchosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Bottle jaw is a soft, fluid-filled, doughy swelling under the jaw that often shrinks during the day when the goat grazes head-down. The goat also has pale eyelids and gums from blood loss to barber's pole worm. A CL abscess is a firm, defined lump at a lymph node, and the eyelids are normally pink.

lookalikes.name: Goitre or salivary cysts
lookalikes.howToTell: Goitre is an enlarged thyroid gland caused by iodine deficiency. It shows as a smooth swelling on both sides of the upper throat, most often in young kids, and does not burst or produce pus. Salivary cysts are soft and fluid-filled. A vet can tell them apart with a needle sample.

lookalikes.name: Tuberculosis, tumours or other causes of wasting
lookalikes.howToTell: Goats with internal CL lose weight much like goats with TB, Johne's disease, heavy worm burdens or tumours such as lymphoma. Outside abscesses elsewhere in the herd point towards CL. Faecal tests, blood tests, worm egg counts or post-mortem by your vet are needed to be sure.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects CL from the typical firm lumps at lymph node sites and the thick cheesy pus. To confirm it, the vet takes a sample of pus with a sterile needle from an abscess that has not yet burst. The sample goes to a laboratory, such as a County or regional veterinary lab or a KALRO or university lab, to culture and identify Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis. This matters because other bacteria can produce similar abscesses. Some laboratories offer blood tests, such as ELISA, that detect antibodies to CL. These help find infected goats that have no visible lumps and are useful when screening a herd or animals you plan to buy. The blood tests are not perfect, and availability in Kenya varies. Internal abscesses can sometimes be seen by ultrasound or X-ray, but often they are only found at post-mortem or at the slaughter slab. Before the vet visits, write down which goats have lumps, where the lumps are, when you first noticed them and whether any have burst. Also note any goats that are losing weight. Keep the affected goat penned separately, and do not burst or squeeze the abscess, because a closed abscess gives the best lab sample. Have clean water, a secure place to hold the goat and records of recent purchases, tagging, castration and treatments ready.
firstSteps: Separate any goat with a lump or a burst abscess from the rest of the herd straight away. Keep it in a pen that can be cleaned easily, away from shared feeders and water points.
Do not squeeze, cut or burst the abscess yourself. This spreads millions of bacteria onto the ground and your hands, and spoils the sample the vet needs to confirm the disease.
If an abscess has already burst, wear gloves. Wipe away the pus with paper or cloth, then burn or bury the waste deeply. Keep the goat isolated until the wound has fully healed and dried.
Clean and disinfect the area where the goat stood, as well as any feeder, wall or post it rubbed against. Remove the bedding and burn it if you can, and wash your hands and boots afterwards.
Check every goat in the herd by running your hands over the jaw, neck, shoulders, flanks and udder or scrotum. Write down each goat with a lump, the site and the date.
Stop selling, buying, lending or sharing animals, especially breeding bucks, until your vet has advised you. This avoids spreading CL to other farms or bringing more in.
Make sure the isolated goat has clean water, good feed, shade and shelter so it keeps its condition while you wait for the vet.
Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer to examine the goat, take a pus sample and plan how to handle the abscess and protect the rest of the herd.
detail.vetTreatment: There is no quick cure for CL. The bacteria hide inside a thick capsule where medicines reach poorly. Treatment aims to reduce suffering, limit spread and help you decide which goats to keep. For a mature outside abscess, the vet may lance and drain it in an isolated area away from the herd. The vet collects and destroys all the pus and flushes the cavity with an antiseptic, often an iodine-based solution. The goat then stays isolated until the wound has healed completely, which can take a few weeks. Sometimes the vet removes the whole lymph node surgically under local anaesthetic, or uses other techniques to manage the abscess. Antibiotics, for example penicillin-type drugs, macrolides or tetracyclines, are sometimes used alongside drainage, especially for valuable animals. They often do not clear the infection on their own, and abscesses commonly come back. Responsible antibiotic use matters: using antibiotics that are unlikely to work, or not completing the course your vet prescribes, adds to antimicrobial resistance and wastes money. Any medicine must be prescribed by a vet, who will decide the drug, dose and length of treatment. All treatments carry milk and meat withdrawal periods. These are the time after treatment during which milk must be thrown away and the animal must not be slaughtered. Ask your vet for the exact periods and follow them. For goats with repeated abscesses, internal abscesses or severe weight loss, the vet will often advise culling, because these animals keep infecting others and rarely recover fully. Your vet can also help you plan a herd control programme. This may include blood testing, culling positive animals, cleaning and, where a licensed vaccine is available, vaccination.
prevention: Buy goats only from herds known to be free of CL. Check every new animal carefully for lumps, and ask for blood test results if available. Keep newcomers in a separate pen for at least a month and check them again before they join your herd.
Check all goats regularly for lumps at the jaw, neck, shoulder, flank, udder and scrotum, for example once a month and at every handling. Isolate any goat with a lump at once, before it bursts.
Handle abscesses only under vet guidance, away from the herd. Collect and burn or deeply bury all pus, dressings and bedding from affected goats.
Cull goats that have repeated abscesses or are wasting from suspected internal CL. Do not keep or sell them as breeding stock, because they keep the disease going.
Reduce skin wounds. Remove or cover nails, sharp wire and broken boards in pens, and trim thorny branches near paths and feeding areas. Avoid overcrowding, which leads to fighting and butting.

Use clean, disinfected equipment for ear-tagging, castration, dehorning, hoof trimming and clipping. Use a new or sterilised needle for each animal, and handle the youngest and healthy goats first and any suspect goats last.
Clean and disinfect pens, feeders, water troughs and rubbing posts regularly. Allow sunlight into goat houses, because sunlight and drying help reduce bacteria in the environment.

Ask your vet whether a CL vaccine is available and licensed for goats in Kenya, because availability is limited and changes over time. Where vaccines are used, they reduce new cases but do not cure goats already infected.
Keep good records of purchases, lumps found, treatments and culling. These help you and your vet see whether control is working.
detail.impact: CL is a slow, money-losing disease rather than a sudden killer. Goats with internal abscesses lose weight and give less milk, which hurts dairy goat farmers in particular. Meat goats grow more slowly and fetch lower prices. At slaughter, abscessed carcasses or parts of carcasses may be trimmed or condemned by meat inspectors, and scarred skins lose value for the leather trade. Breeding stock from a herd known to have CL is harder to sell, and buyers increasingly check for lumps. Repeated vet visits, drainage, isolation and the loss of culled goats all add cost. Infected animals sold through markets carry the disease to other farms, which damages the seller's reputation and spreads losses across the community.
detail.humanHealth: CL can occasionally infect people, though this is rare. It mainly affects people who handle pus or infected tissue, such as farmers, vets, butchers and slaughterhouse workers, and can cause swollen, painful lymph nodes that need medical treatment. Always wear gloves when touching a burst abscess or cleaning affected pens, cover any cuts on your hands, and wash well with soap afterwards. Keep children away from goats with burst abscesses. The bacteria can occasionally be found in milk from goats with abscesses near the udder, so always boil or pasteurise goat milk before drinking it. Meat from goats with abscesses should be inspected, and abscessed parts should be removed and not eaten. If you develop a painful swelling after handling infected goats, see a doctor and tell them you work with goats. Where antibiotics are used, follow the milk and meat withdrawal periods to avoid drug residues in food.
detail.outlook: For one goat with a single outside abscess, the outlook is fair. After proper drainage and isolation the wound usually heals within a few weeks, and the goat can stay productive. However, the goat remains infected, and new abscesses commonly appear later at the same or another site. Goats with many abscesses, abscesses that keep coming back or internal abscesses causing weight loss have a poor outlook and are usually best culled. At herd level, CL tends to stay once it is established, because the bacteria survive in the environment and in goats without visible lumps. With steady effort over several years, it can be brought under control and sometimes cleared. That effort means regular checking, isolating and culling, strict hygiene, careful buying and vaccination where available. Success depends mostly on how consistent the farmer is.

faqs.q: Can I just burst the lump myself and squeeze out the pus?
faqs.a: Please don't. Bursting an abscess in the herd spreads huge numbers of bacteria onto the ground, feeders and your hands. Other goats can then be infected for months. It also destroys the closed abscess your vet needs for a lab sample. Isolate the goat and let the vet drain it away from the herd, with all the pus collected and destroyed.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics from the agrovet cure CL?
faqs.a: Usually not on their own. The bacteria sit inside a thick capsule where antibiotics reach poorly, so lumps often come back even after injections. Using antibiotics without a vet's advice wastes money, can leave residues in milk and meat, and adds to drug resistance. Your vet may use antibiotics alongside drainage in some cases, and will tell you the correct drug and withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat meat or drink milk from a goat with CL?
faqs.a: Meat from a goat with CL should be inspected. Abscessed parts must be cut away and destroyed, and badly affected carcasses may be condemned. Never eat the pus or abscessed tissue. Always boil or pasteurise goat milk, and do not use milk from goats with abscesses on or near the udder until your vet advises. If the goat has been treated, wait until the full withdrawal period has passed.

faqs.q: Should I cull every goat that gets a lump?
faqs.a: Not always, but often it is the wisest choice. A goat with one abscess that heals well after vet drainage may be kept, isolated and watched closely, especially if it is valuable. Goats with repeat abscesses, several lumps or weight loss from internal abscesses keep infecting the herd and rarely recover, so culling them protects the rest. Discuss each case with your vet.

faqs.q: Can my sheep or cattle catch CL from my goats?
faqs.a: Sheep can easily catch the same infection from goats, and the two species often pass it back and forth on mixed farms. Cattle, camels and horses can be affected by related strains of the same bacterium, but they are less commonly part of goat outbreaks. On mixed farms, check your sheep for lumps too and apply the same hygiene and isolation rules.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for CL in Kenya?
faqs.a: Vaccines against CL exist in some countries, sometimes combined with clostridial vaccines, but they are not always available or licensed for goats in Kenya. Availability changes, so ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer what is currently approved. Even where a vaccine is used, it reduces new infections rather than curing infected goats. Buying clean stock, early isolation, hygiene and culling remain the backbone of control.

card.headline: Constant scratching with bald, crusty patches
card.look: The goat rubs against walls, posts and fences, bites at its legs and flanks, and has patches of hair loss with grey, thick, wrinkled or scaly skin, often starting on the head, ears, neck or legs. With lice you may see tiny moving insects and white eggs stuck to the hairs when you part the coat.
card.action: Separate the itchy goat from the herd, check every other goat closely, and call your vet or animal health officer to confirm whether it is mites or lice before any treatment is used.

detail.summary: Mange is a skin disease caused by tiny mites that live on or in the skin, while lice are small wingless insects that live in the coat. Both cause itching, rubbing, hair loss and damaged skin, and the two problems are often found together on the same farm. They rarely kill adult goats outright, but they steal weight, milk and hide value, weaken kids and make goats more likely to fall sick from other diseases. Sarcoptic mange can also cause an itchy rash in people who handle affected goats.
detail.cause: Several different parasites cause these problems. Sarcoptes mites (Sarcoptes scabiei) burrow into the top layer of the skin to lay eggs; their burrowing and droppings cause an intense allergic itch, and the skin becomes thick, wrinkled, grey and crusty, usually starting on the face, around the eyes, ears, neck and inner legs before spreading over the body. Psoroptes mites live on the skin surface, mainly inside the ears in goats, where they cause head shaking, ear scratching and brown crusty wax, sometimes spreading to the head and neck. Chorioptes mites, a close relative, often affect the lower legs, feet and udder area. Demodex mites live deep inside hair follicles and skin glands; instead of a bad itch they cause small, firm lumps (nodules) the size of a pea or bigger, mostly on the face, neck, shoulders and flanks, which contain a cheesy grey-white paste and leave holes in the hide. Lice are divided into biting (chewing) lice, which feed on skin flakes and cause itching and a rough, scruffy coat, and sucking lice, which pierce the skin and drink blood. Heavy sucking lice numbers can cause anaemia (a shortage of red blood cells), which shows as pale gums and eyelids and weakness, especially in kids. In all cases, broken skin from rubbing and biting can become infected by bacteria, and constant irritation stops goats from feeding and resting well.
spread: Direct contact between goats is the main route: mites and lice crawl from one animal to another when goats sleep together, feed side by side or are crowded in a small house.
Buying or borrowing goats, including breeding bucks, that carry mites or lice brings the parasites into a clean herd, sometimes before any signs show.

Shared rubbing posts, walls, feeders, bedding, ropes, brushes and transport vehicles can carry mites and lice for a short time, so a goat can pick them up from a place where an infested goat has been.
Crowded, dark, damp or poorly cleaned housing, common in zero-grazing units and night bomas, keeps parasites close to many animals and helps numbers build quickly.
Mothers pass lice and mites to their kids during suckling and close contact in the first weeks of life.
Poor nutrition, worm burdens, pregnancy and other illness weaken the goat's defences and allow mite and lice numbers to explode.
Lice numbers usually rise in the cooler months, such as the cold season around June to August in Kenya, when coats are longer and goats huddle together; they often drop when the weather warms.
Markets, shows and communal grazing or watering points in pastoral areas bring many herds together and are common places for spread.
detail.atRisk: Any goat can get mange or lice, but the most at risk are kids, young weaners, old goats, pregnant and heavily milking does, and any goat that is thin, wormy or recovering from illness. Goats in crowded houses or bomas, and herds that often mix with other flocks at markets, communal grazing or water points, are at high risk. Newly bought goats and visiting bucks are a common source. Demodectic mange is more common in some dairy breeds and their crosses, such as Saanen and Toggenburg types, and usually shows in younger animals, though it can appear in any breed including Galla and small East African goats. Lice tend to build up in the cool, dry season and in goats with poor feeding during dry periods, while mange can strike at any time of year. Farms that only treat sick-looking goats, rather than the whole herd, often see the problem keep coming back.

early: The goat scratches with its hind feet, rubs against walls, posts, trees or fences, and nibbles or bites at its legs, flanks and tail more than normal.
Small patches of thin or broken hair appear, often on the face, around the eyes and ears, on the neck, or inside the legs.
The coat looks dull, rough and scruffy, and you may see white flakes like dandruff when you part the hair.
When you part the hair along the neck, back and tail base in good light, you may see tiny grey or brown lice moving and white or cream eggs (nits) glued to the hairs.
With ear mites, the goat shakes its head, scratches its ears and holds an ear lower than the other, and you may see brown crusts or wax inside the ear.
With Demodex, you feel or see small, firm, painless lumps under the skin, often without much itching.
Small red bumps and scabs appear where the goat has been scratching.
advanced: Large areas of hair loss with thick, grey, wrinkled, leathery skin, especially over the head, neck, shoulders and legs, typical of sarcoptic mange.
Heavy, cracked crusts that may ooze or bleed, with bacterial infection causing a bad smell or pus in the skin folds.
Constant restlessness and itching so severe that the goat stops feeding properly, loses weight and becomes very thin.
Pale gums and inner eyelids, weakness and poor growth in kids carrying many sucking lice, due to blood loss.
Demodex nodules become numerous and larger, and when squeezed they release a thick, cheesy grey-white paste.
Ear mange spreading from the ears onto the face and neck, with thick crusts and head tilt in some goats.
Drop in milk yield, stunted kids, abortion or weak kids in very run-down does, and in rare severe cases death from exhaustion and secondary infection.

lookalikes.name: Ringworm (fungal skin infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ringworm makes round, grey, crusty bald patches, often on the face, ears and neck, but goats usually itch only a little or not at all. Mange is usually very itchy and spreads in wider areas of thickened skin. A vet can tell them apart with skin scrapings and hair samples. Ringworm also spreads to people as round red rings.

lookalikes.name: Dermatophilosis (streptothricosis, rain scald)
lookalikes.howToTell: This bacterial skin disease causes raised, thick scabs that matt the hair into 'paintbrush' tufts, often along the back and ears after long periods of rain. When pulled off, the scabs leave a moist raw area underneath. It is usually less itchy than mange and is linked to wet weather and ticks.

lookalikes.name: Orf (contagious ecthyma)
lookalikes.howToTell: Orf is a viral disease causing crusty, warty scabs mainly on the lips, mouth corners, nostrils and sometimes the udder and feet, mostly in kids. It is not mainly itchy and does not cause hair loss over the body. Orf can also infect people's hands, so wear gloves.

lookalikes.name: Sheep and goat pox
lookalikes.howToTell: Pox causes fever, dullness, runny eyes and nose, and many raised round lumps over the skin, especially where hair is thin, followed by scabs. Goats are clearly sick, not just itchy, and several may die. Sheep and goat pox is a notifiable disease, so if you see fever with widespread lumps, report it to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

detail.diagnosis: A vet or animal health officer will look at where the hair loss and crusts are, how itchy the goat is, and how many goats are affected. Lice can usually be seen with the naked eye or a magnifying glass by parting the hair, and the type (biting or sucking) can be identified. For mange, the vet takes a deep skin scraping from the edge of a fresh lesion with a blade until a little blood oozes, then looks at it under a microscope to find mites or eggs; Sarcoptes can be hard to find, so several scrapings may be needed and a negative result does not always rule it out. Ear wax and crusts are examined for Psoroptes. For Demodex, the vet squeezes or cuts into a nodule and checks the cheesy contents for the long, cigar-shaped mites. The vet may also take hair or crusts to rule out ringworm or dermatophilosis, and check gums for anaemia. To help, keep the affected goat in a pen without washing or treating it first, note when the itching started, which goats are affected, any recent purchases or visits to markets, what dips or sprays you have used and when, and whether you see the same signs on people in the household.
firstSteps: Separate the itchy or bald goats from the rest of the herd in a clean, dry, well-aired pen, and keep kids with their mothers only if both are being watched.
Check every goat in the herd, including kids and bucks, by parting the hair along the neck, back, tail base and legs and looking inside the ears, and write down which goats show signs.
Wear gloves or wash your hands and arms well with soap after handling affected goats, because sarcoptic mites can cause an itchy rash in people.
Stop buying, selling, lending or borrowing goats, and keep your goats away from communal grazing or markets, until the vet has confirmed the problem and treatment has started.
Give clean water and good-quality feed, and make sure the goats are not hungry, because well-fed goats cope better and recover faster.
Clean out old bedding, dung and hair from the house, burn or bury it away from the goats, and let the house dry out in the sun if possible.
Do not use engine oil, used motor oil, paraffin, battery acid or strong home-made chemicals on the skin, as these can burn the skin, poison the goat and contaminate milk and meat.

Call your vet, County Veterinary Officer or a trained animal health officer to confirm whether it is mites, lice or another skin disease, and do not use any dip, spray, pour-on or injection until they advise you.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on which parasite is found, so getting the right diagnosis first saves money and avoids failure. The vet usually treats the whole herd, not just the goats showing signs, because others may be carrying parasites without obvious signs. Common options include injectable or pour-on macrocyclic lactones such as ivermectin, doramectin or moxidectin, which work well against Sarcoptes mites and sucking lice but less reliably against biting lice; dips, sprays or washes containing amitraz, or synthetic pyrethroids such as cypermethrin, deltamethrin or flumethrin, which are used for lice and surface mites; and older options such as organophosphates or lime sulphur washes in some situations. Most products do not kill eggs, so a second and sometimes third treatment is needed after a gap set by the vet to kill newly hatched mites or lice. For dips and sprays, the coat must be soaked thoroughly, including the head, ears, legs and under the belly, and crusts may need softening first. Ear mange may need treatment applied into the ears. Demodectic mange is difficult to treat; the vet may drain or treat individual nodules and may advise culling badly affected goats from breeding, as the problem can run in families. If the skin has become badly infected, the vet may prescribe antibiotics; these treat only the bacterial infection, not the mites or lice, and should be used only when needed and exactly as prescribed to help prevent antimicrobial resistance. All these medicines have milk and meat withdrawal periods, meaning milk must be thrown away and goats must not be slaughtered for a set time after treatment. Some products are not allowed at all in goats producing milk for people, so tell the vet if your does are milking. Wear gloves and protective clothing when dipping or spraying, and never use more or less than the vet advises, because underdosing helps parasites become resistant to acaricides (mite and tick killers). Itching usually reduces within one to two weeks of effective treatment, but hair and skin can take several weeks to recover.
prevention: Quarantine every newly bought or returning goat, including breeding bucks, for at least two to three weeks in a separate pen, check its skin and ears carefully, and have it treated on vet advice before it joins the herd.
Check the whole herd for itching, hair loss, lice and nits regularly, for example once a month and more often in the cool season, so you catch problems while only one or two goats are affected.
When mange or lice are found, treat all the goats that share housing or grazing at the same time, and repeat treatment as advised, rather than treating only the worst-looking animals.
Keep goat houses clean, dry, well ventilated and not overcrowded; raised slatted floors help, and old bedding and droppings should be removed often.
Clean and, where possible, spray or wash housing, rubbing posts, feeders and handling equipment after an outbreak, and leave the house empty and sunny for some days if you can.
Feed goats well all year with enough energy, protein, minerals and vitamins, including supplementation during the dry season, because thin, poorly fed goats carry much heavier parasite loads.
Control worms and ticks under your vet's or extension officer's guidance, since goats weakened by other parasites are more likely to develop severe mange or lice.
Avoid sharing ropes, brushes and transport with other farmers' goats, and limit contact with other herds at markets, water points and communal grazing where possible.
Rotate the type of acaricide only on professional advice and always use the correct strength, to slow the development of resistance in mites, lice and ticks.
Consider culling goats that repeatedly get Demodex nodules or chronic mange, and avoid breeding from them, to reduce the problem in future generations.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan farm, mange and lice quietly cost money even when no goats die. Itching goats spend less time feeding and resting, so they grow slowly, lose condition and take longer to reach market weight. Dairy goats produce less milk, and kids from run-down does are smaller and weaker. Kids with heavy sucking lice can become anaemic and stunted, and some may die if other diseases strike at the same time. Goats with bald, crusty skin fetch lower prices at the market because buyers see them as sick, and the skin is worth less or nothing to tanners because mites, lice and Demodex nodules leave holes and scars in the leather. Treating a whole herd several times, plus labour, adds cost, and a single infested goat brought in from a market can spread the problem to the whole herd. In pastoral areas where goats mix at water points and markets, mange can spread widely between herds.
detail.humanHealth: Sarcoptic mange mites from goats can pass to people who handle infested animals, causing small, very itchy red spots, usually on the arms, hands, chest and waist. In most people this is temporary because the goat mite does not survive long on human skin, but it can be very uncomfortable, and anyone with a persistent itchy rash should see a health worker and mention contact with mangy goats. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling affected goats, wash hands and arms with soap afterwards, and wash work clothes. Goat lice are host-specific and do not live on people. Ringworm, which can look like mange, does spread to people. The dips, sprays and injections used to treat mange and lice can be harmful to people: wear gloves and protective clothing, avoid splashing eyes and skin, keep children away, never mix chemicals near food or water sources, and strictly follow milk and meat withdrawal periods so that no drug residues reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: The outlook for sarcoptic, psoroptic and chorioptic mange and for lice is good when the problem is confirmed early and the whole herd is treated properly, including repeat treatments. Most goats stop itching within a couple of weeks and regrow hair over the following weeks, though very thickened skin can take longer to return to normal. Recovery is slower and less certain in goats that are very thin, old, heavily wormed or have badly infected skin. Re-infestation is common if only some goats are treated, if repeat treatments are skipped, if housing is not cleaned, or if new animals are brought in without quarantine. Demodectic mange has a less predictable outlook; some goats improve on their own as they mature, but others keep getting new nodules and may be better culled from breeding. Hide damage from mites, lice and nodules may be permanent.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my goat has mange or just lice?
faqs.a: Part the hair along the neck, back and tail base in bright light. If you see small moving insects and white eggs glued to the hair, lice are present. Mange mites are too small to see with the naked eye, and mange usually causes thicker, grey, wrinkled or crusty skin, often on the face, ears and legs, with intense itching. Goats can have both at once, so a vet's skin scraping is the best way to be sure before you treat.

faqs.q: Why does the itching come back after I spray my goats?
faqs.a: This is very common. Most sprays and dips do not kill eggs, so a new generation hatches days later unless you repeat the treatment at the interval your vet advises. Other reasons include treating only the itchy goats while others still carry parasites, not soaking the coat fully, using the wrong product for that parasite, diluting it too weakly, parasites resistant to the chemical, or bringing in new goats without quarantine.

faqs.q: Can I use engine oil or paraffin on mangy goats?
faqs.a: No. Used engine oil, paraffin and similar home remedies can burn and crack the skin, poison the goat if it licks itself, and leave harmful residues in milk and meat. They also do not reliably kill mites. Ask your vet or animal health officer for a proper product and how to use it safely.

faqs.q: Can I drink milk from a goat that is being treated for mange or lice?
faqs.a: Only after the withdrawal period on the product has passed, as advised by your vet. Many mange and lice medicines pass into milk, and some are not allowed in goats producing milk for people at all. Tell the vet that the goat is milking so they can choose a suitable product and tell you exactly how long to throw milk away.

faqs.q: Will mange spread to my children?
faqs.a: Sarcoptic mites from goats can cause an itchy rash in people, especially those who hold or carry affected goats. It usually clears once contact stops and the goats are treated, but anyone with a lasting rash should see a health worker. Keep children from handling mangy goats, use gloves, and wash hands and clothes well. Lice from goats do not live on people.

faqs.q: Do vitamins or good feeding cure mange?
faqs.a: No. Good feeding and vitamins cannot kill mites or lice, so a proper vet-advised treatment is still needed. However, well-fed goats with enough vitamins and minerals have healthier skin, resist heavy infestations better and recover faster after treatment, so nutrition is an important part of both treatment and prevention.

products.role: Vitamins A and E help maintain healthy skin and support the body's natural defences, so on your vet's advice AD3E can help run-down or poorly fed goats recover skin condition and body condition after the mites or lice have been treated. It does not kill mites or lice and is only a support alongside proper treatment, whole-herd control and good feeding.
