card.headline: Hot, swollen, hard udder half
card.look: One side of the doe's udder is bigger, hot, hard and painful to touch, and the milk from that teat is watery, clotted, yellow or blood-stained. In the severe gangrenous form the half turns blue or purple-black and feels cold.
card.action: Separate the doe, check the milk from both teats, and call your vet the same day, urgently if the udder is cold or blue or the doe is weak and off feed.

aka: Blue bag or gangrenous mastitis (severe form)
detail.summary: Mastitis is inflammation of the udder, almost always caused by bacteria entering through the teat canal. In goats it ranges from a hidden (subclinical) infection that quietly lowers milk yield, to a hot, painful, swollen half with abnormal milk, to a life-threatening gangrenous form where the udder tissue dies. It is one of the most common and costly problems in dairy goats and in meat and kienyeji does nursing kids. Early detection and prompt vet treatment give the best chance of saving the doe and her milk.
detail.cause: Mastitis starts when germs get past the teat opening and multiply inside the milk-producing tissue. The most common culprits in goats are Staphylococcus bacteria. Staphylococcus aureus causes many of the severe cases, including gangrenous mastitis. Other staphylococci often cause low-grade, subclinical infections. Streptococcus, E. coli, Mannheimia and Trueperella (pus-forming bacteria) are also involved, and Mycoplasma can cause mastitis as part of contagious agalactia. Once inside, the bacteria damage the cells lining the milk glands. The body sends white blood cells to fight them, which causes the heat, swelling, pain and clots you see. The milk changes because it fills with pus, fluid and blood. In gangrenous mastitis, toxins from the bacteria block the blood supply to part of the udder. That tissue dies, turns blue-black and goes cold, and the toxins entering the bloodstream make the whole doe very sick. Some infections become chronic. The gland turns hard and lumpy with scar tissue (fibrosis) and may stop producing milk permanently, leaving a 'blind' half.
spread: Dirty hands, cloths or milking equipment carry bacteria from an infected doe to healthy ones during milking, especially when the infected doe is milked first.
Wet, muddy or manure-soaked bedding and floors put bacteria directly onto the teats when the doe lies down.
Teat injuries from thorns, sharp wire, rough pen edges, dog bites or hard-suckling kids give bacteria an easy way in.
Kids with orf (sore mouth) or teething kids can damage teats and carry infection from one doe to another when they steal milk.
Incomplete or irregular milking leaves milk sitting in the udder, which helps bacteria grow. Weaning kids suddenly or a doe losing her kids can do the same.
The days around kidding and drying off are high-risk times because the teat canal is more open and the doe's immunity is lower.
Flies feeding on teat sores can spread bacteria between animals, especially in the warm, wet months.
Poor nutrition, including low vitamin E, vitamin A and selenium, weakens the udder's natural defences.
detail.atRisk: Any female goat that is producing milk can get mastitis, but high-yielding dairy does such as Saanen, Toggenburg, Alpine, Anglo-Nubian and their crosses are most at risk. This is especially true in zero-grazing units where many does are hand-milked. Older does and those with large, pendulous udders or long teats that touch the ground are more likely to be injured and infected. The first weeks after kidding and the drying-off period carry the highest risk. Does whose kids have died or been weaned suddenly are also vulnerable, as are does with a past case of mastitis. Cases usually rise during the long and short rains, when pens and paths are wet and muddy and flies breed. Meat goats and kienyeji does in free-range and pastoral systems are also affected, often unnoticed until a kid is starving or the udder is badly damaged. Poorly fed does and those in crowded, dirty housing are at higher risk.

early: One half of the udder looks slightly bigger than the other and feels warmer to the back of your hand.
The affected half is firmer than normal, and the doe flinches, kicks or moves away when you touch or milk it.
Milk from that teat has small flakes, clots or strings when squirted onto a dark cup or plate (a strip cup).
Milk yield drops from one side, or the doe gives less milk overall for no clear reason.
Kids keep nursing on one side only, cry often or look hungry because the sore side is painful or giving bad milk.
The doe may walk stiffly with a hind leg held out from the swollen side.
advanced: The half is very swollen, hard, red and hot, and the milk is watery, yellow, brownish, pus-like or stained with blood.
The doe has a fever, stops eating and chewing the cud, looks dull and stands apart from the herd.
In gangrenous (blue bag) mastitis, the udder skin and teat turn blue, purple or black and feel cold and clammy. The doe may become weak, go down and die within a day or two without treatment.
Thin, reddish, foul-smelling fluid comes from the gangrenous teat. Later the dead tissue may crack, ooze and slough away.
Long-standing cases leave a shrunken, hard or lumpy half that gives little or no milk (a blind quarter).
Abscesses may form as soft swellings on the udder that burst and drain pus.

lookalikes.name: Udder oedema (fluid swelling) at kidding
lookalikes.howToTell: Oedema usually affects both halves evenly. It feels soft and leaves a dent when you press it, and the milk is normal. The doe is bright and eating. Mastitis is usually one-sided, hot and painful, with abnormal milk.

lookalikes.name: Hard udder from caprine arthritis encephalitis (CAE)
lookalikes.howToTell: CAE, a viral infection, can cause a firm, 'woody' udder that produces little milk right from kidding. Both halves are often affected, and it is not hot or painful. The milk looks normal and the doe is not feverish. Affected herds may also have goats with swollen knees. A blood test confirms it.

lookalikes.name: Contagious agalactia (Mycoplasma)
lookalikes.howToTell: Several does in the herd develop mastitis and their milk dries up. This often comes with lameness or swollen joints, and with eye inflammation in does or kids. If many goats are affected at once with joints and eyes involved, tell your vet so samples can be taken.

lookalikes.name: Teat injuries, orf or warts
lookalikes.howToTell: The problem is on the teat skin: cuts, scabs or crusty lesions. The udder itself is soft and the milk is normal. These lesions can lead to mastitis, so treat and watch them closely.

detail.diagnosis: A vet confirms mastitis by examining the whole doe and feeling both udder halves. The vet checks temperature, appetite, colour and warmth of the udder, and looks at milk from each teat. The California Mastitis Test (CMT) is a cheap paddle test in which milk is mixed with a reagent and thickens if it is full of white cells. It helps find hidden subclinical cases. Healthy goat milk naturally has more cells than cow milk, so goat results must be read with care and compared between the two halves. For repeat or herd problems, the vet may collect clean milk samples for culture and antibiotic sensitivity testing at a county or private laboratory. This shows which bacteria are present and which drugs will work. If a doe dies, a post-mortem helps protect the rest of the herd. Before the vet arrives, write down which half is affected, when you first noticed it, and how the milk looks. Note when she kidded, any past mastitis, and any treatments already given, including tubes or injections bought from the agrovet. Keep a clean container of her milk aside, unmixed, so the vet can see it.
firstSteps: Separate the affected doe into a clean, dry, shaded pen with soft bedding so she is comfortable and cannot spread infection to other does.
Give her clean, fresh water at all times and good-quality fodder. A sick doe with fever loses fluid quickly and needs to keep drinking.
Milk the healthy does first and the sick doe last. Wear gloves or wash and dry your hands well afterwards, and use a separate cloth for her udder.
Strip out the affected half gently and often if she allows it, into a container. Discard that milk safely, for example by burying it away from water sources, not on the ground where animals walk.
Do not let kids suckle the infected half. Bottle-feed them with milk from healthy does or a suitable replacer until the vet advises.
Check the udder colour and warmth. If it is turning blue, purple or cold, or the doe is weak, treat it as an emergency and call the vet immediately.
Record her temperature if you have a thermometer (normal for goats is roughly 38.5 to 40 °C), along with appetite, milk changes and the date. Share this with the vet.
Do not buy and use antibiotic tubes or injections without a vet's advice. The wrong drug wastes money, adds to antibiotic resistance and leaves residues in the milk.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how severe the case is and which bacteria are involved, and it must be prescribed by a vet. For mild to moderate cases, vets usually use antibiotics infused into the teat (intramammary tubes). Systemic antibiotics by injection are added for more serious cases. Commonly used drug classes include penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides and tetracyclines, ideally chosen after culture and sensitivity testing. Anti-inflammatory pain relief such as meloxicam or flunixin is often given to reduce pain, swelling and fever, which helps the doe eat and let down milk. Frequent stripping out of the infected half is an important part of treatment. Gangrenous mastitis needs aggressive emergency care: strong systemic antibiotics, pain relief, fluids and supportive care. Sometimes the vet amputates the teat or removes the dead half surgically so it can drain and heal. Even when the doe survives, that half will not produce milk again. Chronic, hard, recurring cases may respond poorly, and the vet may advise drying off the half with dry-cow therapy or culling the doe. Many mastitis products are labelled for cattle, not goats, so the vet will set a safe milk and meat withdrawal period. This is the time you must throw away milk and not sell or slaughter the animal. Follow it strictly. Always finish the full course as prescribed, and never use antibiotics 'just in case'. Misuse breeds resistant bacteria that no longer respond to treatment.
prevention: Milk in a clean place with clean, dry hands, and use a clean individual cloth or paper towel to wipe each doe's teats before milking.
Use a strip cup at every milking to check the first squirts of milk from each teat for clots or changes. This catches mastitis days before the udder swells.
Dip each teat in a suitable teat dip right after milking, and keep the doe standing for a while afterwards by giving her feed, so the teat canal closes before she lies down.
Keep the milking order: young and healthy does first, does with past mastitis next, and any infected doe last.
Keep housing dry and clean. Raised slatted floors, regular removal of manure and wet bedding, and good drainage during the long and short rains make a big difference.
Remove sharp wire, nails, thorny branches and rough edges from pens and feeding areas, and control dogs to prevent teat injuries.
Test the herd with the CMT regularly, for example monthly, to find hidden infections. Ask your vet about treating or culling does that keep getting mastitis.
Dry off does properly at the end of lactation as your vet advises. Selective dry-off treatment may be recommended for does with past infections.
Feed a balanced diet with enough energy, protein, minerals and vitamins, especially vitamins A and E and selenium, to support the udder's natural defences.
Control flies and treat orf and teat sores in kids and does promptly. Wean kids gradually so the udder is not left suddenly full.
detail.impact: Mastitis hits a goat farm in several ways. Milk yield drops, often for the rest of the lactation, and milk from treated does must be thrown away during treatment and the withdrawal period. For a smallholder selling goat milk to neighbours, a cooperative or a processor, that is lost daily income. A damaged half may never milk again, so the doe's value as a dairy animal falls. Kids of affected does grow poorly or die from hunger unless they are hand-fed, which adds cost and labour. Vet visits, drugs and lab tests add up, and gangrenous cases can kill a valuable doe within days. Chronic carriers keep spreading infection in the herd, and repeated cases often end in early culling, losing years of production and breeding value. Hidden subclinical mastitis is especially costly because it quietly lowers yields across the herd without the farmer noticing.
detail.humanHealth: Milk from a doe with mastitis can contain bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus. This germ can produce toxins that cause vomiting and diarrhoea in people, and some of these toxins are not destroyed by boiling. Do not drink, sell or feed to children milk from an infected half or a sick doe, and dispose of it safely. Milk from does treated with antibiotics contains drug residues until the withdrawal period is over. Residues can trigger allergies and contribute to antibiotic resistance in people, so never sell or drink this milk early. Raw goat milk can also carry other diseases such as brucellosis, so always boil or pasteurise milk from healthy does before drinking. Wear gloves or wash your hands well after handling an infected udder, especially if you have cuts on your hands, and keep gangrenous fluid away from your skin.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how early mastitis is caught and what type it is. Mild cases found early with the strip cup or CMT and treated promptly often recover well, and the half may return to normal or near-normal production. Moderate cases usually save the doe, but milk from that side may stay lower. Gangrenous mastitis is serious. Many does die without fast treatment, and even survivors lose the affected half permanently, though some can still raise kids on the other side. Chronic infections with hard, lumpy tissue rarely clear fully and often come back. Fast action, the right drug chosen with your vet, good nursing and a clean environment all improve the chances.

faqs.q: Can I drink or sell milk from the healthy half while the other half is infected?
faqs.a: It is safest not to. Infection and treatment affect the whole doe, and antibiotics given by injection or into one teat can appear in milk from both halves. Discard all her milk until your vet confirms the infection has cleared and the withdrawal period is over. Then boil or pasteurise it as you would any goat milk.

faqs.q: Will the doe milk again on the infected side?
faqs.a: After a mild case treated early, usually yes, though yield may be a bit lower. After severe, chronic or gangrenous mastitis, the half is often permanently damaged or lost. Many such does can still feed kids or give milk from the healthy side, so talk to your vet about whether to keep her for breeding or cull her.

faqs.q: Can I use the mastitis tubes the agrovet sells for cows?
faqs.a: Only if a vet prescribes them. Goat teats are smaller and need careful, clean insertion, and the wrong drug may not work against the bacteria involved. Cow products are not set up for goats, so the vet must give a safe withdrawal period. Using tubes without advice also adds to antibiotic resistance.

faqs.q: Why does mastitis keep coming back in my herd?
faqs.a: Repeat cases usually point to hygiene or management problems. Common causes are wet, dirty bedding, poor milking routine, infected does milked before healthy ones, teat injuries, or chronic carrier does spreading bacteria. Ask your vet for milk culture to identify the germ. Review your milking routine and housing, use teat dips and the CMT, and consider culling does that never fully clear.

faqs.q: Can the kids still suckle a doe with mastitis?
faqs.a: Keep kids off the infected half. The milk is poor, may carry germs that make them sick, and suckling causes the doe pain. Kids can also spread infection to other does. If both halves are affected or the doe is very ill, bottle-feed the kids with milk from healthy does or a goat-suitable replacer, and make sure newborns get colostrum.

faqs.q: Is blue bag the same as ordinary mastitis?
faqs.a: It is the most severe form of mastitis, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus toxins that kill the udder tissue. The udder turns blue or black and goes cold, and the doe becomes very sick. It is an emergency. Call your vet immediately, because without fast treatment many does die.

products.role: An oral rehydration solution that can help a feverish, off-feed doe keep up her fluid and electrolyte intake during recovery, especially in hot weather. It is used alongside, not instead of, the treatment your vet prescribes.

A vitamin A, D3 and E supplement that can help correct deficiencies on poor or dry-season diets. Vitamins A and E support healthy udder skin and natural immune defences, so it can form part of a wider prevention and recovery plan with good hygiene and vet care. It does not treat infection.

card.headline: Heavily pregnant doe dull, alone, stargazing
card.look: A doe in the last weeks of pregnancy, often carrying twins or triplets, stops eating, stands apart from the herd and seems blind or confused. She may grind her teeth, tremble, press her head against walls and later lie down and refuse to rise.
card.action: Call your vet at once, because this is an emergency and treatment works best in the first hours, before she goes down.

detail.summary: Pregnancy toxaemia is an energy shortage in a doe during the last four to six weeks of pregnancy. The growing kids take more sugar than the doe can supply from her feed, so she breaks down her body fat too fast and becomes poisoned by the by-products. It is common in does carrying twins or triplets. Once she is down, many does die, and kids are often lost too, so early action and good late-pregnancy feeding are vital.
detail.cause: In late pregnancy most of the kids' growth happens, and they use large amounts of glucose (blood sugar) from the mother. Twins and triplets need much more than a single kid. At the same time the womb takes up space in the belly, so the doe cannot eat as much. If her feed does not give enough energy, her body breaks down stored fat to make up the gap. The liver cannot process this flood of fat properly. Fat builds up in the liver (fatty liver), and the liver produces ketones, which are acid substances that build up in the blood. High ketones and low blood sugar affect the brain, which is why the doe becomes dull, blind, wobbly and confused. As the disease goes on, her kidneys and liver begin to fail, the kids may die inside her, and dead kids release toxins that make her worse. Very fat does are at high risk because they eat less and have large fat stores to break down, but thin does in poor condition are also at risk because they simply do not have enough energy coming in.
spread: It is not infectious and does not spread from goat to goat, but several does in the same herd can be affected at the same time because they share the same poor feeding.
A drop in feed quality or quantity in late pregnancy is the main trigger, for example in the dry season or during drought when pasture is poor.
Sudden changes in feed, running out of hay, or delays in feeding can tip a doe that is already on the edge into disease.
Stress can trigger it, including transport, heavy rain and cold, chasing by dogs, rough handling, moving to new housing, or fighting at a crowded feeding trough.
Other illnesses reduce appetite and can start it off, such as heavy worm burdens (especially wireworm, which causes anaemia), foot rot or lameness, bad teeth, or a tick-borne fever.
Being overfat at mating and in early pregnancy, often from too much concentrate, raises the risk later in pregnancy.
Timid, old or low-ranking does that are pushed away from feed by stronger goats are more likely to be affected.
detail.atRisk: Does in the last four to six weeks of pregnancy are at risk, especially those carrying twins, triplets or more. High-producing dairy breeds and their crosses kept in zero-grazing units (for example Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine and Anglo-Nubian crosses) are commonly affected, but local breeds such as Galla and Small East African goats can also suffer, especially in pastoral and free-range systems during the long dry season or drought, when kidding falls at a time of poor grazing. Very fat does, very thin does, older does, does with bad teeth or lameness, and does with heavy worm loads are at higher risk. Herds where kidding is not planned, so farmers do not know which does are close to kidding, often miss the early signs.

early: She is slow to come to feed, leaves her concentrate or eats less than usual, often refusing grain or dairy meal first.
She separates from the group, lags behind when the herd moves, or stands alone in a corner of the pen.
She looks dull and sleepy and is less alert to people, dogs or noise around her.
She may seem unable to see well, bumping into walls, feeders or other goats, or not reacting when a hand moves near her eye.
Her breath or urine may have a sweet, nail-polish-like smell from the ketones, though not everyone can smell this.
She may have mild muscle tremors, especially around the ears, lips and face.
Her droppings may become fewer, small and dry.
advanced: She grinds her teeth, which you can hear as a scraping sound, a sign of pain and distress.
She holds her head up in a stargazing position, presses her head against a wall, walks in circles, or twitches and has fits.
She becomes fully blind and does not respond to her surroundings.
She lies down most of the time, rests her head on her side or flank, and cannot or will not get up.
Her belly may become swollen and she may breathe fast, with signs of dehydration such as sunken eyes and dry gums.
She may abort or the kids may die inside her, which often makes her decline faster.
Without treatment she slips into a coma and usually dies within a few days.

lookalikes.name: Hypocalcaemia (milk fever, low blood calcium)
lookalikes.howToTell: Also strikes does around late pregnancy and kidding and can occur together with pregnancy toxaemia. Does with low calcium are often weak and wobbly with cold ears, and a vet's calcium treatment usually brings quick improvement. Pregnancy toxaemia develops more slowly, with blindness, confusion and ketones in urine, and does not fully respond to calcium alone. Your vet may treat for both.

lookalikes.name: Polioencephalomalacia (thiamine or vitamin B1 deficiency)
lookalikes.howToTell: Causes blindness, stargazing and fits, but can affect goats of any age or sex, not only heavily pregnant does. It often follows a sudden switch to rich feed or grain. Affected goats usually improve quickly with thiamine injections from a vet, and urine ketone tests are normally not high.

lookalikes.name: Listeriosis (circling disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Often linked to spoiled silage or rotting feed. Goats circle in one direction and have one-sided signs such as a drooping ear, eyelid or lip and dribbling saliva from one side. It can affect any goat, not only late-pregnant ones, and it can also infect people, so wear gloves.

lookalikes.name: Heartwater (East Coast heartwater, a tick-borne disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Spread by bont ticks and causes a high fever, chewing movements, high-stepping walk, fits and sudden death in goats of any age. Pregnancy toxaemia does not usually cause a high fever at the start. Check for ticks, take her temperature and tell the vet about tick control.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects pregnancy toxaemia from the history: a doe in the last weeks of pregnancy, often with a big belly suggesting twins or triplets, who has stopped eating and shows nervous signs. The vet will examine her, check her temperature, hydration, eyesight and reflexes, and may feel or scan the belly to count the kids and check if they are alive. The most useful quick tests measure ketones. A drop of blood can be tested with a hand-held ketone meter, or urine can be tested with ketone strips, and high levels confirm the diagnosis. Blood sugar may be low or, later in the disease, unexpectedly high. Blood tests in a laboratory can also check calcium, kidney and liver function. Ultrasound, where available, helps the vet decide whether the kids are alive and whether to induce kidding or do a caesarean. If a doe dies, a post-mortem usually shows a pale, yellow, greasy fatty liver and two or more kids in the womb. To help your vet, write down her mating or expected kidding date if known, what she has been fed in the last month and any recent changes, when she last ate, any recent deworming or stress, and whether other does are off feed. If she passes urine, you can collect some in a clean container for testing.
firstSteps: Call your vet or animal health provider immediately, and tell them the doe is heavily pregnant and showing nervous signs, because this is treated as an emergency.
Move her gently to a quiet, clean, dry, shaded pen with soft bedding, away from stronger goats that may push or butt her, but within sight or sound of a companion to reduce stress.

If she is lying down, prop her up on her chest using bags of feed or bales on either side, and turn her to the other side every few hours, as lying flat on her side can cause bloat and breathing problems.

Offer clean fresh water within easy reach, and tempt her with her favourite palatable feeds such as good leafy hay, fresh sweet potato vines, lucerne or fresh browse, but never force feed or pour liquids into the mouth of a doe that cannot swallow properly, as it can go into her lungs.
Do not give any drug, injection or home remedy on your own, and do not try to pull kids out unless she is actually in labour and your vet has guided you, to avoid tearing or infection.
Check all the other does in late pregnancy straight away, as they are on the same feed and may be in the early stage, and tell your vet about any that are eating less or standing apart.
Wear gloves if she aborts or kids, handle dead kids and afterbirth carefully, bury or dispose of them properly, and wash your hands well, because birth fluids can carry other infections.
Write down when the signs started, what she has eaten, her expected kidding date, and any changes you notice, so the vet can act quickly.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment aims to give the doe energy quickly, correct dehydration and acid build-up, and often to remove the cause, which is the heavy pregnancy. In early cases a vet commonly prescribes an oral energy source such as propylene glycol or glycerol, given by drench for several days, often with calcium, as low calcium frequently occurs at the same time. Sicker does may need glucose (dextrose) and fluids given into the vein, B vitamins, and sometimes insulin or other supportive drugs. If the doe is close to her due date, or not responding, the vet may decide to end the pregnancy. In goats this is usually done by inducing kidding with a prostaglandin injection, sometimes with a corticosteroid such as dexamethasone, and kids are typically born a day or two later. In very sick does, or where kids are dead, a caesarean section may be the best option to save the doe. Kids born early may be weak and need warmth, colostrum and careful nursing. Antibiotics may be used if there are dead kids, a retained afterbirth or surgery, because of the risk of infection, and these should only be used when a vet decides they are needed, at the full prescribed course, to avoid antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to drugs). All treatments, doses and schedules must be prescribed by a vet. Many of the drugs used, including antibiotics and some hormones, have milk and meat withdrawal periods, so ask your vet how long to discard milk and how long before the doe can be slaughtered. Expect daily check-ups in the first days; improvement, if it comes, is usually seen as a return of appetite.
prevention: Plan breeding and keep records of mating dates so you know which does are in the last six weeks of pregnancy and can feed and watch them more closely.
Aim for does in moderate body condition at mating, neither fat nor thin, by checking body condition regularly by feeling over the back and ribs, and adjust feeding gradually.

In the last four to six weeks of pregnancy, slowly increase the energy in the diet with good quality hay, legumes such as lucerne or desmodium, and a small, gradually rising amount of concentrate such as dairy meal or maize germ, as advised by your extension officer or vet.

Avoid sudden feed changes and never let late-pregnant does go hungry, especially during the dry season or drought; store hay, silage or crop residues ahead of time and use them before pasture runs out.
Give enough trough space so all does can eat at the same time, and separate late-pregnant does or timid, old and thin does so stronger goats do not push them away from feed.
Control worms, especially wireworm, with a planned programme based on vet advice, and check eyelids for paleness, as anaemic does eat less and are at higher risk.
Keep feet trimmed and treat lameness, check teeth of older does, and control ticks, because any illness that reduces appetite can trigger the disease.
Reduce stress in late pregnancy by avoiding long transport, rough handling, overcrowding, cold and wet housing, and attacks by dogs, and provide dry, draught-free shelter during the rains.
Where possible, ask your vet about scanning does to find those carrying multiple kids, and give them extra attention and feed.
Provide a balanced mineral lick with salt, calcium and phosphorus, and fresh clean water at all times.
detail.impact: Pregnancy toxaemia can cost a smallholder dearly. A doe that dies takes with her the kids she was carrying, so one case can mean the loss of two or three animals at once. For dairy goat keepers, losing a good doe also means losing a whole lactation of milk, which is often a key source of household nutrition and cash. Treatment, vet visits, possible caesarean and nursing of weak premature kids add costs. Does that survive may have a slow recovery, produce less milk, have a retained afterbirth, or take longer to get back in kid. When several does are affected in a herd, especially in drought years in pastoral areas, it can wipe out a season's kid crop. Because it is largely caused by feeding, good planning of late-pregnancy nutrition is one of the best-value investments a goat farmer can make.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends strongly on how early treatment begins. Does treated in the early stage, while still standing and eating a little, have a reasonable chance of recovery, especially if the kids are born or removed soon after. Once a doe is lying down, blind or in a coma, the chances fall sharply and many die even with intensive vet care. Does carrying dead kids, very fat does, and those with liver or kidney failure have a poorer outlook. Kids may survive if they are close to full term and delivered in time, but premature or weak kids need careful nursing. A doe that recovers can kid normally in future, but she should be managed carefully in her next pregnancy, as the same feeding and conditions can cause it again.

faqs.q: Why does it mostly happen to does carrying twins or triplets?
faqs.a: Kids grow fastest in the last weeks of pregnancy and need a lot of sugar from the mother. Two or three kids need much more energy than one, while the big womb presses on the stomach so the doe cannot eat more to keep up. That gap between what she eats and what the kids need is what leads to the disease.

faqs.q: My doe is very fat. Isn't that good for pregnancy?
faqs.a: No. Very fat does are actually at higher risk. Fat inside the belly reduces the space for feed, so they eat less, and when they start breaking down their large fat stores, the liver gets overloaded. The goal is moderate body condition, where you can feel the backbone and ribs with gentle pressure but they are not sharp.

faqs.q: Can I just give her sugar or glucose water at home?
faqs.a: Do not give home remedies or drugs without your vet, and never pour liquid into the mouth of a doe that is dull or lying down, as it can go into her lungs and cause pneumonia. Ordinary sugar is also not an effective treatment for this condition in goats. Your vet can prescribe the right energy drench and other treatment, and will tell you how to give it safely.

faqs.q: Will the vet have to remove the kids?
faqs.a: Not always. If treatment starts early, some does recover and kid normally. But if she is close to her due date, not improving, or the kids have died, the vet may induce kidding or do a caesarean, because removing the pregnancy is often what saves the doe. The vet will explain the chances for both the doe and the kids.

faqs.q: Is it contagious? Should I worry about my other goats?
faqs.a: It is not contagious, so other goats cannot catch it from her. But other late-pregnant does on the same feed are at the same risk, so check them all at once, look for any that are eating less or standing alone, and improve the feeding of the whole group straight away.

faqs.q: How much concentrate should I give in late pregnancy?
faqs.a: It depends on the breed, body condition, number of kids expected, and the quality of the forage you have. Increase concentrate slowly over the last four to six weeks, never in sudden large amounts, and make sure good hay or browse is always available. Your extension officer or vet can help you work out a ration that suits your goats and your feeds.

products.role: Can be used as a supportive aid for liver function and digestive stress in late-pregnant does and during recovery, as advised by your vet, alongside proper energy feeding and vet treatment; it does not treat pregnancy toxaemia or replace the vet's energy and fluid therapy.

An oral rehydration solution that may help a recovering doe stay hydrated when she is alert and swallowing normally, used only with your vet's guidance and never forced into a doe that is dull or lying down; it supports recovery but does not cure the condition.

pregnancy-toxaemia.seoDescription: Pregnancy toxaemia in goats: spot dullness, blindness and teeth grinding in late-pregnant does, act fast, and prevent it with good late-pregnancy feeding.

card.headline: Swollen, drum-tight left side of belly
card.look: The goat's left side, just behind the ribs and below the backbone, bulges outwards and feels tight like a drum when you tap it. The goat is restless, may kick at its belly, grunt, and breathe fast with its mouth open.
card.action: Stop all feeding at once, keep the goat standing and walking gently, and call your vet immediately, because bloat can kill within hours.

detail.summary: Bloat is when gas builds up in the rumen, the goat's large first stomach, faster than the goat can burp it out. The rumen swells, presses on the lungs and heart, and the goat can die from lack of air within a few hours. It usually follows a sudden feed of lush legumes such as lucerne, desmodium or sweet potato vines, or a large amount of grain. It is a true emergency, but it is also largely preventable with careful feeding.
detail.cause: A goat's rumen works like a fermentation tank. Microbes break down feed and make large amounts of gas, which the goat normally gets rid of by belching many times an hour. Bloat happens when that gas cannot escape. There are two main types. In frothy bloat, the most common type in goats, lush legumes or young wet pasture release substances that create a stable foam, a bit like soap bubbles. The gas is trapped inside millions of tiny bubbles, so the goat cannot belch it up. Grain overload can also produce froth and makes the rumen acidic (sour), which slows the rumen down further. In free-gas bloat, the gas forms a normal pocket but something stops it coming out. This can be a blockage in the throat or food pipe (called choke), for example a piece of avocado, Irish potato, mango, maize cob or plastic, or the goat lying stuck on its side or back, or a rumen that has stopped moving because of illness or acidosis. As the rumen swells it pushes forward against the diaphragm (the muscle sheet between chest and belly). The lungs cannot fill properly and blood flow back to the heart is squeezed, so the goat struggles to breathe, becomes weak, collapses and can die of suffocation and heart failure.
spread: Bloat is not infectious and does not spread from goat to goat, but several goats can bloat at the same time because they ate the same feed.
Sudden access to lush legumes such as lucerne, desmodium, clover or bean leaves, especially when the goats are hungry, is the most common trigger of frothy bloat.
Grazing or feeding fresh, wet fodder, for example morning dew, or forage cut after rain in the long or short rains, makes frothy bloat more likely.
Overeating grain, maize bran, dairy meal, leftover ugali, bread or kitchen waste, for example when goats break into a feed store, can cause bloat and acid indigestion.
Large pieces of root crops or fruits such as potatoes, avocados, mangoes or carrots can lodge in the throat and block belching, causing free-gas bloat.
Sudden changes in diet, irregular feeding times, and feeding cut fodder that has heated or started to ferment in a heap can all upset the rumen.
A goat that is cast, meaning stuck lying on its side or back, cannot belch properly and may bloat quickly.
detail.atRisk: Any goat can bloat, but the risk is highest in zero-grazed and semi-zero-grazed dairy goats such as Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine and their crosses, which are often fed cut lucerne, desmodium or sweet potato vines. Goats that are greedy eaters, very hungry after a long time without feed, or newly moved onto lush pasture are at high risk. Weaned kids and young goats moved suddenly onto concentrates are also vulnerable. Risk rises during the long and short rains, when pasture is young, wet and growing fast. Free-range and pastoral goats are less often affected by legume bloat, but can bloat after raiding crops, grain stores or kitchen waste, or after choking on fruit or plastic. Goats that are sick, heavily pregnant or weak may struggle to belch normally and are more likely to bloat or to die from it.

early: The left side of the belly, high up just behind the last rib, starts to bulge outwards and looks fuller than the right side.
When you tap the swollen left side with your fingers it sounds hollow, like a drum, and feels tight.
The goat stops eating and stops chewing the cud, and you hear little or no belching.
The goat is restless, gets up and lies down often, stamps its feet, kicks at its belly, or looks round at its flank.
The goat may grunt, groan or cry, and may grind its teeth because of pain.
You may see frequent passing of small amounts of dung or urine as the goat strains.
advanced: The whole belly becomes very swollen, and the left side may stick out above the line of the backbone.
Breathing becomes fast and difficult, with the mouth open, tongue sticking out, neck stretched forward and drooling.
The goat stands with its legs spread apart, staggers, or becomes unwilling to move.
Gums and the inside of the eyelids may turn bluish or dark because of poor oxygen.
The goat collapses, lies flat and cannot rise.
Without help, death can follow quickly, sometimes within an hour or two of severe signs appearing, and goats are sometimes simply found dead with a hugely swollen belly.

lookalikes.name: Grain overload (rumen acidosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: This often comes together with bloat after goats eat too much grain or concentrate. The belly may look full but often feels more doughy or sloshy than drum-tight, and the goat usually has watery, sour-smelling diarrhoea, looks dull and dehydrated, and may stagger or seem blind. A history of breaking into the feed store is a strong clue.

lookalikes.name: Choke (blocked food pipe)
lookalikes.howToTell: Choke can cause free-gas bloat, but the main signs come first: heavy drooling, repeated swallowing or retching, coughing, stretching the neck, and feed or saliva coming out of the nose or mouth. You may feel a lump on the left side of the neck. Do not push your hand down the throat; call the vet.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia (pulpy kidney or overeating disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is a bacterial toxin disease that also follows sudden rich feeding. Goats may show diarrhoea, nervous signs such as head pressing, circling or convulsions, and often die suddenly. The belly swelling is usually less marked than in bloat and the left side is not drum-tight early on. A post-mortem by a vet is often needed to tell them apart. Vaccination helps prevent it.

lookalikes.name: Late pregnancy or pregnancy toxaemia
lookalikes.howToTell: A heavily pregnant doe has a large belly on both sides, it does not sound like a drum when tapped, and it develops over weeks, not hours. Pregnancy toxaemia causes dullness, poor appetite, trembling and lying down, but without the sudden tight, hollow left-sided swelling of bloat.

detail.diagnosis: Bloat is usually diagnosed on the farm from the signs and the feeding history. The vet looks at the shape of the belly, taps the left flank to hear the drum-like sound, and listens for rumen movements and belching. Passing a stomach tube through the mouth into the rumen is both a test and a treatment. If a lot of gas rushes out and the swelling goes down, it is free-gas bloat. If little gas comes out and froth blocks the tube, it is frothy bloat. If the tube will not pass, it points to choke. The vet may smell or check the rumen fluid for sourness if grain overload is suspected. If a goat dies, a post-mortem can confirm bloat and rule out conditions like enterotoxaemia. To help the vet, note exactly what the goat ate in the last 24 hours, including any new fodder, wet forage or grain; when the signs started; how many goats are affected; and any recent feed changes. Keep a sample of the suspect feed aside.
firstSteps: Remove all feed immediately from the affected goat and from any other goats that ate the same fodder, and move the group off the lush pasture or legume plot.
Phone your vet or the nearest animal health assistant at once and tell them it is bloat, as minutes matter, and be ready to describe the feed and how fast the swelling is growing.
Keep the goat standing and walk it slowly and gently, because movement helps the rumen work and helps gas escape, but never chase or run it.
Stand the goat with its front legs higher than its back legs, for example on a slope or with front feet on a low raised platform, which takes pressure off the lungs and helps belching.
Place a clean, smooth stick or a piece of rope across the mouth like a horse's bit and tie it gently behind the horns, as this makes the goat chew and salivate and can help it belch.
Gently massage the left side of the belly with a flat hand, unless this causes clear pain.
If the goat is lying on its side or back, help it roll up to rest on its chest or stand, as it cannot belch properly lying flat.

Do not pour liquids, oils or home remedies into the mouth unless your vet tells you to by phone, because a distressed goat can easily inhale liquid into its lungs, and never try to puncture the belly with a knife or sharp object yourself, as this can cause fatal infection and does not release frothy bloat.
Check all other goats that shared the feed every 15 to 30 minutes for the next several hours, because more cases often appear.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on the type of bloat and how severe it is. For free-gas bloat, the vet usually passes a stomach tube through the mouth into the rumen to let the gas out, which often gives quick relief. If there is choke, the vet will try to carefully move or remove the blockage. For frothy bloat, the tube alone does not work well because the gas is trapped in foam, so the vet gives an anti-foaming agent through the tube or by drench. Commonly used products include poloxalene, dimethicone or other silicone-based anti-foams, surfactants such as docusate, and vegetable or mineral oils. These break the froth so the goat can burp the gas out. Where grain overload is part of the problem, the vet may give an antacid such as magnesium oxide or magnesium hydroxide into the rumen, fluids into a vein to correct dehydration and acid, and sometimes B vitamins such as thiamine, pain relief or anti-inflammatory drugs. Antibiotics are not a treatment for bloat itself. A vet may only use them where there is a real risk of secondary infection, for example after severe acidosis or after an emergency puncture, and they should never be used routinely, because unnecessary antibiotic use builds antimicrobial resistance. In a life-threatening case where the goat is about to collapse, the vet may make an emergency puncture of the rumen with a trocar and cannula (a hollow spike placed through the left flank) or perform a rumenotomy, which is surgery to open the rumen and empty it. All treatments, including doses and products, must be chosen and prescribed by a vet. Any drug used will carry milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time you must wait before milk or meat can be sold or eaten, and you must follow these exactly. After treatment, expect the goat to be kept on good quality grass hay and water only for a day or more, with fresh legumes and grain reintroduced slowly as the vet advises. Recovery can take a few days, especially after grain overload.
prevention: Always give goats a feed of dry grass hay or mature grass before giving lucerne, desmodium, sweet potato vines or other legumes, so they are not hungry and greedy when they reach the rich feed.
Wilt freshly cut legumes in the shade for several hours before feeding, and avoid feeding forage that is wet with dew or rain, especially during the long and short rains.
Mix legumes with grass or other fibre, rather than feeding legumes alone, and introduce any new legume plot or lush pasture gradually over one to two weeks.
Introduce grain, dairy meal, maize bran and other concentrates slowly over several weeks, split them into small feeds through the day, and never let goats eat large amounts at once.
Store grain, concentrates and kitchen waste securely in a goat-proof store, because goats that break in can bloat or develop acidosis quickly.
Chop root crops and fruits such as potatoes, carrots and avocados into small pieces, or avoid feeding them, to prevent choke, and keep plastic bags and string away from goats.
Keep feeding times regular, provide clean water at all times, and avoid feeding cut fodder that has heated up or started fermenting in a pile.

Watch goats closely for the first hour or two after they are let onto new pasture or fed a new feed, so you can catch early swelling, and speak to your vet about anti-bloat products if you must graze high-risk legume pasture regularly.
Keep goats vaccinated against enterotoxaemia as advised by your vet, because the same rich feeding that causes bloat also raises the risk of this deadly disease.
detail.impact: Bloat can kill a healthy, well-fed goat in a few hours, and it often strikes the best animals, such as high-yielding dairy does that are fed the richest fodder. Losing a dairy goat means losing its milk income, its future kids and the money spent raising it, which is a heavy blow for a smallholder with only a few animals. Several goats can be affected at once when a whole group eats the same lucerne or breaks into the grain store. Goats that survive may drop sharply in milk yield for some days, and pregnant does may abort after severe stress. Severe grain overload can leave lasting damage to the rumen wall and liver, causing poor growth and condition afterwards. There are also costs of emergency vet call-outs, often at night and over long distances, and milk that must be discarded during drug withdrawal periods. Because bloat is mostly caused by feeding practices, good feed management protects both the animals and the farm income.
detail.humanHealth: Bloat itself does not infect people, and meat from a goat that died of bloat should not be eaten because the cause of death cannot be confirmed without a vet and the carcass spoils quickly. If your goat is treated with drugs, follow the milk and meat withdrawal periods your vet gives you, and do not sell or consume milk or meat before that time, to avoid drug residues reaching your family or customers.
detail.outlook: If bloat is caught early and the goat is treated quickly, most goats recover well, often within hours once the gas is released. Free-gas bloat is usually easier to relieve with a stomach tube. Frothy bloat needs anti-foaming treatment and can be harder to resolve. The outlook becomes poor once the goat is struggling badly for breath, has bluish gums or has collapsed, and some goats die even with treatment. Goats with bloat caused by grain overload may take several days to recover and can have lasting rumen or liver damage. A goat that bloated once can bloat again if the feeding causes are not corrected, so changing how you feed is the key to preventing repeat cases.

faqs.q: Can I use cooking oil to treat bloat?
faqs.a: Vegetable oils are one of the anti-foaming agents vets sometimes use for frothy bloat, because they break up the foam. However, a bloated goat is distressed and short of breath, and liquids poured into the mouth can easily go down into the lungs and cause pneumonia or choking. Oil also does little for free-gas bloat or choke. Only give anything by mouth if your vet tells you to over the phone and explains how, and get the vet to the goat as quickly as possible.

faqs.q: Should I stab the goat's belly to let the gas out?
faqs.a: No, not unless you have been trained and it is the only way to save a goat that is collapsing with no vet on the way. Stabbing with a knife or sharp object often causes deadly infection in the belly, can hit the wrong organ, and does not release frothy bloat, which is the most common type, because the gas is trapped in foam. Vets use a proper trocar and cannula in the right place on the left flank, and only as an emergency measure. Ask your vet or extension officer for training if you farm far from veterinary help.

faqs.q: Is lucerne or desmodium bad for goats?
faqs.a: No. These legumes are excellent, protein-rich feeds that boost milk and growth. The problem is how they are fed. Feed hay or grass first, wilt fresh legumes before feeding, avoid wet forage, mix legumes with grass and make changes gradually. With these steps, most farmers can feed legumes safely.

faqs.q: Why did my goat bloat after the rains started?
faqs.a: During the long and short rains pasture and fodder grow fast, are young, soft and full of water and protein. This type of forage is the most likely to form a stable froth in the rumen. Forage wet with rain or dew adds to the risk. Take extra care during the rains by giving dry hay before turning goats out, letting dew dry before grazing and wilting cut fodder.

faqs.q: How can I tell bloat from a goat that is just full or pregnant?
faqs.a: A goat that has eaten well is round on both sides but stays bright, chews cud and breathes normally. A pregnant doe gets bigger slowly over weeks and does not sound like a drum when tapped. Bloat comes on over hours, the swelling is mainly high on the left side, it sounds hollow and tight when tapped, and the goat is restless, stops chewing cud and may struggle to breathe. If in doubt, treat it as bloat and call the vet.

faqs.q: Can bloat spread to my other goats?
faqs.a: Bloat is not contagious, so a bloated goat will not infect the others. But goats that ate the same feed are at the same risk and can bloat at the same time or shortly after. Remove the suspect feed from all goats and keep checking them every 15 to 30 minutes for several hours.

products.role: Can be used during recovery, once the vet has relieved the bloat and advised that the goat can be fed again, to support digestion and the liver after the digestive stress of bloat or grain overload; it does not treat bloat and must never be given to a goat that is still bloated.

An oral rehydration solution the vet may advise offering after the bloat has been relieved, particularly where grain overload has caused diarrhoea or dehydration, to help the goat replace lost fluids and salts while it recovers; it is not a treatment for bloat and should not be drenched into a distressed, bloated goat.
