card.headline: High fever, then circling and paddling
card.look: The goat stops eating, breathes fast and feels very hot. Within a day or two it may walk with high, unsteady steps, chew constantly, circle, then fall on its side paddling its legs. Some goats are simply found dead.
card.action: Call your vet immediately at the first sign of fever, especially if there are bont ticks on the herd. Early treatment is the only real chance of saving the goat.

detail.summary: Heartwater is a serious disease of goats, sheep and cattle caused by a tiny germ called Ehrlichia ruminantium. It is spread by the bont tick, the large tick with colourful striped legs. Goats get a high fever and then brain signs such as circling, twitching and paddling, and many die within days without fast treatment. It is one of the most important tick-borne killers of exotic and crossbred dairy goats in Kenya.
detail.cause: Heartwater is caused by Ehrlichia ruminantium, a rickettsia. A rickettsia is a very small germ that can only live inside the cells of an animal. When an infected bont tick feeds on a goat, the germ passes into the blood. It then enters and multiplies inside the cells lining the small blood vessels, especially in the brain, lungs and around the heart. The damaged vessels become leaky, so fluid seeps out into the tissues. Fluid collects around the heart (this is where the name 'heartwater' comes from), in the chest and in the lungs, which makes breathing hard. Swelling and leaking vessels in the brain cause the nervous signs: unsteady walking, circling, chewing movements, twitching and fits. Signs usually appear about two to three weeks after the infected tick bite, although this period varies. By the time nervous signs show, brain damage is often severe, which is why the disease kills so quickly.
spread: The main carrier in Kenya and East Africa is the bont tick, Amblyomma variegatum, a large tick with a hard, ornamented back and striped legs.
Bont ticks pick up the germ by feeding on an infected or carrier animal as young ticks, then pass it on when they feed again at the next stage of their life.
Bont ticks prefer the lower parts of the body, so check the udder, groin, armpits, under the tail, around the feet and the brisket.
Recovered animals and wild ruminants can carry the germ quietly for a long time, keeping it in the tick population on that land.
Buying goats, or moving goats into an area with bont ticks, is a common trigger for outbreaks, because the new animals have no immunity.
Tick numbers rise during and after the long and short rains, so cases often increase in these seasons.
Heartwater does not spread directly from goat to goat by contact; ticks are needed, although infected blood (for example from shared needles) can in theory carry the germ.
detail.atRisk: Exotic dairy and meat breeds such as Saanen, Toggenburg, Alpine, Anglo-Nubian and Boer, and their crosses, are the most at risk, particularly when they come from tick-free or well-dipped farms into bont tick areas. Indigenous goats such as the Small East African and Galla are generally more resistant, though they can still fall sick and die. Very young kids often have some natural resistance for a short time after birth, especially when born to immune mothers, so older kids and young adults moved onto infected pasture are a common group to fall sick. Goats that graze bushy or grassy land in warm, wetter areas, free-range and pastoral herds mixing with cattle, and zero-grazed goats fed with cut grass carrying ticks are all exposed. Farms where tick control suddenly stops after years of heavy dipping can also see outbreaks, because the animals never built immunity.

early: High fever: the goat feels hot, and a rectal thermometer often reads above 40°C, sometimes over 41°C (normal is roughly 38.5–39.5°C).
Loss of appetite, standing apart from the herd and looking dull or sleepy.
Fast or laboured breathing, sometimes with a slight cough.
Drop in milk yield in milking does.
Bont ticks attached to the udder, groin, feet, tail area or brisket.
Some goats have soft dung or diarrhoea.
advanced: Constant chewing movements, tongue flicking in and out, and twitching of the eyelids or face.
High-stepping, stiff or wobbly walk, as if stepping over objects.
Walking in circles, pressing the head against walls, or standing with the head held oddly.
Falling on the side with legs paddling as if running, head thrown back, and eyes flicking from side to side.
Frothy fluid from the nose or very difficult breathing as the lungs fill with fluid.
Sudden death, sometimes with no signs seen beforehand, especially in highly susceptible exotic goats.

lookalikes.name: Rabies
lookalikes.howToTell: Rabies also causes strange behaviour and paralysis, but there is often a history of a dog or wild animal bite, the goat may be aggressive, drool heavily, bleat strangely, and fever is not usually so marked. Rabies is deadly to people and must be reported. If in doubt, do not touch the mouth and tell your vet.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia (pulpy kidney)
lookalikes.howToTell: Caused by Clostridium bacteria after a sudden change to rich feed or grain. It also causes fits and sudden death, but usually in well-fed, fast-growing goats, often with diarrhoea and without a high fever. Vaccination history and recent feed changes help tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Polioencephalomalacia (thiamine deficiency)
lookalikes.howToTell: Goats appear blind, star-gaze with the head bent backwards and may fall, but usually have a normal temperature and no ticks need be involved. It often follows feed changes and goats may improve quickly when a vet gives vitamin B1 (thiamine).

lookalikes.name: Listeriosis (circling disease)
lookalikes.howToTell: Linked to spoiled silage or feed. The goat often circles in one direction and has a one-sided droopy ear, eyelid or lip with drooling. It develops more slowly over several days than heartwater.

detail.diagnosis: Your vet will suspect heartwater from high fever followed by nervous signs in goats carrying bont ticks, especially newly bought or exotic animals. In a live goat, a blood sample can be tested by PCR, a laboratory test that detects the germ's genetic material, but results take time, so treatment usually starts on suspicion. After death, a post-mortem is very helpful. The vet often finds yellowish fluid around the heart and in the chest, wet, swollen lungs and froth in the windpipe. The most reliable field test is a brain smear: a small piece of brain is crushed on a glass slide and stained, and under the microscope the germ can be seen as clusters inside the brain's small blood vessel cells. To help your vet, record the temperatures you have taken, when signs started, which goats are affected, any recent purchases or movements, and your tick control and dipping dates. Keep a few ticks in a closed container if possible, and if a goat dies, keep the carcass cool and covered and call the vet quickly for a post-mortem rather than opening it yourself.
firstSteps: Call your vet or County Veterinary Officer immediately; with heartwater, hours matter, and treatment works best before nervous signs appear.
Move the sick goat to a quiet, shaded, well-ventilated pen with soft bedding such as dry straw, away from walls or objects it could hit during fits.
Do not force-drench a goat that is chewing, fitting or lying down, because liquid can go into the lungs and kill it; offer clean water in a shallow container only if it can swallow normally.
Wear gloves when handling a goat with nervous signs and keep your hands out of its mouth, because rabies can look similar.
Take the rectal temperature of every goat in the herd, morning and evening, and tell the vet about any goat above about 40°C so they can treat early.
Check all goats for bont ticks and remove them carefully with gloves, gripping close to the skin; burn or crush them in a closed container, and do not squeeze ticks with bare fingers.
Stop buying, selling or moving goats until the vet has seen the herd, and keep the herd off the bushiest, most tick-infested grazing for now.
Write down dates, signs, temperatures, deaths and recent tick treatments so you can give the vet a clear history.
detail.vetTreatment: Heartwater can be treated, but only if treatment starts early, ideally while the goat has fever and before nervous signs are severe. The usual treatment is an antibiotic from the tetracycline group, most commonly oxytetracycline, given by injection; the vet decides the product, route, dose and how many days. Goats that already have fits or are lying paddling often die even with treatment, and some that survive have lasting brain damage. The vet may also give supportive care, such as anti-inflammatory drugs, fluids and careful nursing, and may treat other at-risk goats in the herd that have fever. All treatment must be prescribed by a vet; do not inject leftover or shop-bought antibiotics on your own, because the wrong drug, dose or timing wastes precious time and encourages antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines. Tetracyclines leave residues, so milk and meat from treated goats must not be used or sold until the withdrawal period on the product label, as advised by your vet, has passed. Recovered goats usually develop immunity that lasts for some time, often helped by continued natural low-level tick challenge.
prevention: Control bont ticks with regular spraying, dipping or pour-on acaricides (tick-killing chemicals) recommended by your vet or agrovet, paying special attention to the udder, groin, feet and tail area.
Follow the label exactly for dilution and timing, and rotate acaricide types on your vet's advice to slow tick resistance.
Hand-pick or spot-treat ticks on valuable goats between dips, especially in the long and short rains when tick numbers peak.

Be careful when introducing exotic or crossbred goats from tick-free areas: keep them under strict tick control, check temperatures daily for the first month or more, and have a vet ready to treat early.
In zero-grazing units, cut fodder away from bushy edges where possible, and keep the shed and surroundings clear of long grass and bush that shelter ticks.

Ask your County Veterinary Officer whether any heartwater vaccine or controlled immunisation is available in your area; at present there is no widely used commercial vaccine in Kenya, and the methods used elsewhere in Africa need careful vet supervision.
Keep goats well fed, watered and dewormed so their bodies cope better with any infection, and avoid stressing new arrivals.

Talk to your vet about 'endemic stability' if you keep indigenous goats in an area where heartwater is common: completely stopping tick contact can leave animals without immunity, so tick control should be planned rather than suddenly started or stopped.
detail.impact: Heartwater is one of the costliest diseases for Kenyan dairy goat keepers. A single exotic Saanen or Toggenburg doe represents a large investment, and losing her means losing milk income, future kids and breeding stock. Deaths can be sudden and several goats may be lost in an outbreak, especially soon after buying new animals. Sick goats that survive often lose weight, stop milking for a time and may be left with nervous damage. There are also costs for vet visits, antibiotics, milk discarded during withdrawal periods, and regular acaricides. The fear of heartwater also limits farmers' ability to upgrade herds with improved breeds in tick-infested areas, which holds back productivity.
detail.humanHealth: Heartwater is not considered a meaningful risk to people; human infection with this germ is very rare and not well proven. However, bont ticks can bite people and can carry other germs, such as the one causing African tick-bite fever, so wear gloves when removing ticks and check yourself after working with the herd. Because rabies can look similar, never put bare hands in the mouth of a goat with nervous signs and seek medical advice if you are bitten. Do not use milk or meat from goats treated with antibiotics until the withdrawal period advised by your vet is over, to avoid drug residues in food.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends mostly on how early treatment starts. Goats treated during the fever stage, before nervous signs, have a reasonable chance of recovery. Once a goat is circling, fitting or paddling on its side, the chance of survival is poor, and some survivors have lasting problems. Sudden-death cases cannot be saved. Indigenous goats and those with previous exposure tend to have milder disease than newly introduced exotic breeds. Good nursing in a quiet, shaded pen, with water and soft feed once the goat can swallow, helps recovery. Herds with planned tick control and daily temperature checks on at-risk goats lose far fewer animals.

faqs.q: How can I tell heartwater from other diseases before the vet comes?
faqs.a: The typical pattern is a goat with bont ticks that first gets a high fever and stops eating, and then within a day or two starts chewing constantly, walking with high steps, circling and falling with paddling legs. Other diseases such as rabies, pulpy kidney and thiamine deficiency can look similar, so only a vet can confirm it. Take the temperature, note the signs and timing, and call the vet straight away.

faqs.q: Can I treat heartwater myself with oxytetracycline from the agrovet?
faqs.a: You should not. Oxytetracycline is the antibiotic vets commonly use, but the right product, dose, route and length of treatment must be decided by a vet. Wrong use can fail to save the goat, leave residues in milk and meat, and build antibiotic resistance. Call the vet early instead, because early professional treatment gives the best chance.

faqs.q: Why do my new Saanen goats die of heartwater while my local goats stay healthy?
faqs.a: Exotic goats from tick-free or heavily dipped farms have never met the germ, so they have no immunity. Local goats have usually been exposed when young and many have natural resistance. New exotic goats need strict tick control, daily temperature checks for the first weeks, and quick vet treatment at the first fever.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine for heartwater in Kenya?
faqs.a: There is no widely used commercial heartwater vaccine in Kenya at present. Some other countries use a live blood-based immunisation followed by antibiotic treatment, but it needs careful vet supervision and cold storage. Ask your County Veterinary Officer about what is available. For now, tick control and early treatment are the main tools.

faqs.q: Can a goat that recovers from heartwater get it again?
faqs.a: Goats that recover usually develop immunity that protects them for some time, especially if they keep meeting low numbers of infected ticks. Immunity may weaken if tick contact stops completely, and there are different strains of the germ, so reinfection is possible. Keep up sensible tick control and watch recovered goats for fever.

faqs.q: Does heartwater spread from a sick goat to the rest of my herd?
faqs.a: Not by direct contact. It needs bont ticks to carry it. But if one goat has heartwater, infected ticks are probably on your land, so other goats are also at risk. Check every goat for ticks and fever, and treat the herd against ticks as your vet advises.

products.role: Once the vet has started treatment and the goat can swallow normally again, RE-COVER rehydration solution offered in drinking water can help replace fluids and support recovery after days of fever and poor intake. It does not treat heartwater, and it must never be drenched into a goat that is fitting, chewing uncontrollably or lying down.

heartwater.imagePrompt: A white Saanen dairy goat lying on its side on dry straw in a shaded wooden pen, legs stretched out in a paddling motion and head slightly arched back, with a few large colourful bont ticks visible on its udder and groin.
heartwater.seoDescription: Heartwater in goats: spot the fever, circling and paddling early, act fast before the vet arrives, and prevent it with bont tick control. Kenya farmer guide.

card.headline: Stiff, weak kids that struggle to stand
card.look: Young kids walk stiffly on trembling legs, stand hunched, or lie down and cannot rise or suckle properly. Some kids that seemed healthy collapse and die suddenly, often after running or being excited.
card.action: Keep the weak kid quiet, warm and resting, make sure it gets colostrum or milk, and call your vet the same day.

aka: Upungufu wa vitamini E na seleniamu
detail.summary: White muscle disease is muscle damage caused by a shortage of selenium and/or vitamin E in the diet. It mostly affects young kids, from birth to a few months old, and can damage both the leg muscles and the heart. Kids may be born weak, become stiff and unable to suckle, or die suddenly. It matters because it kills kids that look like they should thrive, and because the same deficiency quietly lowers growth, fertility and immunity across the whole herd.
detail.cause: Selenium is a trace mineral and vitamin E is a vitamin. Working together, they protect the walls of body cells from damage by harmful by-products of normal energy use, called free radicals (unstable molecules that attack cells). Muscle cells work hard and produce many of these by-products. When a kid lacks selenium, vitamin E, or both, the muscle cells are not protected. They break down and are replaced by scar-like tissue that looks pale or chalky white. This is where the name 'white muscle' comes from. When the leg and back muscles are hit, the kid becomes stiff, weak and shaky. When the muscles used for breathing or swallowing are hit, the kid struggles to breathe or suckle. When the heart muscle is hit, the heart can fail suddenly, often after exercise or stress. The deficiency usually starts in the doe. If her feed and soil are low in selenium, or her feed is low in vitamin E, she cannot pass enough to the kid in the womb or through her colostrum and milk.
spread: White muscle disease is not infectious and does not spread from goat to goat; it appears in several kids at once because they share the same deficient diet.

Soils low in selenium grow pasture and crops low in selenium. Some soils in East Africa are low in selenium, but levels vary widely and are not well mapped, so a farm may be deficient without the farmer knowing.
Vitamin E is high in fresh green grass and browse but falls quickly in dry hay, old stored feed, crop residues and dry-season pasture. Long dry spells and stall feeding on poor hay increase the risk.
Does fed poorly in late pregnancy give birth to kids with low reserves, and their colostrum and milk carry less selenium and vitamin E.
Sudden exercise or stress can trigger signs in a kid that is already deficient, for example being chased, moved, transported, or released to run after being penned.
Feeds that are mouldy or rancid, or high in certain oils, can use up the vitamin E the animal has and make deficiency worse.
Heavy use of sulphur-containing fertilisers on pasture can reduce how much selenium plants take up from the soil.
detail.atRisk: Kids are most at risk, from birth up to about two to three months old, although older kids and occasionally adults can be affected. Fast-growing kids, twins and triplets, and kids of improved dairy breeds such as Toggenburg, Saanen, Alpine and their crosses are often noticed first because they grow quickly and need more. Goats are thought to be at least as sensitive as sheep. Risk is highest where does are kept on poor dry-season grazing, crop residues or old hay in late pregnancy, especially at the end of a long dry season before the long or short rains bring green growth. Zero-grazed dairy goats fed mainly on stored feed with no mineral supplement, and pastoral or free-range flocks on known low-selenium soils, are both at risk. Kids that miss colostrum are at greater risk.

early: The kid walks stiffly, with short, stilted steps, like it is walking on hot ground.
Legs tremble or shake when the kid stands, and it may stand with its back arched and legs bunched under it.
The kid tires quickly, lies down a lot and is slow to follow its mother.
It has trouble suckling: it may want to drink but cannot grip the teat well, or milk dribbles from the mouth because the tongue and throat muscles are weak.
Muscles of the hind legs or shoulders may feel firmer or swollen and the kid may seem sore when you handle them.
The kid stays bright and alert even though its body is weak, which helps tell it apart from infections that make kids dull.
advanced: The kid cannot stand at all and lies on its side or chest, though it may still try to get up.
Fast, laboured breathing or flank breathing when the breathing muscles or heart are affected.
Milk coming from the nose or coughing after feeding, which can lead to pneumonia from inhaled milk.
Kids born weak, unable to stand, or born dead in a group of kids from the same herd.
Sudden collapse and death, sometimes with no warning, especially after running, handling or transport, due to heart damage.
Urine may be darker than normal in some cases because of breakdown products from damaged muscle.

lookalikes.name: Navel ill / joint ill (bacterial infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Joint ill causes hot, swollen, painful joints, often with a swollen or wet navel and fever. The kid is usually dull and off feed. White muscle kids have stiffness without hot swollen joints and are often bright despite weakness.

lookalikes.name: Swayback (copper deficiency, enzootic ataxia)
lookalikes.howToTell: Swayback kids wobble and sway, especially in the hind end, because the nerves are affected, not the muscles. They do not usually have firm, sore muscles, and they do not improve after a vitamin E/selenium treatment. A vet may need blood or post-mortem tests to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Tetanus
lookalikes.howToTell: Tetanus usually follows a wound, castration or disbudding. The kid becomes rigid all over, with a 'sawhorse' stance, a stiff tail, a locked jaw and a third eyelid that flicks across the eye. It overreacts sharply to noise and touch. White muscle kids are weak and stiff but not rigid and jumpy.

lookalikes.name: Starvation, hypothermia or pneumonia in newborns
lookalikes.howToTell: Kids that have not had enough milk are cold, hollow-bellied and dull. Pneumonia causes fever, cough and nasal discharge. These can occur together with white muscle disease, so a vet check is important.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects white muscle disease from the signs, the age of the kids, the season and the feeding history. The vet will examine the muscles, listen to the heart and lungs, and check for fever to rule out infection. Blood tests can show high levels of muscle enzymes (substances that leak out of damaged muscle, such as creatine kinase and AST) and can measure selenium or a selenium-dependent enzyme called glutathione peroxidase. A quick improvement after vet treatment also supports the diagnosis. If a kid dies, a post-mortem is very useful: the vet looks for pale, white or chalky streaks in the leg muscles, diaphragm and heart, and may send liver samples to a laboratory to measure selenium. To help the vet, note how many kids are affected and their ages, when signs started, what the does were fed in late pregnancy, whether they had a mineral lick and which one, any recent vitamin or mineral injections, and whether kids got colostrum. Keep any dead kid cool and covered, not buried, until the vet advises.
firstSteps: Keep the affected kid quiet and still; do not chase it, force it to walk, or let it run, because exercise can cause fatal heart failure.
Move the kid and its mother to a clean, dry, draught-free pen with soft bedding, and keep the kid warm, especially at night.

Make sure the kid gets colostrum in its first hours and milk after that. If it cannot suckle, gently hold it up to the teat or bottle-feed slowly, letting it swallow at its own pace to avoid milk going into the lungs.
If the kid cannot swallow at all, do not pour milk into its mouth; call the vet, who can tube-feed safely.
Turn a kid that is lying down from side to side every few hours and prop it on its chest so it can breathe easier.
Check the other kids and the does for stiffness or weakness and handle all young kids calmly.
Write down the kids affected, their ages, signs and what the does have been eating, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer the same day.
Do not give selenium injections or extra selenium powders on your own, because selenium is poisonous in overdose and the safe range is narrow.
detail.vetTreatment: The vet will usually treat affected kids with a prescribed injectable vitamin E and selenium product, and will often advise treating other kids and pregnant does in the same group. The dose depends on the animal's weight and the product, and must only be decided by a vet, because too much selenium can poison and kill goats. Kids with mainly leg-muscle damage often start to improve within a few days of treatment, but recovery of damaged muscle takes longer. Kids with heart damage may not respond and can still die suddenly. The vet may also give supportive care, such as tube feeding, warmth, and fluids. If milk has entered the lungs or the kid has a secondary pneumonia, the vet may prescribe an antibiotic; antibiotics do not treat the deficiency itself, so they should only be used when a vet finds an infection, and the full prescribed course should be completed to reduce antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to drugs). Ask your vet about milk and meat withdrawal periods, the time after treatment before milk or meat can safely be used, for every product given. The vet will also help you plan herd-level prevention, such as mineral supplements and pre-kidding injections.
prevention: Give goats free access to a good-quality goat or ruminant mineral lick or mineral mix that contains selenium, all year round, and check the label to be sure selenium is included.

Ask your vet whether pregnant does should receive a vitamin E and selenium injection in the last weeks of pregnancy, and whether newborn kids should be treated, especially if you have had cases before.
Do not combine several selenium sources (licks, premixes and injections) without vet advice, because too much selenium is poisonous.

Feed does well in late pregnancy, with green forage, browse or good leafy fodder where possible, since fresh green feed is rich in vitamin E. Plan fodder conservation so that late-pregnant does are not left on dry stalks at the end of the dry season.
Avoid feeding mouldy or rancid feeds, stale concentrates, or old poorly stored hay, which lose vitamin E and can increase the body's need for it.
Make sure every kid gets enough colostrum within the first hours of life, as this is a key source of vitamin E, selenium and protective antibodies.
Handle young kids calmly, avoid sudden hard exercise, and take care when moving, transporting or releasing kids after they have been confined.
If you suspect your area is low in selenium, ask your County Veterinary Officer or KALRO about soil or blood testing, and share results with neighbours, as the problem is often regional.
detail.impact: White muscle disease causes losses through kid deaths, weak kids that need extra labour and feed, slow growth and poor weight at sale. Kids from valuable dairy breeds are costly to lose. The underlying deficiency also affects adults: low selenium and vitamin E are linked to retained afterbirth, poorer fertility, weaker immunity and more infections such as mastitis and diarrhoea in kids, which together reduce milk and meat income. Because it is not infectious, many farmers do not notice the pattern and keep losing kids each kidding season. The good news is that prevention with proper minerals and feeding is usually cheaper than losing even one kid.
detail.humanHealth: White muscle disease itself does not infect people. However, the vitamin E/selenium products and any antibiotics used in treatment can leave residues in milk and meat. Follow the withdrawal periods your vet gives before drinking or selling milk or slaughtering a treated goat. Store selenium products safely away from children and other animals.
detail.outlook: Kids with mild to moderate stiffness that are treated early by a vet often recover well and can grow normally, although muscle healing takes time. Kids that cannot stand, cannot swallow or have breathing problems have a poorer outlook, and those with heart damage may die suddenly even after treatment. Kids born weak or that miss colostrum also do less well. Recovery is helped by early treatment, rest, warmth, good feeding and preventing pneumonia. Once you know your herd is at risk, good prevention can greatly reduce future cases.

faqs.q: Can I just buy a selenium injection at the agrovet and treat my kids myself?
faqs.a: It is not safe to do this without a vet. Selenium has a very narrow safe range, and a small overdose can poison and kill a goat, especially a small kid. The right product and dose depend on weight, age and what else the goats are getting. Call your vet, who can confirm the diagnosis, prescribe the right treatment and advise on withdrawal periods.

faqs.q: Why did my healthy-looking kid die suddenly after I let it out to run?
faqs.a: In white muscle disease, the heart muscle can be damaged before you see any stiffness. When the kid suddenly runs or gets excited, the weak heart cannot cope and fails. This is why deficient kids should be handled calmly, and why a sudden death in a young kid should be checked by a vet, ideally with a post-mortem.

faqs.q: I give my goats a salt lick. Is that enough?
faqs.a: Plain salt licks give sodium only and do not contain selenium. Choose a mineral lick or mix made for goats or ruminants that lists selenium on the label. Ask your vet or agrovet to help you choose one, and do not add other selenium products on top without advice.

faqs.q: Does this only happen in the dry season?
faqs.a: It can happen at any time, but it is more common when does have been on dry pasture, old hay or crop residues in late pregnancy, because vitamin E levels in dry feed are low. Many cases appear in kids born near the end of a long dry season, before the rains bring fresh green growth. Selenium deficiency depends on the soil, so it can occur all year on low-selenium land.

faqs.q: Will my other goats catch it?
faqs.a: No, white muscle disease is not contagious. But if one kid has it, others on the same farm are likely low too because they share the same feed and soil. Ask your vet whether the other kids and pregnant does should be checked or treated, and improve minerals and feeding for the whole herd.

faqs.q: Can adult goats get white muscle disease?
faqs.a: It is mainly a disease of young kids, but older goats can sometimes show stiffness or heart problems. More often, adults with low selenium and vitamin E show poor fertility, retained afterbirth and weaker resistance to infections. Correcting the deficiency benefits the whole herd.

products.role: Supplies vitamin E (with vitamins A and D3) to help top up vitamin E in does in late pregnancy and in growing kids during the dry season or on stored feed, as part of a vet-guided prevention plan. It does not contain selenium, so it does not replace a selenium-containing mineral or any vitamin E/selenium treatment your vet prescribes.

white-muscle-disease.seoDescription: White muscle disease in goats: spot stiff, weak kids early, act safely before the vet arrives, and prevent vitamin E and selenium deficiency on your farm.

card.headline: Abortion in the last months of pregnancy
card.look: A doe loses her kid in the fourth or fifth month of pregnancy, or gives birth to dead or very weak kids, and the afterbirth often stays hanging from her for many hours. Several does in the same herd may abort around the same time.
card.action: Do not touch the aborted kid or afterbirth with bare hands; isolate the doe, boil all milk from the herd, and call your vet to arrange testing.

detail.summary: Brucellosis is a long-lasting bacterial infection of goats, sheep and other livestock caused mainly by Brucella melitensis. In goats it causes abortions late in pregnancy, retained afterbirth, weak or dead kids, lower milk yield and swollen testicles in bucks. Many infected goats look healthy but carry the bacteria for life and shed it in milk and birth fluids. It matters greatly because B. melitensis is the most dangerous Brucella type for people, causing Malta fever, a serious and long-lasting illness picked up from raw milk and from handling births and abortions. Kenya treats brucellosis as a priority zoonotic disease (a disease that passes between animals and people).
detail.cause: The disease is caused by Brucella melitensis, a small bacterium that lives inside the animal's cells, where it can hide from the immune system and from many medicines. Bacteria usually enter through the mouth when a goat licks an aborted kid, afterbirth or contaminated ground, or drinks contaminated water; they can also enter through the eye, nose or broken skin. From there they travel to the lymph nodes (the glands that filter infection) and spread through the blood. In a pregnant doe the bacteria multiply heavily in the placenta (afterbirth) and the womb, damaging the placenta so the unborn kid no longer gets enough food and oxygen. This leads to abortion, stillbirth or the birth of weak kids. The bacteria also settle in the udder and the lymph nodes near it, so they are passed out in milk, sometimes for months or years. In bucks they can settle in the testicles and the tubes beside them, causing swelling, pain and poor fertility. Once infected, most goats remain carriers for life, even if they never abort again.
spread: The biggest source of infection is an aborted kid, the afterbirth and the fluids that come out during abortion or kidding, which contain very large numbers of bacteria.
Healthy goats pick up the infection by sniffing, licking or grazing pasture and bedding contaminated by these birth materials, or by drinking from shared water points and pans.
Infected does shed bacteria in vaginal discharge for several weeks after aborting or kidding, and in milk, often for a long time.
Kids can become infected by suckling milk from infected mothers, and some become hidden carriers that show signs only when they become pregnant later.
Buying or borrowing goats from markets, other herds or neighbours without testing is a common way the disease enters a clean herd.
Shared grazing, communal watering points, and mixing goats with sheep and cattle during migration or at markets spread the disease between herds, especially in pastoral areas.
Dogs, wild animals and birds can drag aborted kids and afterbirths around the homestead and pasture, spreading contamination.

Bucks used for breeding across several herds can carry infection, and contaminated hands, ropes, boots and tools can move bacteria between pens. The bacteria can survive for weeks to months in cool, damp, shaded places and manure, but are killed faster by direct sunlight, drying and disinfectants.
detail.atRisk: Sexually mature goats, especially does in their first pregnancy after infection, are most at risk of aborting. Young kids can be infected but usually show no signs until they are older. All breeds can be affected, including local East African and Galla goats and dairy breeds such as Toggenburg, Saanen and Alpine crosses. Risk is highest in pastoral and agro-pastoral systems in arid and semi-arid areas, where large mixed herds of goats, sheep, cattle and camels share grazing and watering points and where stock is frequently bought and sold at markets. Herds that kid together in crowded bomas, and seasons when many does kid at once (often linked to the long and short rains), see more spread because many birth materials are produced in one place. Zero-grazing and small dairy goat units are at risk mainly when they bring in new animals, use an untested breeding buck, or share a buck with neighbours. Families who drink raw goat milk or help with kidding without protection are the people most at risk.

early: Abortion, usually in the last one to two months of pregnancy (about the fourth or fifth month), often with little warning and with the doe otherwise appearing fairly normal.
Afterbirth that does not come out within a few hours of aborting or kidding (retained afterbirth), sometimes with a dirty, smelly discharge from the vulva afterwards.
Kids born dead, or born weak, small and unable to stand or suckle properly, with some dying in the first days of life.
Several does in the herd aborting over a few weeks, which is often called an abortion storm when the disease first enters a herd.
Many infected goats show no visible signs at all, which is why testing is so important.
advanced: A drop in milk yield in infected does, sometimes with hard, lumpy areas in the udder or signs of mastitis (udder inflammation).
Repeated breeding failures, does that do not conceive easily, or a herd with far fewer kids than expected.
Swollen, hard, hot or painful testicles in bucks, sometimes only on one side, with reduced interest in mating and poor fertility.
Occasional lameness from swollen, painful joints in some goats.
A long-term pattern in the herd where abortions become less frequent but the herd never fully clears, with new does aborting in their first pregnancy and milk remaining infectious.

lookalikes.name: Q fever (Coxiella burnetii infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Q fever also causes late abortions and weak kids in goats and is also dangerous to people, often spreading through dust from dried birth materials. It is impossible to tell apart from brucellosis by looking at the goats; only laboratory tests on blood, the aborted kid or afterbirth can separate them, so treat both with the same protective precautions.

lookalikes.name: Enzootic abortion (chlamydial abortion)
lookalikes.howToTell: Caused by Chlamydia abortus, it also causes abortion in the last two to three weeks of pregnancy and stillborn kids. The afterbirth is often thick, leathery and reddish-brown. Buck swelling and long-term milk shedding are more typical of brucellosis, but a lab test is needed to be sure, and it can also infect pregnant women.

lookalikes.name: Toxoplasmosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Caused by a parasite carried by cats, it leads to abortions, mummified (dried, shrunken) kids and weak kids, often in herds where cats contaminate feed or stores. Small white spots on the afterbirth may be seen. There is no buck testicle swelling. Laboratory testing confirms which disease is present.

lookalikes.name: Rift Valley fever
lookalikes.howToTell: This viral disease causes sudden abortion storms in goats, sheep and cattle together, usually after unusually heavy rains and flooding when mosquitoes increase, along with high death rates in young kids and lambs and illness in people. It spreads fast across many herds in an area. It is notifiable, so suspected cases must be reported to the County Veterinary Officer immediately.

detail.diagnosis: Brucellosis cannot be confirmed by signs alone, because several other diseases cause similar abortions. A vet will examine the herd, ask about abortions, kidding records, new animals and milk use, and take samples. Blood is commonly screened with the Rose Bengal test, a quick test that detects antibodies (the body's defence proteins against the infection), and positive samples are usually confirmed with more specific laboratory tests such as ELISA or the complement fixation test. The strongest proof comes from growing the bacteria (culture) or detecting their genetic material (PCR) from the aborted kid's stomach contents, the afterbirth, vaginal swabs or milk; this work must be done in a properly equipped laboratory because the bacteria are dangerous to lab staff. Testing is usually done at herd level, since single negative results in one goat can miss early infections. Your vet may send samples through the County Veterinary Office to government or research laboratories. To help, keep any fresh aborted kid and afterbirth for the vet if you can do so safely: use gloves or plastic bags over your hands, place them in two sealed plastic bags, keep them cool and in shade away from dogs, and do not open them. Also prepare a simple record of which does aborted, when, at what stage of pregnancy, where new goats came from and whether any family members have had recurring fevers.
firstSteps: Protect yourself first: wear gloves (or plastic bags over your hands), cover cuts, avoid splashing fluids into your eyes or mouth, and wash hands and arms with soap and clean water afterwards.

Move the doe that aborted or has retained afterbirth into a separate pen or tethering area away from other pregnant does, and keep her there until the vet advises, because she sheds bacteria for weeks.
Do not pull on a retained afterbirth yourself; leave it for the vet, keep the doe calm with shade, clean water and good feed, and keep flies away as best you can.

Collect the aborted kid and afterbirth safely in double sealed bags for the vet; if the vet does not need them, bury them deep with quicklime away from water sources or burn them completely, so dogs and other animals cannot reach them.
Clean the spot where the abortion happened: remove contaminated bedding and soil, burn or bury it, and treat the area with a suitable farm disinfectant or lime, then allow sunlight to dry it.
Boil all milk from the herd before anyone drinks it or makes mala or other milk products, and stop selling raw milk until your vet has tested the herd.
Keep children, pregnant women and anyone with a weak immune system away from kidding, abortions and the sick doe.

Stop buying, selling, lending or mixing goats, and do not share your buck with neighbours, until the vet has assessed the herd; then call your vet or County Veterinary Officer and give them your records.
detail.vetTreatment: Treating infected goats is generally not recommended and is rarely successful. Because Brucella hides inside the animal's cells, even long courses of combined antibiotics, typically a tetracycline-type drug together with an aminoglycoside such as streptomycin, may reduce signs but often fail to clear the infection, and treated goats may continue to shed bacteria in milk and birth fluids. For this reason, most vets advise identifying infected goats through testing and removing them from the herd, usually by slaughter under veterinary guidance, rather than treating them. In some situations a vet may treat a doe for a secondary womb infection after retained afterbirth or abortion, but this is to manage the complication, not to cure brucellosis. Any antibiotic must be prescribed by a vet, who will decide whether it is appropriate; using antibiotics casually or in incomplete courses wastes money and encourages antimicrobial resistance, where bacteria stop responding to medicines that people and animals depend on. If any drug is given, observe the milk and meat withdrawal periods on the label and as advised by your vet, meaning milk and meat from that goat must not be used or sold until the period has passed. At herd level, your vet may recommend a control plan that combines testing, removing positive animals, vaccinating young replacement does where the vaccine is available, and strict hygiene at kidding time. Expect this to take time, often with repeated testing over months.
prevention: Buy new goats only from herds known or tested to be free of brucellosis, ask your vet to test them before purchase where possible, and keep all new arrivals separate for at least a few weeks and until tested.

Ask your vet or County Veterinary Officer about vaccination with the Rev.1 vaccine, a live vaccine for goats and sheep that is usually given to young females before their first pregnancy; availability in Kenya varies, it must be given by a trained person because it can cause abortion in pregnant goats and can infect people if accidentally injected, and it can interfere with later blood tests.
Set up a clean kidding area away from the main herd and water sources, and remove and safely dispose of all afterbirths and dead kids immediately, using gloves.
Isolate any doe that aborts at once and get every abortion investigated by a vet, rather than assuming it was caused by stress or bad luck.
Use your own tested breeding buck instead of borrowing or sharing bucks between herds.
Avoid communal watering points and shared grazing where abortions are happening in neighbouring herds, and keep dogs from carrying birth materials around the homestead.
Clean and disinfect kidding pens, boots, ropes and tools regularly, and let sunlight dry out pens, since sunlight and drying kill the bacteria faster.
Always boil milk before drinking it or making milk products, and teach everyone on the farm, including herders and children, about the human risk.
detail.impact: Brucellosis causes heavy, often hidden losses on Kenyan goat farms. Each abortion means a lost kid, a lost season of production and, for dairy goat farmers, a shortened or poorer lactation and less milk to sell. Weak kids that die soon after birth add to the loss, and infertile does and bucks slow herd growth and genetic improvement. Culling infected goats removes valuable breeding stock, and farmers may struggle to sell breeding animals or milk if their herd is known to be infected. In pastoral communities, where goats are savings, food and a source of school fees, repeated abortions directly reduce household income and food security. There are also human costs: family members who catch Malta fever may be unable to work for weeks or months and face medical bills, sometimes after being misdiagnosed with malaria or typhoid. Control programmes require testing, vet visits and replacement stock, but these costs are usually far smaller than the long-term losses from a herd that stays infected.
detail.humanHealth: Brucella melitensis is the most serious Brucella type for people and causes brucellosis, also called Malta fever or undulant fever. People catch it mainly by drinking raw goat milk or eating products made from raw milk, by handling aborted kids, afterbirths and birth fluids, by helping with difficult kidding, and when slaughtering infected animals; laboratory workers and anyone accidentally injected with the live Rev.1 vaccine are also at risk. In people it causes fever that comes and goes, night sweats, headache, severe tiredness, back and joint pain and weight loss, and it can become a long-lasting illness affecting joints, the heart, the nervous system or the reproductive organs. It may cause miscarriage in pregnant women. It is often mistaken for malaria or typhoid, so if anyone on the farm has recurring fevers, tell the doctor or clinic that you keep goats and that abortions have occurred. Human brucellosis is treated by doctors with long courses of specific medicines, and early treatment works best. To protect your family: boil all milk before use, wear gloves and cover cuts when handling births or abortions, wash thoroughly afterwards, keep children and pregnant women away from kidding and aborted material, and buy milk and meat from safe, inspected sources. Thorough cooking of meat reduces risk, but handling raw carcasses and organs of infected goats still carries some risk.
detail.outlook: For the individual goat, the outlook for full recovery is poor. Most infected goats stay infected for life, even though many do not abort again and may later kid normally, which can falsely suggest they have recovered while they continue shedding bacteria in milk and birth fluids. Does with retained afterbirth may recover from that complication with vet care, but remain carriers. Bucks with damaged testicles may stay infertile. For the herd, the outlook is much better when the farmer acts early: testing, removing infected animals, vaccinating replacement does where possible, strict kidding hygiene and buying only tested stock can gradually reduce and, over time, may clear the disease from a herd. Success depends on how widespread infection is, how often new animals are brought in, contact with neighbouring herds, and how consistently the control plan is followed.

faqs.q: Can I just inject my goats with antibiotics from the agrovet to stop the abortions?
faqs.a: No. Brucellosis bacteria hide inside the goat's cells, so antibiotics rarely clear the infection, even when given for a long time. A treated goat often keeps carrying and shedding the bacteria, so your family and herd stay at risk. Using antibiotics without a vet also leaves drug residues in milk and meat and helps create resistant bacteria. Talk to your vet, who will usually recommend testing and removing infected goats rather than treatment.

faqs.q: My doe aborted once but kidded normally the next year. Is she now healthy?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many does abort only once and then kid normally, but they usually remain infected and can shed large numbers of bacteria in milk and at every kidding. The only way to know is to have her tested by a vet. Until then, boil her milk and handle her kidding with gloves.

faqs.q: Is boiling milk really enough to make it safe?
faqs.a: Bringing milk to a full rolling boil kills Brucella and makes it safe to drink. Do this every time, including milk used for tea, mala, yoghurt or for feeding kids. Warming milk only slightly is not enough. Raw milk cheeses and fermented products made from unboiled milk can still carry the bacteria.

faqs.q: Can my cattle, sheep or dogs catch brucellosis from my goats?
faqs.a: Yes. Brucella melitensis mainly affects goats and sheep, but it can also infect cattle, camels and dogs that are in close contact, especially if they share grazing, water or come into contact with aborted material. Cattle are more commonly affected by another type, Brucella abortus. If you keep mixed livestock, ask your vet to consider testing all species and keep dogs away from afterbirths and aborted kids.

faqs.q: Should I vaccinate my goats against brucellosis?
faqs.a: Vaccination can help a lot in infected areas, but it must be planned with your vet or County Veterinary Officer. The Rev.1 vaccine is usually given to young female goats before their first pregnancy. It is a live vaccine, so it can cause abortion if given to pregnant does and can infect the person giving it if they are accidentally injected. Availability in Kenya varies by area, so ask your County Veterinary Office what is possible where you farm.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat meat from a goat that tested positive?
faqs.a: Infected goats should be slaughtered only under veterinary guidance, with meat inspection. The highest risk is to the people doing the slaughter, through contact with blood, the udder, the reproductive organs and lymph nodes, so they should wear gloves and cover cuts. Meat that passes inspection and is thoroughly cooked carries low risk, but organs such as the udder, womb and testicles should not be eaten and should be safely disposed of.
